source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of a knoll which is surrounded by marshy ground E-W. A level oval area (26.7m N-S; 20m E-W) defined by a broad steep scarp (H 2m) S-N with a ramp-like extension (L c. 50m E-W) tapering towards E. The scarp is most pronounced along the S arc where it merges with the broad natural slope of the knoll (H c. 4.5m). A raised oval area (Wth 4m), flanked to E and W by natural depressions, projects northwards from the NE end of the extension. The base of the knoll is defined by a steep scarp separating it from the surrounding marshy ground. There is a souterrain (SL019-16002-) in the S half of the interior. Described by O'Rorke (1878, 275-6) as '...a beautiful sod fort, with three lines of circumvallation, the innermost circle being ten yards[9.14m] in diameter, the next thirty-two [29.26m], and the outer one sixty [54.86m]'. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an embanked circular area with a trackway leading to it from S and on the 1913 OS 6-inch map only by an arc of hachures S-NNW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

artefact typology - souterrains are characteristic Early Medieval features

source_data.original_text:
Located in the interior of a rath (SL019-160001-), close to the enclosing scarp at S. This souterrain was recorded by O'Rorke (1878, 275-6) as '...a cave ten or twelve feet [3.66m] long and four or five feet [1.22-1.52m] wide; roofed with flags resting on sidewalls of uncemented stones'. The accessible remains consists of two intact, interconnecting chambers (chambers 1 and 2) on a roughly N–S axis, and a ruined, roofless chamber/passage (chamber 3), c. 3-4m to W of these. The current access is at surface level through an opening (max. dim. c. 0.45-0.5m) in the roof of chamber 1, the southernmost of the two intact chambers. The opening is the result of the collapse of a roof lintel. Chamber 1 (L 5.2m NNE–SSW; Wth 1.45m; H 2m) is oblong in plan. The walls are constructed of random rubble incorporating large, irregular-shaped stones and boulders. They incline inwards towards the top to support a roof of massive overlapping slabs. An air vent was noted in the SW wall(pers. comm. M.A. Timoney 2003). Two lintel-roofed creeps open off the chamber at ground level. A creep (L 2.2 N−S; H 0.9-0.95m) at the NNE end of the chamber opens into the S end of chamber 2. In chamber 1, the opening to this creep forms a short lobby (L 0.7m NNE–SSW; Wth 0.76m) roofed by a massive boulder. Beyond this, the creep narrows (Wth 0.54m), before widening and rising in height (Wth 0.8m; H 1.6m) at the point where it merges with the S wall of the chamber 2. Chamber 2 (max. Wth 1.6m; H 2.2m) is of similar construction to chamber 1, but is considerably longer, extending to N for at least 10m. It appears to narrow towards its N end, where it is blocked by a sloping heap of stone rubble. The lintelled opening (Wth 0.71m; H 0.62m) to the second creep in Chamber 1 is located at the SW end of the chamber. This creep extends for at least 2m to NW but is blocked by collapsed soil. It may lead to the ruined chamber 3 which is exposed at surface level to W of chamber 1. Chamber 3 consists of a sub-rectangular depression (L c. 3.6m E–W; Wth 1.7m N–S; D c. 0.9m at E end) with drystone walling on the N, E and S sides, and one in situ lintel at its E end. It may be the original entrance passage/chamber to the souterrain. It is engulfed in overgrowth, and partly filled with soil and stones, which may obscure a creep leading to chamber 1. During an inspection in 1994 a large stone slab was noted protruding from the ground c. 3m E of the chamber 3 possibly indicating another chamber or passage.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of revised upload: 12 December 2016

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified as 'Enclosure'. In rocky pasture, on the lower N-facing slopes of the Ox Mountains and within the N half of an 18th/19th-century field system (SL019-161004-). Oval area (16m N-S; 21.7m E-W) enclosed by a roughly-built wall (Wth 1.5m; H 0.5m) of stones and boulders. The interior and surrounding land is planted with coniferous trees. Upon inspection in 1994 it was concluded that this was an animal holding enclosure dating to the post-1700 AD period.

Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified as 'Field System'. A number of roughly parallel walls which extend upslope on a roughly N-S axis (as indicated on the 1837 edition of the OS 6-inch map) are crossed on an E-W axis by numerous drystone walls and form small rectangular fields (as indicated on the 1913 edition of the OS 6-inch map). The fields are associated with a number of ruined rectangular stone-built huts and houses. Many of the fields are laid out to conform with the natural terraces of the mountain slope. Two passageways, flanked by stone walls, follow a curving roughly N-S line through the fields. There are three enclosures for holding animals (SL019-161001-, SL019-161002-, SL019-161003-) and a rath (SL019-162----) within the field system. Upon inspection in 1994 it was concluded that the field system and the enclosures for holding animals noted above, date to the post-1700 period.

source_data.original_text:
In rocky pasture, on the lower N-facing slopes of the Ox Mountains and straddling a narrow terrace with a steep N-facing slope. A roughly circular area (23.3m N-S; 26m E-W) defined NE-NW by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse (Wth 3.8m) and NW-NE by a steep curving scarp (H 3.7m). The inner bank is substantial (Wth 5.6m; int. H 0.9m; ext. H 2.8m) apart from along the S arc and an internal revetment of drystone walling (H 0.6m) is evident at SSE. The entrance (Wth 3m) is at S, partially obscured by a pile of field clearance stones, with a causeway (Wth 1.8m) across the fosse. The outer bank (Wth 5.5m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H 1.5m) has an entrance at S blocked with stones. Both banks are capped by the low remains of a wall (Wth 1.2m) along the W arc. The interior slopes slightly down to N and S from the centre. A low N-S field boundary crosses the interior just W of the centre. This field boundary forms the W side of a roughly square structure (6m E-W; 7.3m N-S) which is defined by low sod-covered wall footings (Wth 1.1m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.55m) on its N, E and S sides. A narrow terrace (Wth 1.7m), the outer edge of which is marked by stones, skirts the base of the scarp NW-NE. An E-W field boundary lies immediately to S of the rath. The surrounding slopes have recently been planted with trees.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On a slight rise, on a broad undulating shelf on the lower N-facing slopes of the Ox Mountains. The immediate vicinity is heather-covered and broken by rock outcrops while further to W and E there are coniferous plantations. A circular area (int. diam. 25m N-S; 26m E-W) enclosed by a substantial inner drystone wall (Wth 4m) and encircled at a distance of 10m by the remains of an outer stone wall. The inner wall consists of internal and external stone facing with a rubble core. Its external face (H 1.3m) incorporates large roughly rectangular blocks of stone while the upper courses have collapsed outwards and spreads of stone tumble obscure the wall face around much of the circuit. The internal wall face (H 1.6m) is better preserved though it is partially rebuilt. In the interior, at the base of the internal face of the wall SW-NNE is a sod-covered terrace (Wth 2m; H 0.6m), probably the result of wall collapse. The internal face of the cashel wall rises to a height of 2m above this terrace but this is the result of rebuilding when the W arc of the cashel was incorporated into a property boundary. At ground level in the inner wall face at ENE there is a low opening (Wth 1m; H 0.4m) giving access to a niche (1m N-S; 1.5m E-W; H 0.7-0.75m) built into the thickness of the wall. The entrance (Wth c. 1m) is a dilapidated break at ESE. 
The outer enclosing wall (Wth 2.5m) consists of a low pile of rubble covered with heather and ferns. From N-E where it coincides with a natural break of slope it has an external height of c. 1m and from SSE-SSW it is incorporated into a field boundary wall that extends to E of the cashel. A ruined townland boundary wall bisects the interior on a N-S axis and crosses both cashel walls. 
In the intervening space between the two cashel walls at SSE is a ruined 18th/19th-century stone-built gable-ended house (int. dims.: 8.8m E-W; 3.5m N-S). A more ruinous but similar structure lies a short distance to W. Several small divisions of the space between the cashel walls are probably fields associated with these structures.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'Field System'. A ruined 18th/19th-century rectangular house (int. 8.8m E-W; 3.5m N-S) is located in the intervening space between the SE walls of the cashel (SL019-176001-). The stone-built house is gable-ended and is sub-divided into three rooms. There are wall cupboards in the thickness of the walls but no fireplace is evident. There is a window and doorway in the S wall. A second structure of similar size but of irregular in plan is located a few meters to W. The modification/rebuilding of the cashel walls, and various small subdivisions of the intervening space between the two cashel walls, are most likely associated with this settlement. A pattern of subrectangular fields, indicated on the 1913 edition of the OS 6-inch map, links this house with the ruins of another settlement of two houses located on a terrace, c. 300-400m upslope to SE. The fields, on a NE-SW axis, are generally subrectangular and are enclosed by ruined drystone walls (Wth 0.8-1m). They conform to the undulating local topography of irregular bedrock terraces and scarps.

source_data.original_text:
Towards the N end and highest point of relatively flat-topped Doomore Mountain. The site overlooks Ballysadare Bay and commands a magnificent outlook in all directions. This is a circular cairn (diam. 21m; H c. 2m) the perimeter of which is under peat-grown heather. Towards the western edge of the flat top of the cairn there is a roughly constructed heap of stones, circular in plan (diam. 7m; H 1.5m). The age and purpose of this feature is uncertain but it may be a 19th-century OS trigonometrical station. Just E of the centre of the cairn there is a 20th-century OS concrete-built trigonometrical pillar. At the NNE a line of four large stones extends towards the centre of the cairn from a point c. 3m inside the perimeter. These stones, which are substantially buried, are of uncertain status but could represent tomb structure, possibly a passage tomb. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 94)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On the S side of Ballysadare Bay, c. 350m W of an Augustinian abbey (SL020-108----). The minerals galena (lead sulphide) and sphalerite (zinc sulphide) occur in flat bands in the limestone beds at Abbeytown and silver occurs in the lead as an impurity. The earliest documentary evidence for mining at Abbeytown dates to the mid-18th century when Charles O'Hara of Annaghmore (see SL026-049----) commenced lead mining operations at Abbeytown and Lugawarry (3.2km to SW of Abbeytown) (McTernan 1998, 571-3). However, it is possible that these mines were worked by the monks at the 7th-century monastic site (SL020-109005-) c. 500m to E at a much earlier period for the production of lead and silver (ibid., 571). Some of the smaller mine shafts 'are known as The Monks' Tunnels … and may be Medieval or Early Christian in date' (M. B. Timoney 2002, 150). No remains of these early shafts were noted when the site was inspected in 1992. The mines indicated on the 1838 and 1913 OS 6-inch maps with several shafts shown are the 19th and 20th-century mines.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Close to the shoreline of Ballysadare Bay, in the grounds of the limestone quarry and concrete works complex at Abbeytown. This Augustinian abbey is surrounded and largely covered by quarry debris. The visible remains consist of the N wall of the nave (L 13.6m) and chancel (L c. 6m) of the church, and the lower part of a tower (6.35m N-S; 3.7m E-W; H c. 6m) which was inserted between them. The walls are built of random-rubble set in a lime mortar. The N wall of the church is covered by debris and ivy, but a drawing made in 1917 (SMR (1989) file) shows an arched recess or opening just E of the tower. The crossing-tower rises from two substantial cross-walls. In the centre of each cross-wall is an opening (Wth 3.55m) covered by a pointed arch of dressed stone; these openings link the nave with the chancel. The underside of each arch has a rib rising from tapering corbels; on the chancel side the corbels have a terminal vine-leaf motif. A barrel vault (H 3.5m) covers the central area of the tower between the openings. The internal ground level is raised with quarry debris to the level of the corbels. The remains are those of the abbey of St Mary of the Canons Regular of St Augustine which existed by the middle of the 13th century but whose foundation date is not known (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 160; M. B. Timoney 2002, 150). The N wall could be 13th century, though no datable features are evident, but the tower is a 15th/16th century insertion. In 1585-6 the abbey consisted of 'a partly thatched church, a dormitory, two ruined buildings, three cottages, with gardens, cemetery, etc.' (ibid.). A large piece of window tracery (SL020-109016-), probably from here, is in the graveyard of St Fechin's church on the site of an early monastery (SL020-109005 -) c. 250m to the E (M. B. Timoney 2002, 157-8, n. 14). There is a lead and silver mine (SL020-107----) c. 350m to the W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

This monument is subject to a preservation order made under the National Monuments Acts 1930 to 2014 (PO no. 1/1994).

raw_items.raw_text: St Fechin of Billa, and later of Fore, who died in 665 or 668
early monastery founded by St Fechin
It is 13th century or later and incorporates 12th-century features
FÁS graveyard clean-up scheme in 1995 and 1996

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the top of a SW-facing slope overlooking the Ballysadare River to the E; in the N side of Kilboglashy graveyard (SL020-109002-). The roofless ruin of a rectangular gable-ended church (int. dims. 19.38m E-W; 7.9m N-S), covered with ivy, built of random-rubble limestone with shaped quoins. The apex of the E gable has collapsed but the base of a central splayed window ope (Wth c. 1.7m) is visible through the ivy (M. B. Timoney 2002, 154-5). According to O'Rorke (1878, 21), 'this window had a mullion, and consisted of two lights'. The W gable and the N wall (H c. 5m) are densely covered with overgrowth. A blocked lintelled window (max. Wth 0.9m) in the centre of the W gable and a recess (0.5m x 0.5m; D 0.5m) at its S end were recorded during a previous site inspection in 1992 (SMR (1989) file). A sketch by Wakeman (1885-6, 49) depicts a blocked-up trabeate doorway in this wall. There is a round-headed window embrasure in the E end of the S wall with a narrow round-headed light, and a similar partially blocked ope at its centre. A Romanesque doorway occurs W of the centre in this wall. The surround has two orders composed of blocks of eroded grainy light red sandstone. Both orders have moulded corners and capitals decorated with animal motifs. Springing from the capitals of the outer order is a semicircular arch with eleven voussoirs, each ornamented with a worn face in bold relief, with a plain chamfered hood-moulding. Two similar heads occur on either side of the doorway. The space under the arch is filled with random dark-red sandstone rubble and the doorway is lintelled (Wth 1.22m; H 1.8m). Internally to the W of it is a series of niches that would have held timbers to support a gallery, lit by a lintelled rectangular light high up near the W end of the S wall. The interior of the church contains many 19th-century headstones and chest-tombs. During a FÁS graveyard clean-up scheme in 1995 and 1996 a number of architectural pieces were found, including a Romanesque font, a stone head and a medieval graveslab (SL020-109010-) (M. B. Timoney 2002, 149-59). The architectural pieces included a Romanesque window hood (in the NMI), a sandstone voussoir, a round window head, a limestone window sill and an ogee window head (ibid., 152-3). The baptismal font consists of half of a hemispherical sandstone block (H 0.22m; diam. 0.6m), which is decorated on the underside with a series of ten leaves; it is in the NMI (ibid.). The sandstone head (H 0.07m; max. T 0.06m; D 0.32m) was found on the ground W of the church; it is also in the NMI. It has indications of a head-dress, the eyes slant downwards with the left eye lower than the right, the mouth is down-turned, the nose is chipped and there are indications of the left ear (ibid.). This church is on the site of an early monastery founded by St Fechin of Billa, and later of Fore, who died in 665 or 668 (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 160). An early ecclesiastical enclosure (SL020-109005-) may be preserved in the field boundaries to the S and W of it. It is 13th century or later and incorporates 12th-century features including the doorway and mouldings at the corners (Harbison 1972, 212; M. B. Timoney 2002, 149-50). O'Rorke (1878, 22) noted a number of breaches in the N and S walls which indicate that the church underwent a number of phases of reconstruction. Adjacent rectangular buildings (SL020-109003-, SL020-109004- and SL020-109015-) may be associated with it. An Augustinian abbey (SL020-108----) lies 250m to the W. Two enclosures (SL020-109006- and SL020-109011-) are to the SE and N, respectively.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

raw_items.raw_text: mid-19th century to the present day

source_data.original_text:
Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an irregular area (c. 50m NW-SE; c. 30m NE-SW) with a church (SL020-109001-) in its N half. It has since been extended to the SE and SW. The remains of the original enclosing wall are evident on the W and N sides. Headstones in the older section date from the 18th century to the present day and include some vaults and chest-tombs. Numerous low uninscribed grave-markers are also present. The extension is enclosed by a stone wall with two roadside gateways in the SW wall. The headstones in this section date from the mid-19th century to the present day. During a graveyard clean up in 1995 and 1996, a number of architectural pieces, a Romanesque font and a medieval graveslab were found (SL020-10910-) (M. B. Timoney 2002, 149-59). One of the architectural pieces included a piece of window tracery (SL020-109016-) that was probably from the Augustinian abbey (SL020-108----), c. 250m to the W in Abbeytown (ibid. 157-8, n. 14). A shell midden (SL020-109012-), consisting mainly of oyster shells, was discovered immediately outside the NE wall and oyster shells were also noted on the surface of the interior during the clean-up scheme (ibid., 150). An ecclesiastical enclosure (SL020-109005-) may be preserved in the field boundaries to the S and W. A rectangular building (SL020-109003-), parallel to the church, lies immediately outside the N wall and there is a similar structure (SL020-109004-) at the SW side, which has foundations of another building (SL020-109015-) on its E side (M. B. Timoney 2002, 151).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
The arc of an ecclesiastical enclosure, as indicated on the 1913 OS 6-inch map, may have been preserved in the field boundaries to the S and W of the church (SL020-109001-) and graveyard (SL020-109002-) (see Keeley 1998, 4 and fig. 3). Evidence from the map suggests that the enclosure was D-shaped with the straight side formed by the Ballysadare River. The field boundaries in the area to the S of the graveyard may have incorporated part of an outer enclosing element, as well as a possible entrance avenue and internal divisions. These field boundaries and structure indicated on the 1913 OS 6-inch map, were levelled in the late 1980s (M. B. Timoney 2002, 149). An Augustinian abbey (SL020-108----) and a silver and lead mine (SL020-107----) lie c. 250m and c. 500m to the W respectively. Two enclosures (SL020-109006- and SL020-109014-) lie within and were possibly part of the monastic settlement.

In pasture, on a rounded hillock overlooking the mouth of the Ballysadare River. The hillock forms the northern extremity of a larger undulating hill to S of which the church and graveyard (SL020-109001-, SL020-109002-) are located. An oval raised area, indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map, is evident as a barely discernible sod-covered stony rise (Wth 0.5-1m) SW-NE. It is most clearly defined NW-N where the external scarp (H 0.5-0.8m) incorporates large stones at intervals. It appears to continue NE-E but due to dense blackthorn scrub it is impossible to confirm this. A quarry pit (8m N-S; 6.6m E-W; D 1.6m) has obliterated the S half of the enclosure. The extant remains suggest that the dimensions of the original oval enclosure were c. 20m N-S by 15m E-W.

source_data.original_text:
In level pasture. The ruin of a rectangular church (int. 12m E-W; 5.3m N-S) built of roughly coursed stonework, the walls (T c. 1m) of which are much reduced in height. Internally a short section of a cross-wall (H 0.3m; Wth 0.7m) extends 0.6m from the S wall, just W of the centre. The church was better preserved when described by O'Rorke (1878, 278-81), who noted an E window 'three feet [0.91m] high, the opening to the outside seeming to have been only four inches [0.1m], but with a splay on the inside of five or six feet [1.52-1.82m]'. He also described a window in the S wall with a square-headed light 'four inches [0.1m] wide to outside, but splayed internally to three feet [0.91m]'. The church was known as Kildalough church (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 336-8). There is a possible graveyard (SL020-135002-) to the E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On sloping pasture about 400m N of the steep slopes of Slieveward with an outlook across Ballysadare Bay. The tomb is in an oval mound (9.7m NE-SW; max. 6m NW-SE). A NE-facing gallery (L 7m; max. Wth 2.5m) is divided by jambs into two chambers. Only the more northerly entrance jamb survives and there is are no remnants of the court. Four sidestones remain of the more northerly side of the gallery and three of the opposite side and it is closed by a large backstone. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 50, no. 77)

source_data.original_text:
On an elongated ridge, which is enclosed on three sides by the Ballysadare River (which emerges through the Collooney gap in the Ox Mountains) and on the fourth side by a silted marshy lake. The S side of the ridge, which rises 4m above the surrounding marsh, was cut off from the remainder by a bank and external fosse, which enclosed an area 85m N-S by at least 75m E-W (cut by a railway line at W). According to local information, this bank and ditch were bulldozed in 1978 (Mount 2002, 106). The inland promontory fort was partially excavated in 1994 (ibid., 103-116) prior to the construction of the Collooney to Carraroe by-pass road (N4). The road was realigned to the E in order to cause minimal damage to the interior of the fort (ibid., 103). Based on evidence from aerial photography and the excavation of the fosse, Mount (ibid., 106-7) concluded that the fort's defences consisted of a stone-faced earthen bank as well as the external fosse and that there was an entrance with a causeway (Wth 6.5m) midway along them. Excavation revealed that the fosse had a maximum width of 5m at the top and of 2.08m at the base. The excavations within the fort also revealed a large quantity of butchered animal remains, iron tools and nails, and vast quantities of iron smelting slag and furnace bottoms, indicating that this was an important industrial centre (ibid., 113). An animal bone found in the fosse produced a radiocarbon determination of 1260+/-40 BP (GrA-2452; 660 to 880 cal AD 2 sigma) (ibid., 106). Within the promontory fort is a burial ground (SL020-166002-), two cairns (SL020-166008-, SL020-166009-) and four hut sites (SL020-166004-). A corn-drying kiln (SL020-166003-) was found within the E half of the interior. Subsequent to Mount's excavation, unauthorised quarrying was carried out at the promontory fort and in 1996 archaeological testing of an undisturbed finger of ground to the N of the area previously excavated, revealed three 'ditches' (Channing 1998b, 156). Though not fully excavated, Channing suggests that these features 'probably relate to [the] inland promontory fort' (ibid.). According to Mount (2002, 105), this promontory fort was well sited to control river traffic from Ballysadare Bay along the Ballysadare River and to guard a possible river crossing between the Barony of Tirerrill to the east and Leyny to the west. (Mount 1994d, 22-3; Mount 1995d, 78-9).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Within an inland promontory fort (SL020-166001-), on an elongated ridge, on the W bank of and at a bend of the Ballysadare River. This burial ground was uncovered in 1994 during the excavation of the promontory fort prior to the construction of the Collooney to Carraroe by-pass road (N4) (Mount 2002, 103). The importance of the discovery resulted in the realignment of the road to the E in order to cause minimal damage to this and adjacent sites (ibid.). The inhumations were of three main types: crouched, flexed and extended. In most cases the heads were oriented to the W or SW. The burials were mainly in pits, which in a few cases were outlined with stones. Some of the burials contained grave-goods, either in metal or stone, and others contained animal bones. A minimum of 185 inhumation burials was recorded, 51 examples were extended inhumations with the heads to the west and the feet to the east, two individuals were extended on their sides, three burials were crouched and three were flexed. There were 11 examples of skulls without any other body parts. Eighty-two burials were disturbed and 13 were disarticulated. Twenty burials were left in situ. At some time the burial ground was enclosed by a subrectangular enclosure (23m N-S; 19m E-W) which is indicated on the 1913 OS 6-inch map in the SE quadrant of the inland promontory fort. The enclosing drystone wall (max. T 2.2m; H 0.95m) is composed of spaced uprights and drystone-walling of boulders with a rubble or earthen core. The earthen core contained a substantial number of artifacts and organic remains that were derived from an occupation surface. The wall overlay the old ground surface where a number of burials, which predate its construction, were excavated. The blocked entrance was discovered during the excavation in the S half of the W side and is marked by two large upright stones, 0.72m apart, with three low jamb-stones. The enclosure was subsequently reinstated to its original form prior to excavation and the entrance feature was reconstructed. There are two cairns (SL020-166008-; SL020-166009-) at the centre of the burial ground. The town of Ballysadare is c. 600m to NW. (Mount 1995d, 78-9; 2002, 103-116)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In the centre of a burial ground (SL020-166002-) which is located in the interior of the inland promontory fort (SL020-166001-). The easternmost of two cairns (see SL020-166009-) discovered and partially excavated during excavation of the complex in 1994 (Mount 1995d, 78-9; 2002, 103-116). A roughly circular cairn (4.5m E-W; 4.2m N-S; max. H 0.54m) situated on the old ground surface, directly under the sod layer, consisting of limestone boulders and flat slabs in a matrix of dark brown humus. A substantial quantity of stone immediately to the E of the cairn may have been tumble from it thus reducing the height of the cairn somewhat. Cremated human bone and charcoal flecks were found on the surface of the cairn directly under the sod but the bulk of it was recovered from a small depression formed by a number of stones. This cremation has been dated to 680 to 880 cal. AD (Mount 2002, 114). Finds included chert, flint, iron nails and a decorated gold and amber disc. In contrast to the surrounding burial ground, no inhumation burials were found in the old ground surface beneath the cairn which 'probably indicates that this feature pre-dates the inhumations' (ibid., 107). The E and W cairns were linked by a 6m long arrangement of angular stones on the northern side, possibly a wall footing, which continued to the E as a collapsed wall partly enclosing the eastern cairn.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

An oval level area (33.4m E-W; 25.9m N-S), formed by levelling the top of the hillock, is enclosed by fragmentary remains of a drystone wall. source_data.original_text:
Some 2km S of Ballysadare Bay on the narrow summit of Croaghaun Mountain which commands an extensive outlook in all directions. A SE-facing undifferentiated passage tomb of rectangular outline (L 1.7m; Wth 0.95m) stands in a circular cairn (diam. 7m; H. c. 0.6m). Three stones form the left-hand side of the structure, one stone of a probable original three stands at the right-hand side and it is closed by a backstone. A sillstone stands at the front of the chamber. The site was excavated in 1985 (Bergh 1986, 35; Bergh 1995, 104-5, 225). Cremated human bone was found in the chamber and also a fragment of a poppy-headed antler/bone pin, one piece of chert with wear-marks and fragments of a coarse ware pottery. Five minor deposits of cremated bone were found in the cairn with one of which there were sherds of food vessel type. A hollow scraper made of chert was also found in the cairn. During the excavation two displaced slabs, likely to have been chamber roofstones, were found S and W of the structure. Radiocarbon dating of charcoal from an in situ cremation suggest it was deposited in the interval 5640 to 5490 BC (calendar years). This date is much earlier than would be expected for a passage-tomb so it may be that charcoal already many centuries old somehow became associated with the burial deposit. Charcoal associated with cremated bone in another part of the chamber has been dated to the interval 4675-4460 cal. BC. This date too, according to the excavator, presents 'problems of interpretation'. A prehistoric wall (Wth 3-8m; H c. 1m; L c. 175m) (SL020-182----) of large boulders, which may have been associated with the passage tomb, lies c. 130m to S where it curves around the base of the mountain roughly SE-SW (Bergh 1986, 34-5). (Ó Nualláin 1989, 93-4)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On the S side of Croaghaun mountain; a passage tomb (SL020-181----) is located on the summit of Croaghaun, c. 130m to N. A heather-covered wall (Wth 3-8m; H c. 1m; L c. 175m), composed of large boulders, curves around the base of the mountain roughly SE-SW ending where the hillside starts to drop abruptly on the downhill side. The remains of a subrectangular sunken area (7m NW-SE; 3m SW-NE) occur in the wall at SW, on relatively flat ground. A second similar feature occurs at the E end of the bank. The function of this wall is not known but it may have been associated with the passage tomb. (Bergh 1986, 34-5)

On a prominent rock outcrop on a NNW-facing slope in rough mountain terrain overlooking the narrow winding Cooney-Glen gap through the Ox Mountains. A relatively flat D-shaped area (dims. c. 16m NNE-SSW; 14.8m WNW-ESE) at the top of a rock outcrop, the straight NNE side of which is defined by a high steep cliff-face. For the remainder of the circuit ENE-NNW the interior is defined by the fragmentary remains of a rough drystone wall (Wth 2.4m, int. H 0.6m; ext. H 1.2m), composed of large rocks and boulders, positioned a short distance below the top of the rock outcrop. At SE, where it is best preserved, the wall is up to three courses high. For much of the remainder of the circuit only its outline is now identifiable, as many of the stones have collapsed down the hill.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a steep S-facing hillside in very rough mountainous terrain with excellent views. The inspection of this cashel was difficult due to dense overgrowth of scrub. An oval area (33.5m NW-SE; 28.2m NE-SW) enclosed by two substantial, although much-denuded, drystone walls. Both walls display evidence of internal and external revetment in places. The inner wall (Wth c. 2.2m; int. H 1.2m; ext. H 0.9m) is much better preserved than the outer (Wth c. 2m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 0.3m). Along the N arc there is a fosse (Wth c. 3.2-4m) between the walls; elsewhere there is a level space (Wth c. 2.5-3.4m). The interior slopes steeply down to S. A number of possible internal divisions, defined by drystone walls of uncertain age, are visible but could not be inspected in any detail due to the overgrowth. According to local information, there is a spring well within the interior but this was not located.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, near the top of a gentle S-facing slope and adjoining another cashel (SL020-197008-) to E. A circular area (int. diam. 18.8m N-S; 19.1m E-W) defined by a collapsed grass-covered stone wall (int. H 0.6m; ext. H 0.5m). The spread of the collapsed wall is widest (Wth 6m) SE-SW where it faces a natural scarp and narrowest (Wth 2.4m) at ESE where only a narrow fosse (Wth 0.6m) separates it from the bank of the adjoining cashel. There is a possible entrance (Wth 1m) at ESE. The interior is under pasture and slopes gently down to SE. Cultivation ridges, visible in an aerial photograph (CUCAP, BGM 35) taken in 1971, are not visible at ground level. A possible cashel (SL020-197009-) abuts the SE edge. Mentioned by Wood-Martin (1882, 21) as one of three raths in a 'trefoil arrangement'.

In the Annals of the Four Masters, under the year 1360, it is recorded that 'a bridge of lime and stone was built by Cathal O'Conor across the river of Eas-dara' and 'Eas-dara' is equated in a footnote with Ballysadare (O'Donovan 1848, vol. 3, 619). According to O'Keeffe and Simington (1991, 28), this is the first reference in any annal to the erection of such a bridge in Gaelic Ireland. The exact location of this bridge is not known. Wood-Martin (1892, 200) noted that 'the present modern bridge [see SL020-268----] at Ballysadare is much higher up the stream than its predecessor; for the remains of an old bridge-perhaps that erected in 1360 or in 1586-was discovered when workmen were sinking foundations for the eel-house, which is situated just over the last fall made by the river before mingling its waters with the tide'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and the RMP (1995) and classified 'Salt Workings'. In pasture, on the S shore of Ballysadare Bay. The salt workings comprise a series of overgrown ruined buildings. One of the buildings (on an E-W axis) is a residential, two-storey, gable-ended house (7.3m E-W; 5m N-S) with an enclosed yard (7m E-W) on the E side. There is a chimney on the W gable. There is a small square, single story structure (5.35m x 5.3m) at the E end of the yard with a wide cut-stone arch. There is another building (7.4m N-S; 4.8m E-W) at right-angles to the latter with a door ope at the N end facing onto the seashore. There is the remains of a two-storey building to E with the foundations of other buildings evident. The remains are of 18th/19th century appearance. 


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

source_data.original_text:
On a relatively level patch of rough ground, on the N face of a hill overlooking Ballysadare Bay. The feature, at the junction of three field walls, and partly buried by wall stones, seems to be some form of deliberate structure. It is c. 1m long, 0.75m wide at the S, narrowing to 0.4m at the N. It is represented by two opposed stones, an eastwards leaning example at the W (L 1.1m N-S; T 0.3m; min. H 0.5m) and another opposite it at the E (L 0.95m N-S; T 0.15m; H 0.5m). Between these two there is a displaced slab (1.15m x 0.8m x 0.15m). The role of this stone is unclear but it may have roofed the structure. The nature of the structure is uncertain but it may be some form of cist.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, on the E side of a road, on a W-facing slope of the Ox mountains. A well (D 0.6m from roof slab) with a rectangular drystone slab surround (0.8m E-W; 0.8m N-S; T 0.38m) with an opening (Wth 0.3m) at N. Two lintel slabs cover the S half which is partially collapsed.
There is no indication that this is a holy well. However, this may be the holy well referred to by O'Rorke (1878, 277) as being a little to the east of the cruckawn, called Tubbermurro, 'where stations used to be performed by the people of the neighbourhood. The well lay in a hollow between two bushes and the devotees made a circuit on their knees round the bushes, attaching to one or other of them, at the close of the exercise, a small strip of scrap of cloth, in token, probably, of willingness to make a more valuable offering if circumstances permitted or required. Either by accident or by design the water supply was cut off and the well dried, about thirty years ago, by persons quarrying close to Tubbermurro.' A footnote states that Tubbermurro signifies 'Mary's Well'.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC with revisions by Patrick F. O'Donovan and Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
A bridge over the Ballysadare River is indicated on the Down Survey (1655-6) barony map (1654-57) at the town of Ballysadare. There are now no visible remains of this bridge. The present road bridge (on a NE-SW axis; Wth c. 6m) which is of 18th-century appearance is on the SW side of Ballysadare town. It has seven segmental arches (span c. 6m) increasing in size towards the centre with dressed voussoirs. The low pointed cutwaters have concrete tops. The core of the bridge is rendered and the arches are underpinned. The bridge has been recently widened with a cantilevered support and iron railing. An earlier bridge (SL020-249----) seems to have existed to NW. Also indicated on the Down Survey (1655-6) barony map (1654-57) is a mill (SL020-273----) on the E bank of the Ballysadare River and down stream from this bridge.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Described as a kidney-shaped mound (13.2m E-W; 10.4m N-S; H 0.54m) of heat-shattered stones in a charcoal-enriched soil, indented on its S side (McConway 2000, 280). A rescue excavation was carried out in 2000 (Deevy 2001, 304) as the fulacht fia was in an area proposed as a landfill site. Excavation revealed a series of wooden planks and posts likely to represent the remains of the base of a trough under the S side of the mound and a discontinuous ring of thirty wooden stakes, c. 0.3m apart, which formed an enclosure (diam. 15m) around the mound (ibid.).

source_data.original_text:
On the W bank of the Owenmore River and immediately W of Collooney. A mill is indicated on the Down Survey (1655-6) barony map on the W bank of the river and next to 'a fall' and on the opposite side of the river to a church (SL020-203001-). There is a substantial bleach mill complex still standing on or near this site. This is probably the mill which according to McGarry (1980, 38) was built in 1797 by a Mr Jackson and was later sold to Alexander Sim who built a flour and corn mill on the opposite bank of the river. Most of the flour and corn mill has been demolished though the remains of wheel-pits and arched head and tailraces are evident. Two mills, one each side of the river, are marked here on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, a third, in Bleachgreen, lies c. 200m to N and is set back from the river.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, located on a SE-facing slope in rough hilly terrain. This souterrain was exposed in 2001 during land reclamation works. Inspected in October of that year, it consisted of a circular drystone chamber (diam. at base c. 2m) of corbelled construction. The upper quarter of the chamber was destroyed but the walls of the lower part of the chamber remained intact to a height of c. 1.2m. A passage (Wth c. 0.95m), with drystone walls constructed of relatively small stones, roofed with large, flat slabs, extended to NNE from the NNE end of the chamber. The passage was partly infilled with soil and could not be investigated. 

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Situated in marsh c. 20m NW of a bend in the Ballysadare River. The remains consist of a central pear-shaped sunken area (15m E-W; 27m N-W; D c. 1-1.2m) with the narrow end opening to the N. It is enclosed by a raised, flat berm (W c. 5m) and external bank (W c. 5m; H. 1-1.5m). The bank is best preserved along the E, S and W sides and fades out gradually at the N end where the depression opening is situated. The E side of the monument was planted with trees in 2000 as part of the formal landscaping of the area following on the erection of the art work 'Regeneration' installed after the completion of the N4 roadworks. The exact nature of this feature is unknown and the possibility that it is of modern construction cannot be ruled out. The sides of the depression are relatively steep and it is possible that a pre-existing raised enclosure had its centre excavated. The inland promontory fort excavated by C. Mount in 1994 lies c. 150m to the WSW.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 18 August 2011

source_data.original_text:
Located on the W bank of a tributary stream of the Owenboy River, in an upland river valley on the S slopes of the Ox Mountains. There is a forestry plantation adjacent to E. Ruined rectangular stone-built hut (4.8m N–S; 3m E–W). The walls (Wth 1.2m; H 0.6-0.8m), which appear to be of dry-stone construction using local gneiss stones, are largely covered in sod and moss. A gap (Wth 0.8m) at the N end of the E wall marks the original doorway. A small annex (int. dim. 1.1m E–W; 1-1.5m N–S) is appended to the S wall, defined on the E and W sides by two short lengths of wall, and open on the S side. There are two heaps (max. dim. c. 2m) of loose field stones c. 3m to SW. To S a low, stone wall borders the bank of the stream, built apparently to direct overflow and prevent flooding of the low terrace on which the hut is built. There is a structure (SL024-004001-) located c. 60m to NE.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 7 March 2013

In rough upland pasture on the lower slopes of the Ox Mountains, located on a small terrace scarped out of the S-facing slope of a natural hillock on the S bank of the Owenboy River. Forestry plantation adjacent to SE. Ruined, roughly circular stone-built structure (3.8m E–W; 3.5m N–S). The enclosing wall (Wth c. 1.2m) is constructed of local gneiss stones. Internally the wall appear to have a gentle inward slope towards the base. The interior space (diam. 1.3-1.4m) is partly filled with loose stone and obscured by sod and moss. Appended to the S side of the structure is a rectangular space (2.7m E–W; 1.2m N–S) enclosed on W and S by a wall and open on the E side. This appears to have served as a sheltered access to the circular structure. However, no clearly defined gap into the circular structure is evident. There is a booley hut (MA024-004----) located c. 60m to S.

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

source_data.original_text:
In rough upland pasture, in the Ox Mountains, located on a small ridge or knoll, flanked immediately to N and S by two small, boggy valleys. The knoll is cloaked in blanket bog, with ground cover of moorland grasses, sedges, rushes and mosses, broken by areas of gneiss outcropping. To E ground falls away to the shore of Easkey Lough, overshadowed on its E side by the high main ridge of the Ox Mountains; to W there is a drop to a broad, flat expanse of blanket bog which stretches far to W and NW. The standing stone consists of an upright, narrow flat-topped pillar of schist. It has naturally rounded edges, giving it a roughly oval cross-section (0.2m E–W; 0.12-0.15m N–S). It leans slightly to N so that its vertical height is 0.6m, and the leaning or oblique dimension is 0.75m. There is at least a further 0.5m of the stone embedded in the peat.

source_data.original_text:
On rocky reclaimed pasture below the steeper S slopes of the Ox Mountains and commanding an extensive outlook to the S. A layer of peat covers parts of the structure. 
This wedge tomb is a National Monument in State ownership (no. 523). A well-preserved gallery opens onto a façade and an outer wall. The gallery, facing WNW, is divided by two jamb-like stones inset in the gallery walls and a septal-stone, now in a displaced position just E of them, into a portico (L 1.4m; Wth 1.3m) and main chamber (L 6m; Wth at front 1.6m, at mid-length 2.15m, at rear 0.7m). A single stone forms each side of the portico. There are eight stones on the N side of the main chamber and seven on the S side. There is a small stone immediately outside the easternmost stone at the S. The E end of the structure is covered by three overlapping roofstones resting on the gallery sides. A large stone is interposed between either end of the westernmost roofstone and the top of the S side of the gallery. Outer-walling survives beyond both the sides and back of the gallery. There are ten outer-wall stones at the N, twelve at the S, and a single large orthostat is in position at the E end of the monument. There is a set stone of uncertain function 0.7m outside the E end of the outer-walling at the N. A single facade-stone links the outer wall at the N to the front of the portico. Its counterpart at the S is now prostrate. There is considerable cairn material between the outer-walling and the gallery but no trace of a mound outside the structure. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 54-5, no. 86)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In rough rocky pasture, on a S-facing slope. An oval steep-sided earthen platform (31.2m NE-SW; 35.7m NW-SE; H 3.45m), probably incorporating a natural knoll, with a step (H 1m) around its base. Traces of a possible stone revetment for the step are evident at W and SW. The top of the platform is enclosed by a ruinous sod-covered wall (Wth 3m; int. H 1m; ext. H 1.2m) with a rubble core and facing of large limestone blocks. A berm (Wth 2m) was noted at the external base of the wall W-NNW. The western section of the wall is topped by a post-and-wire fence. A blocked-up gap in the wall at SE is possibly an entrance. A broad fosse (Wth 3.2m) encircles the base of the mound S-N; a low terrace (Wth 3.3m; H 0.6m) is evident E-SE. A sod-covered stony bank (Wth 4.5m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 1.5m) skirts the outer edge of the fosse SSW-NW and is incorporated into a field boundary for a short section at S. A rectangular area (5.3m N-S; 7.5m E-W) enclosed by earthen bank (Wth 3.4m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1.5m) abuts the external face of the outer wall. The interior is level though strewn with sod-covered stones; some coniferous trees grow in the N third. Several field-clearance heaps were noted and at E, adjacent to the enclosing wall, is a small hollow now partially infilled with stones. At SSE, close to the inner side of the enclosing wall, is a circular drystone-built structure (1.4m N-S; 1m E-W; H 0.6m). Drystone field boundaries radiate from the base of the platform at N, S, SW, W and NW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On top of a ridge in rolling drumlin-like country. A well-preserved gallery (L 8.9m), flanked at both sides by the remains of outer-walling, opens onto a flat facade at the W. The front of the monument is incorporated in a field fence. The gallery is divided by a septal-stone into a portico (L 1.6m; Wth 1.4m) and main chamber (L 7m; Wth 1.7m at septal-stone, 1m near the backstone). Single stones form the sides of the portico and each articulates with a facade-stone. A stone stands in the gap between the facade-stones thus dividing the gallery entrance. Eight stones are in position on the N side of the main chamber and six on the S side and these display a general decrease in height from W to E. A roofstone covers the portico and another the rear of the gallery. Between these three others lie displaced along the gallery. A line of three outer-wall stones (the middle one fallen outwards) adjoins the northern facade-stone and a lone outer-wall stone remains on the opposite side of the structure about 1m beyond the front of the main chamber. Outside this there is a displaced slab and there is another outside the N side of the gallery. There is an unclassified megalithic tomb (SL025-009----) c. 300m to SE. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 55-6, no. 87)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
The monument, greatly ruined, stands about 300m SE of a wedge tomb (SL025-008----) and is on similar land at the foot of the ridge occupied by that tomb. It consists of a number of large prostrate slabs and leaning stones along with some small set stones. The remains stretch some 7.5m SE-NW, perhaps the alignment of the ruined structure, and are described here as if they lay E-W. There are two set stones at the W end neither more than 0.8m long or 0.2m high, one set transversely to the long axis of the structure and the other at its more northerly side. Close to the E end there is a large westwards-leaning slab (L 2.3m; H if upright c. 2m) at right angles to the long axis of the structure. West of and at right angles to the S end of this there is a somewhat smaller northwards-leaning slab. At right-angles to the outer face of the former there is a small set stone (L 0.6m; T 0.15m; H 0.25m) and 0.6m S of the latter there is another (L 0.9m; T 0.15m; H 0.4m). Along the N side of structure there are three large displaced slabs, the largest 3.5m x 2.4m x 0.6m T. There are also other smaller displaced and partly buried stones at the site. Traces of mound survive along the N side and W end of the structure. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 56, no. 88)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In rocky pasture, on the S side of a low rise. A slightly raised roughly circular area (34.5m E-W) enclosed by an earth and stone bank NNE-NNW which is levelled for 20m NNW-NNE. The bank is generally low and sod-covered, possibly composed of an earthen base capped by a stone wall with internal and external kerbstones evident in places. It is best preserved S-SW (Wth 3.5m; int. H 0.45m; ext. H 1.5m), obscured by dumped field clearance stones along the E arc and overgrown with vegetation along the S arc. The interior is level; a large slab protrudes from the ground in the S half and two large stones were noted in the W half. There are field boundaries immediately outside the bank to S and W. A rectangular enclosure (SL025-162----) lies c. 70m to S.

source_data.original_text:
In rocky upland pasture, on a rise on the margins of flat boggy ground. A spring rises to N of the rath and flows past it at NE, feeding into the boggy ground. A roughly circular area (c. 40m N-S) defined by a scarp (H 1.5m) SW-NNE and by a steep natural fall of ground S-SW. The enclosing elements are not visible NNE-SE due to a dense overgrowth of blackthorn bushes. The scarp is topped by a rim of loose stones (Wth c. 1-1.5m), stones are also visible in the face of the scarp which may be remains of stone facing. A shallow external flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 2m) is visible SW-NNE. The remains of a stone field boundary (Wth 1m; H 0.3m) skirts the fosse W-NW. The interior is level except in the NE quadrant where it slopes down to NE and is wet underfoot. Much of the interior is engulfed in a thicket of blackthorn, hazel and brambles, but the centre is clear of overgrowth. There is a possible hut site (SL025-011002-) in the NW quadrant of the interior. In the E and SE of the interior are the remains of possible 19th-century structures, consisting of a number of intersecting ruined walls (Wth c. 1m; H 0.4m) enclosing small rectilinear areas. Within one of these areas are the foundations of a rectangular structure (4.3m N-S; c. 5.3m E-W) defined by a sod-covered stone wall (Wth 0.7m; H 0.3m). The interior is partially infilled with stones. It appears to be the ruins of a small house. To S of the structure there are spreads and heaps of fieldstones. There is a possible souterrain (SL025-011001-) in the interior.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, at a break of slope on the SE side of a ridge; the ground falls away steeply to the S and E but rises gently to the NW and W. A raised circular area (30.1m N-S; 32.6m E-W) defined by two banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 6.5m; int. H 0.9m; ext. H 3.1m) is best preserved SSW-NE; it is low or levelled elsewhere. There is a gap (Wth 3m) at SE. The intervening fosse (Wth 5m) is evident SSW-NE. The outer bank (Wth c. 3.5m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H 1m) is evident SW-NE; a field boundary wall is built on top of the bank in places and elsewhere built against the external face of the bank. The outer bank E-SE is possibly truncated by a field boundary. The fosse and parts of the outer bank are partially overgrown with hawthorn bushes. The interior slopes down gently to SSE. There is a possible souterrain (SL025-01201-) in the centre of the W half. A semicircular hollow (c. 3m x 2m) is visible immediately inside the gap at SE. There is a house immediately S of the rath.

Along the E arc, the wall is also low and narrow (Wth 1m; H 0.5m) and c. 1m outside it is a curving field boundary. There are narrow gaps (Wth c. 0.5m) through the wall at NW and WSW. Field boundaries radiate out from the cashel to S and W. A field boundary curves SSW-NW c. 5m outside the enclosing wall. source_data.original_text:
In a level area in rocky pasture, with wet ground immediately to E. A slightly raised circular area (diam. 22m) defined by a scarp (H 1m) with a fosse and external bank. The edge of the scarp is topped NE-SE by the low remains of a field boundary wall. A similar wall (Wth 2m; H 0.4m), set 2.4m in from the edge of the scarp, curves WSW-N. The scarp is low or eroded at SE and SW. The fosse (Wth 3.7m) is crossed at SSE, SSW and SW by the field boundary walls. The outer bank (Wth 3m; int. H 1.1m; ext. H 0.6m) is evident all round as a stony sod-covered rise with traces of stone kerbing. The interior is level and crossed off-centre to W by the remains of a N-S field boundary. H 0.5m), NW-NE by a pile of stones (Wth 5.6m; int. H 1.4m) accumulated against a natural rising slope and NE-S by a drystone wall (Wth 2.5m; H 1.2m). A small irregular field-clearance cairn lies against the enclosing element at NW. source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and the RMP (1995) and classified 'Field System'. Not marked on the 1838 edition of the OS 6-inch map. A system of small fields indicated on the 1914 edition of the OS 6-inch map Many of the field walls are now tumbled but where property boundaries occur the walls are in better repair. The principal walls extend on a roughly N-S axis up the mountain slopes and numerous cross-walls form a patchwork of small irregular fields. That the field system is later than the many raths and enclosures in the vicinity is evident where field walls have bisected or incorporated portions of these enclosures. This field system probably dates to the post-1700 AD period.

In rough pasture, at the base of a S-facing slope. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an embanked circular area (diam. c. 20m) and on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as an arc of bank W-E abutting the N side of an E-W field boundary. The interior is bisected by a second field boundary on a N-S axis. Only the S half of this possible rath is now evident. Remains consist of a slightly raised, roughly D-shaped area (diam. 21m E-W; H c. 1m) covered with mature coniferous trees and strewn with boulders and debris. Traces of a N-S field boundary cross the interior just E of centre and a concrete shed partially overlies the W edge. A concrete wall has been built along the straight N side of the D-shaped area. There are no visible remains of the N half of the rath, a bungalow now occupies this area which is at a slightly lower level than S half.

In pasture, on a low semicircular rise. A substantially raised roughly circular area (25.7m N-S; 28.8m E-W) enclosed on top by an earthen bank and at its base by a fosse and external bank. The inner bank (Wth 6.2m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 3.5m) has traces of possible stone facing on its internal face. There is a gap (Wth 3m) at NE with the remains of an external ramp. The fosse (Wth 3m) and external bank (Wth 6.2m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H 0.6m) are evident SE-NE. A farm track and field boundary lie immediately to E. In the interior, a shallow depression skirts the internal face of the bank N-SE, terminating at each end in an oval hollows (N hollow: 4m x 5m; D 0.45m; SE hollow: 3m x 6m; D 0.35m). A third hollow (1m x 2m) lies adjacent to a large boulder close to the bank at S. There is a field boundary immediately to N of the rath.

source_data.original_text:
At the foot of a NW-facing slope and close to a stream in damp pasture. The structure is damaged and difficult to interpret. The main feature is an uphill- and E-facing chamber (L 4m; Wth c. 2m) with its back to the stream. A large stone (H c. 1.5m) forms each side and it is closed by an inset backstone (L 1.8m; min. T 0.3m; H 1.4m), the jagged top of which indicates it has been broken. In front of the northern sidestone there is the stump of another orthostat (L 1.6m; min. H 1.7m) possibly a broken portal-stone. Part of its detached upper portion lies at the front of the chamber. Some low stones just N of the stump of this orthostat are part of an old field fence. A large flat slab (4m x 3m; T 0.4m), a displaced roofstone, leans against the outer face of the southern sidestone. Both sidestones lean to the S and both are split. There is considerable grass-grown fill in the chamber. The tomb must remain unclassified but its location, facing uphill away from a stream, the use of a single large stone for each side of the chamber, and the presence of a great roofstone would suggest it may be a ruined portal-tomb. 
Five metres W of the chamber there is a large prostrate slab (2.45m x 2.5m; T 0.4m), its W end raised clear of the ground where it rests on a set stone (L 1.1m; H 0.55m; T 0.15m). There are other partly buried slabs here. The indications are that this may have been some form of chamber. Some 7m to the N there is another large prostrate slab (4m x 2.4m; max. T 0.4m).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In rough stony pasture, on a gentle SE-facing slope. A circular area (31m NW-SE; 28m NE-SW) enclosed by a scarp (H 1-1.2m) with a slight internal lip (Wth c. 1.5m) E-SW, by a stone field boundary W-NNE and by a low sod-covered stony rise (int. H 0.4m) NNE-E. The scarp and lip appear to be very stony and with the low rise are heavily overgrown with blackthorn bushes and brambles. A possible entrance (Wth c. 1.2m) is at ESE. The S portion of the interior is raised to compensate for the hillslope. The NW quadrant the interior is fairly level but it slopes down from there to SE, levelling out again close to the scarp SE-S. There is a souterrain (SL025-024002-) in the SW quadrant. A large slab, barely protruding above the sod, is located in the NE quadrant close to the NNE perimeter and appears to overlie a shallow hollow but there is no evidence of a souterrain chamber here.

In rough grazing, at a break of slope on the S side of a ridge. A slightly raised circular area (43.4m E-W) defined by the remains of an earthen bank (Wth 3.7m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1.45m) SW-NW and by a scarp elsewhere. The slope of the scarp (H 2.3m) is enhanced SE-S by the natural slope of the ridge. Gaps occur in the bank at NW (Wth 2m), W (Wth 3m) and WSW (Wth 1.2m). A shallow external depression (Wth 2m; D 0.3m) SW-W is possibly the remains of a silted-up fosse and it is skirted by a flat terrace (Wth 5m; H 0.6m) which may be a natural feature. The interior slopes down to E and is densely overgrown with ferns. Roughly in the centre of the E half is a low gently curving scarp (L c. 6m N-S). At the N end of the interior is an arc of sod-covered stones (6.5m E-W; c. 3m N-S; H 0.5m) W-E terminated at the W end by a field clearance cairn overgrown with bushes. A broad natural terrace surrounds the N perimeter of the rath. Hazel trees grow around the perimeter and there is a small hazel wood on the slope to E and SE.

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on a gentle SE-facing slope; the ground falls away gradually to E and SE towards the Owenboy River. A raised circular area (35m N-S; 33.5m E-W) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 6m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H 2.3m) with an external fosse. The bank is levelled internally NE-SE where a NNE-SSW field boundary crosses the edge of the interior. At WSW there is a 7m long break in the bank and the exposed sections reveal an earthen construction with some large stones incorporated in the core at the base. The external bank face has been eroded or dug away for c. 6m at N. The entrance (Wth 2m), at NE, is stone faced on its N side and partially obscured by a field boundary on its S side. The fosse (Wth 3m; D 1.4m) is evident all round apart from NE-SE where there is a terrace (Wth 3m; H 0.7m) edged with stones. The interior slopes slightly down to SE. There is a hut site (SL025-026002-) in the SW quadrant.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Located c. 2 km WSW of the village of Rockfield. In rough grazing, at the base of a SE-facing slope and in the SW quadrant of an enclosure (SL025-027002-). A rectangular platform (10m WNW-ESE; 5.5m ENE-WSW) defined on three sides by the remains of a stone wall (Wth 1m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.5m) and on the fourth side by the W wall of the enclosure. The surface of the platform is covered with sod-covered stones including some small upright slabs, probably grave-markers. Several more similar stones and slabs were noted in the area to the S and SW of the platform. According to O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 61), unbaptised children were buried here. There is a souterrain (SL025-153----) c. 100m to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the S-facing slope of a ridge. A large rath with a smaller oval enclosure (SL025-033001-) in its N half. The rath consists of a circular area (50.8m N-S; 49m E-W) enclosed by an earthen bank (Wth 1.7m; int. H 1m; ext. H 1.1m) that is incorporated into a field boundary SSE-SSW. There are gaps in the bank at SW (Wth c. 4m) and at NNE (Wth 3.8m); a rough farm track curves across the interior between these gaps. The interior slopes down to S. An area in the centre of the interior has been quarried, in places up to 1m in depth. There is a stone-built shed in the NE quadrant. A dense patch of irises grows on a fairly level part of the interior just inside the bank at S. A rectangular garden surrounding a disused cottage is built onto the N side of both enclosures.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Another field boundary shown on the 1914 OS 6-inch map extending NE from bank at N has been levelled. A bowl-barrow (SL025-035----) lies c. 60m to NE.

source_data.original_text:
At a break of slope, on the S side of a ridge overlooking the valley of the Owenboy River to S; with panoramic views. A slightly raised oval area (21.8m N-S; 24.6m E-W) defined by two enclosing banks/walls with an intervening fosse. The inner bank is evident along the E arc as a low sod-covered stony bank (Wth 2.7m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.5m) with some internal stone kerbing and along the W arc as low wall-footings with internal and external stone facing (Wth 2.3m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.3m). There is a berm (Wth 2m; H 0.5m) outside the bank SW-NW. The outer bank (Wth 3.4m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 0.65m) is well defined SW-NW, degraded E-S and levelled elsewhere. The fosse (Wth 2.3m) best evident SW-NW, less well defined E-S and evident only by a growth of rushes elsewhere. There is a possible entrance (Wth 1.2m), partially lined with stones, through the banks and across the fosse at SE. The entrance is partially obscured by a dense growth of irises. The interior slopes gently down to S and is mostly covered with rushes and irises. There is a wet boggy area in the SE quadrant. A hut site (SL025-037002-) lies to W of centre.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In undulating pasture, on a gentle SE-facing slope. A raised circular area (37.8m N-S; 41.8m E-W) enclosed by two banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 6.8m; int. H 1.1m; ext. H 2.5m) is evident all round. At the SE, partially obscured by a field clearance pile, is a parallel setting of stones (1.2m apart), possibly the remains of a stone-lined entrance passage with a gap (Wth 2m) immediately to S. The deep intervening fosse (Wth 4m), which is evident SW-SE, is reduced to a shallow depression SE-SW. The outer bank is levelled SE-SW but substantial elsewhere (Wth 6m; int. H 1.8m; ext. H 1.45m). There is an eroded gap (Wth 1m) through the inner and outer banks at NNW. The interior is split level; the higher N half is divided from the lower S half by a gentle scarp extending roughly E-W just S of centre. There is a possible souterrain (SL025-038001-) in the NE quadrant. Field boundaries are built against the external face of the inner bank SE-SW and the external face of the outer bank SW-W and NW-NE.

In undulating pasture, straddling a break of slope at the E end of a ridge. A roughly circular raised area (26.3m N-S; 30.3m E-W) defined by two earth and stone banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 5.4m; int. H 0.85m; ext. H 2.45m) is evident all round with traces of possible internal stone revetment. The entrance (Wth 1.1m) is at E and is lined with boulders. Some large boulders at the base of the external face of the inner bank are possibly from field clearance. The outer bank (Wth 5m; int. H 1.9m; ext. H 1.2m) is evident SW-E, though almost levelled NNW-E, and levelled SE-SW. The intervening fosse (Wth 3.5m) is evident SW-NE with a terrace (Wth 2.5m) SE-SW from which the ground slopes away naturally. The interior slopes gently down to E. There is a souterrain (SL025-040002-) in the NW quadrant, a hut site (SL025-040003-) in the NE quadrant and a roughly circular slightly sunken area (c. 10m E-W) in the centre of the S half. Remains of a N-S field boundary are adjacent to the outer bank at W. There are small quarry pits close by to SW and SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In the NW quadrant of a cashel (SL025-089001-). Two openings to the souterrain are evident, one within the W half of the square internal enclosure (SL025-089003-) in the cashel and the other c. 5m to the SW close to the cashel wall. The first mentioned opening reveals a vertical drystone-built shaft, circular in section (diam. 1m; D c. 1m), which may be the original access shaft to the souterrain. The shaft is partially infilled with soil and a possible displaced lintel but a creepway is evident, opening to the SW. The second opening reveals a small oval corbelled chamber (3m x 2m; D c. 1.1m), partially infilled with soil and stones. A creepway is evident at the NE side leading in the direction of the previous opening. A rath (SL025-090001-) lies c. 150m to SSW.

source_data.original_text:
In rolling pasture. A pair of opposed orthostats at the SW and another pair some 4m to the NE represent a ruined gallery (L at least 6m; Wth 2.2m at SW, 1.55m at NE). A displaced roofstone lies between the two pairs of orthostats and there is a shattered roofstone at the NE end of the structure. An outer-wall stone stands 1m outside the more northerly of the two opposed orthostats at the SW. Immediately SW of the structure there is a field fence and beyond this there is an orthostat set transversely to the main axis of the gallery. This stone might be part of a facade and if so indicates an original gallery length of some 11m. Just 1m E of this orthostat there is a prostrate stone. There are no traces of mound around the structure but there are a number of loose slabs scattered at the site. An enclosure (SL025-093----) lies c. 50m to N. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 58, no. 92)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In undulating rough pasture, near the base of a SE-facing slope at the S end of a ridge. A slightly raised roughly circular area (39.8m NNW-SSE; 41.9m ENE-WSW) enclosed by an earthen bank and external fosse. The bank is substantial (Wth 4.8m; int. H 1.3m; ext. H 0.65m) and slightly stepped externally NW-E, has a low internal lip but drops down 1.8m externally E-SW and is narrower (Wth 2m) with a more vertical external face SW-NW. A gap (Wth 2m) at SE and several other eroded areas were noted in the bank. At S a semicircular area has been scooped out of the external face of the bank. The fosse is substantial (Wth 4m; D 0.9m) NW-E, evident as a band (Wth 2m) of irises and denser vegetation E-SW and as a shallow depression (Wth 6m) SW-NW. The SE portion of the interior is raised to compensate for the hillslope though there is still a gentle slope down to SE. There is a possible hut site (SL025-104001-) in the NW quadrant. Some small quarry pits are adjacent to the rath at SE. Levelled field boundaries abut the bank at NW and SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as a embanked circular area and on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as a subrectangular enclosure defined on the E side by a field boundary. Now evident as a slightly raised subrectangular area (57.9m N-S; 71m E-W) defined on the E side by a drain (Wth 1.5m) and field boundary (Wth 1.2m), on the linear S side by a steep scarp (H 1.7m), by the gently curving remains of an earthen bank (Wth 2.1m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 0.95m) SW-W and at NW by a short section of linear bank (Wth 2.8m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 1.1m) at the E end of the N side. An external fosse is evident along the S arc (Wth 3.5m; D 0.9m), for short section at E (Wth 4.3m) and as band of irises (Wth 4.5m) NW-N; a quarry pit has been dug into the line of the fosse at SW. Gaps in bank occur at NE (Wth 3m) and NNW (Wth 4m). The W half of the interior is level while the E half slopes steeply down to E; the ground level in the E half is c. 3m lower than the W half. The following features were noted in the W half of the interior: a hut site (SL025-107002-) in the NW quadrant, a linear sod-covered mound of earth and stone (5.5m E-W; 1.6m N-S; H 0.6m) W of the centre and a similar parallel mound (8m E-W; 4m N-S; H 0.5m) c. 20m to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On gently sloping ground in rolling land. A large flat slab (L 3m SE-NW; Wth 2.7m; T 0.4m) is supported in a more or less horizontal position by four of seven stones set in irregular order under its perimeter. These are up to 1m long, 0.5m thick and 1.1m high. At least five other stones now lie loose under the perimeter of the roofstone. This is clearly an ancient burial chamber but its age and culture context is unclear. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 98, no. 20)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In wet pasture, on top of a low rise, c. 100m SE of Killoran North Lough; in the E half of Killoran graveyard (SL025-112002-). The ivy-covered ruin of a rectangular church of which only the E and S walls stand. Built of roughly coursed stone, the walls are heavily encased with ivy. The E wall (L c. 8m) is broken off just short of the NE corner. In its centre is a window embrasure with a single light. This is flanked by two wall-presses on the internal wall-face. The S wall (L c. 21.5m) is broken off short of the SW corner. Roughly centrally placed in it is a doorway, missing its surround, but an internal edge stone on the W side survives. This block of sandstone is decorated with a plain roll-moulding (M. A. Timoney 2002d, 178). There is a window embrasure near the W end of this wall, which contains a piece of moulded stone, and another similar embrasure near its E end. The ruin is that of the medieval parish church of Killoran. A branch of an ancient road (SL025-159----) extends c. 230m to the SE from it and the graveyard.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008
