source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, at a break of the S-facing slope of a low rise. A raised roughly circular area (32.6m E-W; 34.3m N-S) defined by a low scarp (H 0.9m) NNW-E and elsewhere by a scarp (H 1.5m) enhanced by the natural slope of the rise. A gap (Wth 2.2m) at NE gives machinery access to the interior. The interior slopes gently down to S and SW even though the S portion has been raised to compensate for the hillslope. The external slope of the scarp is quarried into at N and S and overgrown with bushes SE-SW. Immediately outside the scarp at SW, a slight depression (Wth c. 2.7m), bordered on its external side by a low rise (Wth c. 3.7m) which merges into the natural slope, can be traced through overgrowth for c. 8m. A road lies immediately to SW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In undulating pasture, at the top of a SE-facing slope. A raised D-shaped area (42.3m NE-SW; 34m NW-SE) defined by a scarp (H 2.6m) NE-W and on the straight NW side by a road. The scarp is revetted S-W by a drystone wall. The interior is level and bisected NW-SE by the townland boundary. On the NE side of the townland boundary, the interior is used as a dump for old cars and a concrete garage has been built over the perimeter at N. On the SW side of the boundary a barn has been built in the interior and mature coniferous trees grow around the perimeter. There are no visible remains of the enclosure on the NW side of the road.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the SE-facing slope of a ridge. A slightly raised roughly circular area (31m NW-SE; 35m NE-SW) enclosed by an earthen bank and a possible external fosse. The bank (Wth 3.8m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H 1.1m) is evident all round but along the S arc is low internally (H 0.2m) and substantial (H 1.6m) externally to compensate for the natural slope of the ridge. The bank W-N (Wth 2.8m) has an almost vertical external face with a low step (Wth 1.2m; H 0.4m) at its base. Several small eroded gaps were noted in the bank including one at E now obscured by gorse. A depression (Wth 4m) noted at N, between the bank and a sharp natural rise of the ridge, may be the remains of a fosse. The interior is covered with thistles and slopes gently down to S and SE. There is a field boundary immediately to NE and a road immediately to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on the narrow top of a small ridge; the ground slopes away abruptly c. 10m to NW with more gradual slopes to S and SE. A raised oval area (26m NE-SW; 36.7m NW-SE) defined by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 4.3m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 2m) is evident all round except ENE-ESE where the interior is defined by a scarp (H 1.2m), a 5m section of which has been eroded. The outer bank (Wth 2.7m; int. H 0.55m; ext. H 0.4m) and the intervening fosse (Wth 2.6m) are best evident SE-W, less well defined W-NE and levelled and infilled NE-SE. A field boundary truncates the outer bank and the intervening fosse at NE. The interior is divided by an E-W trackway, flanked by field boundaries, just N of centre. There is a low rise roughly in the centre of the interior just S of the trackway. A N-S field boundary crosses the SE quadrant of the interior and the remains of another abuts the outer bank at S. Another rath (SL025-119----) lies c. 50m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on the S end of a ridge with panoramic views of the surrounding countryside. A substantially raised circular area (25.8m NW-SE; 26.9m NE-SW) enclosed on top by an inner earthen bank and at base by a fosse with an outer bank. The inner bank (Wth 5.2m; int. H 0.1m; ext. H 3.4m) is low internally and at N and SE has been levelled. A well-defined fosse (Wth 2.4m) with a narrow base is evident all round. An outer bank (Wth 3.3m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1.4m) is evident all round and its slope is enhanced along the NW and SE arcs by the natural slope of ground. The entrance (Wth 2m) is at SE with a causeway (Wth 4m) across the fosse. Gaps (Wth 2m) occur in the inner and outer banks at W and a low area in the inner bank faces a gap (Wth 6m) in the outer bank at E. The interior is generally level though there is a slightly raised area (c. 11m NW-SE; 15m NE-SW) in the N half at the W end of which is a circular hollow (diam. 3m; D 0.4m). There is a road (SL025-159----) c. 40m to N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at a break of a NW-facing slope of a ridge. Raised roughly rectangular area (31.1m NE-SW; 37.6m NW-SE) defined by an earthen bank on the SE, SW and NW sides and by a scarp on the NE side. The bank is best preserved on the NW side (Wth 6.1m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 3m) where it has a broad steeply sloping external face. On the SW side the bank is incorporated into a field boundary (Wth 2.4m). Some stones protrude from the inner face of the bank on the SE side. There is a gap (Wth c. 1m) at the SW end of the SE side, now flanked by two large unembedded stones set against the external face of the bank. A small quarry pit (5m x 10m) has been dug into the scarp at the SE end of the NE side. The interior is level. An irregular rise (Wth 5m; H 0.3-0.8m) c. 5m outside the bank at the N corner may be of recent origin. There is a disused field boundary immediately outside the enclosure on the SW side. A road (SL025-159----) lies c. 40m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on top of a narrow ridge. A raised circular area (37.1m N-S; 34.8m E-W) enclosed by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 7.1m; int. H 1.7m; ext. H 3.15m) has traces of internal stone revetment along the S and W arcs and at NNE its external slope has been quarried into for a distance of 6m. The intervening fosse (Wth 4m) is evident all round apart from E-ESE. The outer bank (Wth 4.3m; int. H 1m; ext. H 1m) is evident all round apart from N-NNE where it has been incorporated into a field boundary and E-ESE where it is levelled and replaced by a field boundary. At N a small section of the external slope of the outer bank has been quarried into. The S half of the interior is slightly higher than the N half with a gentle slope down to NE and E. The entrance (Wth 1.4m) is at E, with traces of possible stone-facing visible.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on top of the W end of a narrow ridge; the ground slopes steeply down to N and NW, more gradually to S and SW. A raised oval area (20.6m N-S; 25.8m E-W) defined by a scarp (H 2.25m) along the S arc and elsewhere by an earthen bank (Wth 4.3m; int. H 0.6m; ext. H 1.75m) which is low internally in places. A possible entrance (Wth 1.2m) is at SE, outside of which is a slight rise (Wth c. 3m), possibly the remains of a causeway. The interior is uneven in general and the W portion is slightly higher than the rest. Off-centre to S is a linear depression (2.4m E-W; 5.5m N-S; D 0.5m) with a small sod-covered heap of stones at its N end. The rath is encircled by an earth and stone field boundary, generally c. 2-3m outside the bank but merging with it NW-N. Possibly this field boundary respects the line of an infilled fosse. A terrace (Wth 5m) lies outside the bank/field boundary NW-N. The perimeter of the rath is ringed with hawthorn, hazel and scrub.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

The scarp is densely overgrown with hawthorn bushes. There are gaps in the bank at NW (Wth 2m) and at SE (Wth c. 2m). The interior is grass-covered and slopes gently down to S. Drumdivnagh Lough is c. 100m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In wet pasture, on elevated ground at the base of a high ridge. A roughly circular area (c. 84m NNE-SSW; 77m WNW-ESE) defined by a poorly preserved earthen bank and an external fosse. The gently rounded bank (Wth 3.5m; int. H 1.8m; ext. H 0.45m) is clearly defined S-SW and is evident as an intermittent low rise (Wth c. 3m; ext. H 0.6m) NE-S; elsewhere the interior is defined by a scarp (H 0.9m). The flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 2m; D 1.3m) is clearly defined S-SW but is shallow (Wth 3m; D 0.4m) elsewhere. Both the bank and the fosse are cut into rising ground S-SW and are cut by a trackway at SW. 
The N two thirds of the interior are occupied by a small oval hillock (c. 60m NW-SE; 47m NE-SW) with a flattened top and broadly sloping sides. A gap (Wth 5-10m) of level ground separates the base of the hillock from the bank along the E arc. A recently recut stream, with mounds of upcast on its S side, crosses the S third of the interior, cutting through the enclosing elements at SSE and SW. The bank and fosse are obscured by the upcast at SSE. The trackway which cuts the bank and fosse at SW continues into the interior and crosses the stream via a concrete bridge. A N-S field boundary (Wth 2.6m; H 0.7m), flanked by drains (Wth 1m), crosses the interior to W of centre. Another field boundary extends E from this, defining the S side of the hillock. A degraded NNE-SSW field boundary crosses the SE end of the hillock. Linked to this is a low scarp following the curve of the hillock NNE-SSW, thus enclosing a roughly D-shaped area (c. 30m NNE-SSW; 18m E-W), with a pronounced slope down to E. To SW of the enclosure the ground rises sharply in a broad steep NE-facing slope, part of a high ridge that overlooks the enclosure. A moated site (SL025-131----) lies c. 50 m to E and a fulacht fia (SL025-165001-) c. 30m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In level wet pasture with ridges of higher ground to SE and SW; the surrounding area is cut by modern drains. A raised rectangular area (13.9m NE-SW; 15.7m NW-SE) enclosed by the remains of two earthen banks with intervening and outer fosses. Only slight traces of the inner bank are evident, along the NE side and at the S and W corners; elsewhere the interior is defined by a scarp (H 0.8m). The intervening fosse (Wth 1.6m) is marked by a dense growth of rushes. The outer bank (Wth 3.8m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 0.95m) is evident all round. The outer fosse (Wth 4m; D 0.3m) is evident along the NW, SW and SE sides but on the NW side it swings c. 10m wide of the outer bank. A low rise (Wth 4m) is evident on the external side of the outer fosse on the S half of the SW side. A circular enclosure (SL025-130----) lies c. 50m to W and a fulacht fia (SL025-165001-) c. 30m to SSW in the same field.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on a low roughly circular rise with gently sloping sides. An oval area (51m N-S; 36m E-W) enclosed by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 3.5m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 2m) is generally low internally, particularly along the E arc. The entrance (Wth 1.4m) at E is concealed by overgrowth with some stone facing evident. The fosse (Wth 3m) is evident SE-N though very faint SE-S, replaced by a field boundary N-NE and infilled elsewhere. The outer bank (Wth 3.4m; int. H 1.1m; ext. H 0.6m) is evident S-N, replaced by a field boundary N-NE and levelled NE-ESE. The interior is level; an arc of scarp (H 0.3m) N-S faces the entrance in the E half. Both banks are densely overgrown with bushes. There is a rock outcrop close by to E. Another rath (SL025-134----) lies c. 100m to SSW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In undulating pasture, on top of the W side of a low ridge. A slightly raised circular area (30.4m NE-SW) enclosed by an earthen bank and an external fosse. The bank (Wth 5m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1.6m) is evident S-NE, being low internally in places; elsewhere it is incorporated into a linear field boundary which crosses the SE edge of the rath. The fosse (Wth 4m; D 0.9m) is evident S-NE and E-SE on the external side of the linear field boundary. The fosse is most clearly defined SW-NE and evident only as a shallow depression E-SE. The remains of a field boundary (Wth 1.5m; int. H 1.2m; ext. H 0.3m) skirt the outer edge of fosse S-SW. The interior is covered by rushes and crossed by a WNW-ESE field boundary. A farm trackway (Wth 2m) crosses the SE quadrant immediately inside the field boundary.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on a rise and separated from another rath (SL025-132----) c. 100m to NNE by a small marshy pool. A raised circular area (diam. c. 30m) defined by two earthen banks with an intervening fosse (Wth 3m). The inner bank (Wth 4.5m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1.8m) is evident along the W, N and E arcs and the interior is defined by a scarp along the S arc. There is an entrance (Wth 2m) through the inner bank at ESE. Traces of internal stone kerbing were noted on the bank in the vicinity of the entrance. The outer bank (Wth 3.2m; int. H 0.75m; ext. H 0.7m) is levelled along the E arc. The rath is densely overgrown with bushes and the interior is impenetrable.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In undulating pasture, straddling a break of an E-facing slope of a narrow ridge overlooking Fin Lough to SE. A slightly raised oval area (58.6m N-S; 48m E-W) enclosed by the remains of an earthen bank N-E, by a scarp E-S and by a curving field boundary (Wth 2.6m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1.4m) S-N. The interior slopes from the centre down to S and E and is level elsewhere. At N, close to the enclosing field boundary, a roughly circular area (diam. 7.5m; D 0.8m) has been quarried away.

At the boggy shoreline on the S edge of Fin Lough. A circular low-mound crannog (6.4m N-S; 7m E-W; H 0.57m above the lake-bed) on a lake-bed that is firm in places and marshy in others. The surface of the mound is grass-covered and fairly even with some stones visible in places and it slopes gradually down into the water. The E edge is the most well defined. The crannog is surrounded by a band of rushes (Wth c. 2m) that may mark its true edge. The S edge blends into the surrounding water-meadow. A possible crannog (SL025-137001-) is c. 50m to SSE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on the narrow top of an ENE-WSW ridge and overlooking Fin Lough to NW. A raised oval area (31.1m N-S; 32.8m E-W) enclosed by two earthen banks with an intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 3.7m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1.3m) is best preserved along the W arc, only a low internal lip is evident elsewhere. A possible entrance (Wth c. 2m) is at SE, with possible stone kerbing. The fosse (Wth 2.4m) is evident S-NW and is infilled elsewhere. The outer bank (Wth 2.4m; int. H 0.35m; ext. H 0.6m) is evident SE-S, incorporated into a field boundary S-NW and levelled elsewhere. Adjacent to E is a rectangular field planted with young coniferous trees. The inner bank and part of the interior at E have also been planted with coniferous trees. Mature deciduous trees grow on the perimeter S-N and in part of the W half of the interior. A few metres to E is a roughly circular area (diam. c. 6m) defined by an irregular bank of stone (Wth 2m; H 0.5m), on the E side of which is an irregular depression (Wth 2m; D 0.5m) which extends c. 5m to E. Both features may be the result of recent disturbance.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

raw_items.raw_text: A roughly circular area enclosed by an earthen bank with scant remains of an external fosse

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of a ridge. A roughly circular area (25.8m E-W) enclosed by an earthen bank with scant remains of an external fosse. The bank (Wth 3.4m; int. H 0.35m; ext. H 1.5m) is low and degraded internally. There are gaps (Wth 2m) in the bank at SW and NE with ramps to allow vehicles into the interior. The fosse is evident as a shallow depression SSW-SW. A curving field boundary skirts the bank SW-NW, c. 2m outside the bank, probably on the line of the fosse. The interior is level. A quarry pit (diam. c. 12m; D c. 2m) has destroyed most of the NE quadrant. There is a short section of a water-filled drain (Wth 2m; D 0.5m) outside the bank NNE-NE. A rectangular enclosure (SL025-141----) lies c. 30m to SW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, straddling a break of slope on the S side of an E-W ridge; the ground slopes gently down to N and more steeply to S and SE. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an embanked circular area (diam. c. 20m). It is now evident as a raised subcircular area (36.8m NNW-SSE; 36.5m E-W) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 3.3m; int. H 0.55m; ext. H 1.45m) NW-E, by a scarp (H 1.8m) SE-SW and W-NW and by a linear field boundary SW-W. A gap (Wth 2.5m) occurs in the bank at ESE. The N third of the interior is level; in the remainder the ground slopes markedly down to S and SW. Outside the bank NE-E is a 2m wide band of differential growth, probably indicating the line of an external fosse. At the break of slope, a curving scarp (L 6m E-W; H 1.1m) has been cut into the interior and continues indistinctly in a curve to the SE (L c. 8-9m). The perimeter is covered with bushes.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on a low NE-SW ridge. A raised circular area (42.2m NE-SW) defined by two earthen banks and intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 4.6m; int. H 1m; ext. H 2m) is substantial and evident all round with traces of internal stone kerbing noted in places. There is a gap (Wth 1.4m) in the bank at E. The fosse (Wth 4m) is evident SE-NW. The outer bank (Wth 3.6m; int. H 1.45m; ext. H 1.3m) is incorporated into a townland boundary SE-NW and levelled elsewhere, though a slight rise was noted on the line of bank at N and SE. Immediately outside the outer bank is a sloping terrace (Wth 2m; H 0.5m). The interior is mainly grass-covered with a few blackthorn bushes in the NW quadrant. A portion (18.5m NNE-SSW; 25m WNW-ESE) of the S half of the interior, abutting the inner bank SE-SW, is divided off by a low sod covered bank. Within the SW quadrant of this area is a low roughly oval sod-covered rise (2.7m NE-SW; 5.8m NW-SE; H 0.5m). A slightly raised semicircular area (4.5m N-S; 3.5m E-W) built against the internal face of the bank at NNE, is defined by an earthen bank (Wth 1.5m; int. H 0.15m; ext. H 0.5m). The outer bank of the rath is overgrown with blackthorn bushes which are also encroaching on the fosse and inner bank at W and NW. There is a road immediately to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On rough pasture on the lower slopes of the Ox Mountains commanding an outlook to the S. The tomb, well-preserved, is partly obscured by a fence running along its N side and W end. A gallery facing WSW is divided by a jamb-like stone at the N into a portico (L 1.9m) and main chamber (L 7.6m; Wth 1.55m at front, 1.95m towards mid-length, 1.3m at rear). The long axis of the gallery and that of the portico are at a slight angle to each other. A stone at the front of the portico divides the gallery entrance in two. Only one stone, at the S, remains of the portico sides. The main chamber orthostats are partly concealed by fill. Eight are visible on the N side, eleven to the S, and the gallery is closed by a single stone. A slab resting on the S side of the gallery at about mid-length seems to be a displaced roofstone. The facade and outer-walling represented by twelve orthostats merge to form a broad curve around the N side of the gallery. A large orthostat about 1m beyond the gallery backstone seems to represent the back of the outer wall. To the S, four outer-wall stones are in place beyond the middle and back of the gallery and between the easternmost of these and the large orthostat representing the back of the outer wall there are five fallen examples. A lone facade-stone adjoins the S side of the gallery entrance. Two large blocks 3m to the S of the SE corner of the structure do not seem to have formed part of the monument. There are some slight traces of a mound around the structure. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 56-7, no. 89)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and the RMP (1995) and classified 'Bridge'. A partially collapsed road bridge (on a ENE-WSW axis; Wth 7.5m), of 18th-century appearance, over the Owenbeg River to NE of Coolaney village. The remains of two tall semicircular arches (span c. 8m; H 6-7m), with a third collapsed dry arch (span 3.7m; H 1.8m) on the floodplain c. 20m to SW, under a disused approach road from Coolaney. All of the arches have rough voussoirs. The bridge has tall piers (Wth c. 2m) with low pointed cutwaters; there are also cutwaters against the side walls of the road to ENE. The bridge is now overgrown with ash trees, the roots of which are causing severe structural damage. It was replaced by another bridge to SW, closer to Coolaney. The later bridge, dated 1833, is slightly hump-backed and has a single wide segmental arch with a prominent keystone and cutstone voussoirs and string course. This bridge probably dates to the post-1700 AD period.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 11 January 2012

In undulating pasture, on a level terrace just below the top of a NE-SW ridge. A slightly sunken sod-covered track, flanked by substantial earthen field boundaries (Wth 2.2-4.6m; max. H 1.5m), is traceable for c. 500m in a roughly NE-SW line (Pl. 81). Roughly midway along its length, a side branch (Wth 2.8m) (SL025-112003-) extends (L c. 230m) downslope to NW to a church and graveyard (SL025-112001-; SL025-112002-) in Killoran North. The average width of the track is c. 8m but it widens to 12.7m at the branch junction. The side branch is flanked on its S side by a field boundary and on the N side is defined by a scarp (H 0.6m) dug into the side of the ridge. A rectangular enclosure (SL025-121----) lies c. 40m to NW and a rath (SL025-120----) c. 40m to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In level wet pasture, c. 80m SSE of a rath (SL025-041----) and immediately N of a disused railway line. The remains of a circular hut (9m N-S; 7.8m E-W) defined by a low sod-covered bank (Wth 2.1m; int. H 0.25m; ext. H 0.2m). Traces of internal stone kerbing are evident along the NE arc. There are gaps (Wth 2m) in the bank at SE and N. The interior is wet and sparsely covered with rushes. Partially sod-covered stones are scattered throughout the interior with one group forming a shallow E-W arc (C 2m) in the S half.

In rocky pasture, on a slight rise 7m S of a stream. A circular flat-topped mound (diam. at base c. 7m, at top 5m; max. H 1.2m) with a stone kerb (H 0.5m) evident SW-N. The mound is highest NE-SE where it merges with a natural break in slope but is low (H 0.5m) elsewhere. On the flat top of the mound are two roughly parallel lines of stones (long axes NW-SE), c. 2m apart. The NE line consists of two contiguous slabs (NW stone L 1.4m; Wth 0.24m; H 0.1m, SE stone L 0.95m; Wth 0.12m; H 0.15m). The SW line consists of one prominent stone (L 1m; Wth 0.12m; H 0.4m) at the NW end and at least five smaller barely discernible stones. A hawthorn tree grows on the perimeter of the mound at S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, in a thicket of hawthorn and overgrowth, located on the S-facing foothills of the Ox Mountains, a few meters W of a S-flowing stream. The low, partly sod-covered ruins of a vernacular house are located c. 10m to N. Upright stone (1.42m; H 1.05m; T 0.3m at base, 0.20m at top), embedded in the ground, with long axis NW–SE. It is roughly triangular in shape, with the narrow sides inclining inwards towards a gently pointed apex. The broad NE side of the stone is almost entirely covered in moss, and an ash tree grows against this side. According to local tradition, this stone is regarded as marking a special location, possibly the site of a burial.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, located on a natural terrace, on a steep SE-facing slope in the southern foothills of the Ox Mountains. The enclosure is located at the N edge of the terrace where the slope rises steeply to NW. The relatively level terrace extends c. 50m to SE of the enclosure before the ground falls away again in a steep slope. There are extensive views E–SW, with Kesh Corrann and Knocknashee forming prominent landmarks in the distance to SE and S, respectively. The enclosure is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps. It consists of an oval area (16m NE–SW; 14m NW-SE) defined by a collapsed stone wall, with a broad gap (Wth c. 7m) at NE. The wall is evident as a low, largely sod-covered stone bank. The S half of the enclosure is built up slightly to compensate for the natural slope. At SE–SSW the wall/stone bank is flush with interior ground level but has a broadly slumped external slope (Wth slope c. 3m; ext. H 0.8m), at SW–WNW it is evident as low wall footings (Wth 1.2-1.4m), and at NW–N the outer edge is almost flush with exterior ground level but it has a broadly slumped interior slope (H 0.5-0.6m). The NW–N section of the wall appears somewhat linear and may have been incorporated into a NE–SW field boundary in the past, and it also incorporates field clearance stones. 

Attached images:
SL025-168----_01.JPG viewed from SE 
SL025-168----_01.JPG viewed from E, showing broad gap at NE, and field clearance stones piled on bank at NW

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy 

Date of upload: 6 July 2015

source_data.original_text:
At a cliff-edge on the summit of Tullaghan Hill, a prominent rocky peak that rises from a bog-covered plateau NE of Coolaney, in the Ox Mountains. The fort has excellent views and overlooks a mountain pass to NW. A roughly D-shaped area (21m E-W; 19m N-S) defined E-W by two concentric stone walls and on the straight N side by a flat lip of bedrock marking the top of the cliff-face. The inner wall (Wth 2.5m) is collapsed and partially obscured by sod. External wall-facing is evident in places consisting of two to four courses (H 1.2m) of horizontally laid slabs. Outside the wall SW-W is a sod-covered spread (Wth 3m) of stones. A section of the wall at E has been rebuilt and there is a large break (Wth 7m) SSE-SW. There is a possible entrance (Wth 0.95m) at SE, flanked by two stone blocks. On top of the wall at SW is a possible penitential cairn (SL026-001004-). The remains of the outer wall are located 13-18m downslope of the inner wall and the intervening ground slopes down steeply apart from SE-W where it levels out to a natural terrace. The basal courses of the outer wall (Wth 1.55m; H 0.5m) are evident SW-W and are moss-covered. Elsewhere it is marked only by a slightly raised line of moss and heather. A field wall (SL026-001002-), barely discernible as a line of stones protruding through the sod, extends on a NE-SW axis between the inner and outer fort walls, continuing outside the fort limit as a cropmark following a natural scarp or contour to NW, then down the hillside to W.
The interior is level but the surface is uneven, stony and obscured by overgrowth including a dense thicket of blackthorn bushes in the SE quadrant. Slightly W of centre are two parallel linear stone walls (L c. 9m; Wth c. 1m; long axis N-S), 1.4m apart. A cross-wall (long axis NW-SE) may connect them at the S. Close to the fort wall at W is a sunken linear trench (L c. 5m; Wth 0.5m; D 0.4m). 
At the base of the cliff, 12-15m N of the cliff-face is a wall (Wth 1m; H 1.7m on N side), roughly constructed of boulders, which extends for 25m E-W linking two rock outcrops that project from the E and W ends of the cliff. The space between the cliff and the wall appears to be a natural terrace and, beneath dense overgrowth, is covered in stones and boulders. There is a holy well (SL026-001003-), the Hawke's Well, between the inner and outer fort walls on the E side. A possible souterrain (SL026-001007-) lies in the W half.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On the ESE-facing slope of Tullaghan Hill, between the inner and outer enclosing walls of the cliff-edge fort (SL026-001001-) and close to the inner wall. An algae-covered pool (D 0.4m) filling an oval hollow (0.8m NW-SE; 0.6m NE-SW) cut into the hill-slope and enclosed by a roughly constructed U-shaped wall open to SE. The wall is little more than a jumble of stones and forms a substantial heap (Wth 1.5m; int. H 1.7m to the base of the well; ext. H 0.5m) on the upslope side N-NW but tapers off on either side of the pool towards the opening (Wth 0.5m) at SE. A simple modern wooden cross has been erected on top of the wall. This well is said to be one of the Mirabilia Hiberniae, or wonders of Ireland and is mentioned in 1185-6 by Giraldus Cambrensis as being 'in Connacht on the top of a high mountain and some distance from the sea, which in any one day ebbs and overflows three times, imitating the ebbing and flowing of the sea (O'Meara 1951, 44-5). O'Rorke (1878, 226-228) noted that 'pilgrimages to the well have ceased' though he also noted that there were still strong traditions associated with it, including the belief that the well sprang up at the prayer of St Patrick, that its water ebbed and flowed with the tide (the sea is c. 2km to N on the other side of the Ox Mountains) and that it was haunted by two trout. Kilgannon (1926, 276-7) writing over fifty years later noted a small crucifix and a 'little tin porringer...for the convenience of persons wishing to drink or sample the water'. In 1836 it was noted that the well was dedicated to St Patrick (OSL, 344-6). A large stone standing on end, and known locally as an 'altar' (SL026-001005-) was recorded by O'Rorke (1878, 226) 'fourteen feet [4.3m] west of the well' but this can no longer be located. O'Rorke (ibid.) also recorded a possible penitential cairn (SL026-001004-) close to the well.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On a level expanse of blanket bog on a plateau in the Ox Mountains, overlooked to SE by Tullaghan Hill. A semicircular flat area (6m N-S; 7.5m E-W) defined S-N by an arc of a heather-covered wall (Wth 3.6m; H 0.5-0.8m), consisting of loose stones, with broadly slumped sides. There are no visible remains of any enclosing element N-S. There is a break (Wth 2m) in the S 'arm' of the arc. The interior is only marginally drier than the surrounding boggy ground.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In level elevated pasture; the ground falls away gradually to N giving extensive views over broad expanses of low-lying pasture and bog. A slightly raised subrectangular area (42m NNE-SSW; 23m WNW-ESE) defined on the N, E and the N half of the W side by a low bank of earth and stone (Wth 2m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.75m) and elsewhere by a scarp (H 1.4m). A low kerb of stones defines the inner edge of the bank on the N side. On the S half of the E side, the bank expands to a broadly slumped irregular rise (Wth 3.4m) from which stones protrude randomly, possibly the result of recent disturbance. The N half of the enclosure has linear sides and rounded corners while the S half is more generally curving. There is a slight indentation of the scarp midway along the W side and of the bank midway along the E side. The interior is level and covered in rushes. The S half is slightly higher, the change in level being marked slightly N of centre, by a slight dip or depression (Wth c. 3m) extending across the interior. The indentation of the enclosing element and the change in the level of the interior suggest that the S half of this enclosure may have been originally circular and that the more linear N half may have been an addition. Traces of a linear field drain extend to S from the SE corner.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating poorly drained pasture, above a stream. The remains of a rectangular tower (int.: 9.4m N-S; 5.5m E-W) now standing to two storeys, though originally higher, but missing most of its E and S walls; it has been in this condition since at least the late 18th century (Grose 1791, vol. 1, 58-9). The walls are built of uncoursed limestone blocks set in a lime mortar, and have a prominent base batter. Much of the outer face of the tower is covered by ivy. At ground-floor level there is a blocked-up window embrasure in both the N and W walls; the entrance doorway does not survive. Above this is an entresol with a blocked-up window in its N wall. Also at this level is a garderobe chamber in the SW corner of the tower; this is approached by a mural stairs in the S wall rising from ground level but the lower part of the stairs does not survive. Over the entresol was a vault springing from the W wall but only the skewbacks have survived. The first-floor chamber is entered via a lintelled door at the W end of its S wall; this stands at the head of a mural stairs rising through the S wall. There are remains of central window embrasures in the S, W and N walls, at first-floor level. Also at this level is a garderobe chamber in the SW corner of the tower. Due to a build-up of fallen masonry and the fall in ground level, there is a scarped edge (H c. 1m) immediately outside the base of the E wall. Outside this is a sunken area which appears to be the result of surface quarrying for limestone; there is also a spring here. This castle was built by the O'Haras (Grose 1791, vol. 1, 58-9; McParlan 1802, 92-3; O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 627-8).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In damp low-lying pasture, c. 150m S of the Owenbeg River and incorporated into a field boundary. A D-shaped well (0.8m NW-SE; 0.8m NE-SW; D 0.4m) recessed into rising ground SE-NW and faced with stone (H 1.5m). A flat concrete slab, on which the visitor stands, defines the straight side. Outside the slab, a NW-SE mortared stone wall intersects with a curving wall to completely enclose the well. A series of steps built into this wall allows access to the well. Another holy well (SL026-015----) dedicated to St Fechin is c. 1.6km to E in Kilnamanagh townland. St Fechin's church and bed (SL026-011001-; SL026-011002-) are c. 200m to S and St Fechin's stone (SL026-012002-) is c. 350m to E. There are four other wells associated with St Fechin in the vicinity (SL026-015----; SL026-086----; SL026-151----; SL033-062----).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, bordered on the SE side by a road. A roughly trapezoidal-shaped area (18.5m E-W; 10.5m N-S at W end, 4.7m at E end) defined by a scarp (H 0.6m) except on the SE side where it is fringed by the roadside field boundary. The entire platform is grass-covered and though stones protrude randomly from the scarp, no masonry or wall structure is apparent. Its surface is generally level but uneven. On the N side, the scarp drops 0.4m down to a low triangular terrace (5.5m N-S; c. 4-5m E-W), the N corner of which incorporates a sod-covered cairn of loose stones (diam. c. 3m; H 1.2m). Embedded in the terrace is a saint's stone known as 'St Fechin's Bed' (SL026-011002-). There is a holy well (SL026-010----) c. 200m to the N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Embedded in a low terrace abutting the W end of the N side of the platform known as St Fechin's church (SL026-011001-). A prostrate limestone slab (min. dims. 2m E-W; 1.2m N-S) is largely covered by sod. Roughly in the centre of its flat upper surface is an elongated solution fissure (c. 1m N-S; 0.25m E-W; D 0.35m). According to local tradition, the stone could cure backache. The patient had to lie flat with the spine aligned along the central fissure. St Fechin's holy well (SL026-010----) is c. 200m to N and another saint's stone, St Fechin's Stone (SL026-012002-), is c. 400m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, in the NW corner of a field, on a slight rise and c. 100m S of the Owenbeg River. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an oval enclosure. Now levelled; the remains consist of an oval area (c. 30m NW-SE; 23m NE-SW), clipped at NW and N by field boundaries and defined by a degraded scarp (H 1m) extending for c. 15m N-ESE in a gentle curve, coinciding with a low natural break in slope. Occasional stones protrude from the sod along the line of the scarp. The scarp peters out at SE but a barely discernible undulation continues SE-SW, truncated at SW by a linear field boundary on a N-S axis. Where the field boundary (L 12m; Wth 2.5-3m; H on E side 0.8m; H on W side 0.8m) overlies the presumed line of the enclosure W-NW, it has a broad slumped W face and is noticeably stonier and more substantial than elsewhere. St Fechin's Stone (SL026-012002-) lies c. 30m to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Incorporated into a N-S field fence in an area of low-lying pasture to S of the Owenbeg River. A limestone slab (L c. 2.2m; T 1m at W end; 0.12m at E end; H c. 1m), with a rough convoluted moss-covered surface, is set on end in the ground. The long axis of the stone is perpendicular to the line of the fence and the stone protrudes from both the W and E faces of the fence. The stone is wedge-shaped in plan, with the broad W end gradually tapering to a narrow sharp-edged E end. The stone protrudes by c. 0.2-0.3m from the W side of the fence and 1.4m from the E side. A perforation (Wth 0.13m; max. H 0.35m) through the thickness of the stone occurs at the base of the stone close to the E face of the field fence. Due to overgrowth on the fence and the position of the perforation it is difficult to examine but it appears to be a natural solution hole, rather irregular and decreasing in size from S to N. St Fechin's well (SL026-010----) is c. 350m to W and St Fechin's church and bed (SL026-011001- and SL026-011002-) are c. 400m to SW. An enclosure (SL026-012001) lies c. 30m to N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a flat expanse of wet boggy ground bordering the NE side of the Owenbeg River. A shallow circular stone-lined pool (diam. 1m; D 0.4m), the base of which is stone flagged. The top of the stone lining forms a low ledge (Wth 0.4m) at a height of c. 0.3m above the water, on which the visitor can stand, and is in turn enclosed by a mortared roughly coursed stone wall (Wth 0.3-0.4m; H 1m) with vertical stone coping. The wall (relatively modern in appearance) incorporates a stile-like arrangement of stones allowing easy access to the well and encloses an area of 2m in diameter. The water appears oily and murky and is covered with algae. The well is dedicated to St Fechin. There is a church (SL026-016----) c. 350m to NE. There are four other wells associated with St Fechin in the vicinity (SL026-010----; SL026-086----; SL026-151----; SL033-062----).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating rocky pasture, in the immediate vicinity of the partially deserted settlement cluster of Kilnamonagh. According to McParlan (1802, 108) this is the site of an 'ancient abbey' founded by St Fechin and also a 'parish church'; Gwynn and Hadcock (1970, 183) state that 'a small cell' of the Augustinian monastery of Ballysadare (SL020-108----) was founded here shortly after AD 1140 but it does not appear to have survived into the 15th century. According to local tradition, there was an associated graveyard (SL026-016001-). Test trenching, c. 110m NE of the church site, uncovered a pit containing metal slag but no evidence of a monastic enclosure (M. A. Timoney 2001a, 303). St Fechin's well (SL026-015----) is c. 350m to SW. A rectangular enclosure (SL026-017----) lies c. 130m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, straddling the base of a N-facing slope overlooking an expanse of damp pasture to N. A roughly circular level area (33.5m NW-SE; 31m NE-SW) enclosed by an earthen bank with an external fosse and the remnant of an outer bank. The rath is crossed N of centre by a WNW-ESE road, flanked by field boundaries. To S of the road the interior is defined SE-WNW by a substantial earthen bank (Wth 5m; int. H 1m; ext. H 1.4m) with an external fosse (Wth c. 5m, base 2.3m; D 0.9m). The bank is somewhat degraded and flattened on top, broadly slumped internally and obscured in parts by gorse and hawthorn bushes. The fosse is cut into rising ground and marked by a growth of rushes and partially infilled with field clearance debris at SE and SW. A break (Wth 3.2m) in the bank at SSW with a causeway across the fosse appears to be a recent feature. Breaks (Wth 2-3m) in the bank were also noted at SE and WNW at the intersection with the field boundary, bordering the road. To N of the road the interior is enclosed by a degraded earthen bank with a low internal rim (Wth 3m; int. H 0.1m; ext. H 1.5m), a shallow fosse (Wth 3m), marked by rushes, and a gapped, degraded outer bank (Wth 2.5-3m; int. H 0.65m; ext. H 0.45m).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

According to O'Rorke (1878, 221-2; 396-8), when trees were being planted here c. 1840, 'extensive brick foundations' were dug up and the ground was levelled off; there are brickworks 2km to the WNW in Tullaghan. These foundations were thought to be the remains of a church associated with St Lassara, though it is very unlikely that such a church would have had brick foundations. O'Rorke (ibid., 397) associates this church with St Anne's Well (SL026-151----). There are no visible remains of a church in the area.

source_data.original_text:
Annagh More (Annaghmore) was the principal seat of the O'Haras in the later medieval period, though the 'auncient house' which stood there was described as 'being demolished' in 1684 (Ó Muraíle 2002, 240). The O'Haras of Annaghmore were the only family of Gaelic origin in Sligo to survive as landowners through the 17th century (O'Dowd 1991, 138; Bartlett 1982). Little is known about the house which replaced the 'auncient house', but in c. 1820 a new house was built and this was enlarged c. 1860-70 by C. W. O'Hara to the design of James Franklin Fuller (Bence-Jones 1988, 4). According to the present owner of this house, its predecessor lay a short distance to the NW where there is now no trace of it. The 1838 OS 6-inch map shows the present house at the NE end of a long linear avenue (SL026-176----). This avenue consists of a central earthen platform (Wth c. 6m) flanked by a wide drain (D 0.4m) with an outer earthen bank (Wth c. 3m; ext. H c. 1m). There is a similar avenue at Ballindoon House (SL034-213----) and both are probably late 17th/early 18th-century in date. Ardcree Bridge (SL026-172----) is at the S end of the demesne. A bullaun stone (SL026-049001-) is situated opposite the front door of the present house.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On level elevated ground, in a large open pasture field bordered by forestry plantation to the W, N and NE. A very slightly raised subcircular area (34m NW-SE; c. 36m NE-SW) defined by a slight scarp (H c. 0.6m) that slumps into a shallow external fosse (Wth c. 3m; D 0.3m). The scarp is very poorly defined. The fosse survives as a shallow depression, barely discernible in parts to SW and N-NE. At NNW a small quarry pit (Wth 6m) cuts across the line of the fosse. The interior is crossed on a NW-SE axis by four parallel, clearly defined, linear banks (Wth 3-3.6m, H 0.5m) set c. 3m apart. They occupy most of the available interior space and appear to represent ridge and furrow cultivation, levelled traces of which can also be seen in the surrounding field. Remnants of linear field boundaries and part of a levelled rectilinear field system that postdate the rath, clip the outer edge of the fosse at SE and SW. There is another rath (SL026-044----) visible on the top of the hill to NW. O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 66-7) suggests that a fort, known locally as 'Ardcree-fort' and within a thousand yards of Ardcree bridge, was possibly the site of the 'castle of Rath-Ard-creeve' which was burned by Hugh O'Connor in 1265. It is not certain to which of the three forts (SL026-088----; SL026-089----) in the townland O'Rorke was referring.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Prominently sited on the summit of a steep-sided hill with excellent views. An oval platform (30.7m E-W; 23.5m N-S) defined by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank (Wth 5.7m; int. H 0.9m; ext. H 1.8m) has a high broadly sloping external face and a low stony internal lip. Some of the stone protruding from the inner edge of the bank may be remains of kerbing or facing. The fosse (Wth 3-4m) and outer bank (Wth 3.5m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1.2m) are evident WNW-SW, but there is considerable evidence for recent disturbance and modification. Both appear to have been truncated WSW-WNW by the construction of a water reservoir immediately adjacent to the rath. Areas of quarrying occur within the fosse at NE and SE and more extensively SW-W. The outer bank coincides with the natural break of slope N-S. It is levelled WNW-NE to a broad low flat-topped rise (Wth 8m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.4m) defined on its outer edge by a hawthorn hedgerow. It appears as a compact bank of earth and stone (Wth 3-3.5m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.5-1.2m) ENE-SW, that has been modified to serve as a field boundary. The inner face of the outer bank S-W is greatly disturbed by quarrying. A possible entrance occurs at ESE where there is a slumped gap (Wth 1.4m) in the inner bank and a possible causeway across the fosse as well as a narrow break (Wth 1m), eroded by cattle, in the outer bank. A thicket of blackthorn bushes covers the interior and the outer bank is ringed with hawthorn.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In undulating pasture, crowning a prominent ridge with extensive views in all directions. This rath was described in 1992 (SMR (1989) file) as a circular raised area (int. diam. 14.5m; H c. 1m) enclosed by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse (Wth 4m). The inner bank was evident only as a slight lip (Wth 2.5m; int. H 0.2m) around the edge of the interior. The outer bank (Wth 2m; ext. H 0.8m) was evident only along the N arc. There was an entrance (Wth 4.5m) at SW with a causeway/ramp across the fosse. Field boundaries were noted immediately to the E and N. The rath was partially overgrown with bushes. A subsequent site inspection in 2002 found that the rath was engulfed in impenetrable overgrowth and the presence of a possible circular hut site, visible in an aerial photograph (OSAP, 6 4083-4) in the N half of the interior, could not be determined. The entire rath is within the NE corner of a large oblong field (c. 80m NE-SW; c. 45m NW-SE) defined by a substantial field boundary (ext. H 1.3m) with an external ditch (Wth 1.8m).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In level pasture, close to a break of slope. The most south-western of three conjoined raths (see SL026-120002- and SL026-120003-) in a NE-SW row. A slightly raised circular area (24m N-S; 25m E-W) enclosed S-N by an earthen bank (Wth 2.5m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 1.15m) with a well-defined external face and a low internal rim and by a low broadly sloping scarp (Wth 3.5m; H 0.55m) N-NE, petering out to a slight undulation E-S. The bank at N swings wide of the circuit of the enclosure and continues to NE intersecting with the bank of the adjoining rath (SL026-120002-) but this appears to be the result of a later modification of both. The interior has a very slight slope down to E. At N-NE the scarp slumps into a shallow fosse-like depression (Wth 2m) that separates this rath from the bank of the adjoining rath (SL026-120002-).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In level pasture, close to a break of slope. The middle of three conjoined raths (see SL026-120001- and SL026-120003-) in a NE-SW row. A slightly raised subcircular area (30.3m NNW-SSE; 24m E-W) defined S-N by an earthen bank (Wth 3.5m; int. H 0.6m; ext. H 1m), by a discrete section of bank at E and by a slight scarp E-S. The slightly sunken remnants of a NW-SE trackway truncates the NE arc of the rath. The trackway, bordered on the NE side by a field fence, also truncates the interface between this rath and the adjoining rath (SL026-120003-) immediately to NE. The interior is level with traces of ridge and furrow cultivation on a NW-SE axis.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the top of a steep slope down to the Owenmore River to NNE. A roughly wedge-shaped area (14m WNW-ESE at S; 38m WNW-ESE at N; 36.4m NNE-SSW) defined on the straight S and W sides by a bank (Wth 2m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.5m), by a scarp (H 1.35m; Wth slope 3.5m) in a shallow curving arc NNW-NE and on the straight E side by a bank, reduced to scarp at NE end. The scarp NNW-NE is built up to compensate for the natural fall of ground. Large stones protrude from the sod along the top of the scarp at NE. The interior is generally level but roughly in the centre there is a slight rise (diam. c. 10m). Just to N of this is a more pronounced roughly circular, sod-covered stony rise (5m E-W; 4m N-S; H 0.55m). The rath is indicated as an embanked circular area (diam. c. 32m) on the 1838 OS 6-inch map.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In the Owenmore River. This monument was listed in the SMR (1989) as ‘Weir’ and in the RMP (1995) as ‘Weir Site’. This is one of seven records for weirs (SL026-122----; SL026-126-----; SL026-130----; SL026-159-----; SL026-159001-; SL026-159002-; SL026-159003-) recorded in the SMR whose only source is noted as ‘Marked on estate map dated 1618’ (SMR file). It has not proved possible to identify this map. It is marked and named ‘Weir’ on the 1837 edition of the OS 6-inch map. It was not marked on the 1913 edition. On inspection in 1992 there were no visible remains of this weir though it is possible that residual elements survive on the river bed. Although the date of this weir is unknown the possibility that it pre-dates 1700 AD cannot be ruled out.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 18 October 2011

source_data.original_text:
On a very slight rise in an expanse of flat poorly drained pasture. The ground slopes down gently to E towards the Owenmore River. A slightly raised circular platform (23.8m NE-SW; c. 20m NW-SE) defined by a broadly sloping scarp (H 1.2m; Wth slope 4.7m) with traces of an internal lip. A shallow external fosse (Wth 4-5m), marked by soft wet ground and a dense growth of rushes, is evident all round while the outer bank (Wth c. 5m) survives SW-NW as a broad low rise. The outer edge of the fosse is poorly defined and S-SW merges imperceptibly with the very boggy surrounding ground. The top of the platform is level. A bowl-barrow (SL026-125----) lies c. 100m to ENE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On the N edge of Ballynacarrow village, in waste ground wedged between the realigned main road and a lay-by. This possible rath is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an embanked circular area (diam. c. 20m) and on the 1913 OS 6-inch map as a circular raised area truncated at E by a N-S field boundary. According to local information, the rath was partially levelled during the road realignment in the 1950s. Part of the S quadrant remains as a raised triangular area of waste ground but, due to overgrowth, it is very difficult to inspect. The area is defined SE-SW by a scarp (C c. 10m; H c. 0.8m). The NW side (L c. 20m) of the triangle is defined by the main road and the E side by a field boundary.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rocky upland pasture, on a S-facing slope of the Ox Mountains. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as circular enclosure (diam. c. 20m). Indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as a semicircular area, represented by a solid line S-NW, abutting the W side of a NW-SE field boundary. The remains consist of a curving field boundary wall at the W end of a rectangular field. The remainder of the enclosure is not visible at ground level. A small D-shaped field is indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map immediately to NW in the adjoining field. This survives as an arc W-NNW formed by a derelict stone-faced scarp cut into the upslope and enclosing the SE corner (23m x 14m) of a field. A cashel (SL031-017----) lies c. 50m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough upland pasture, on a S-facing slope of the Ox Mountains and adjacent to a cashel (SL031-017----). A low heather and scrub-covered rise (L c. 15m), from which an occasional stone protrudes, extends from the cashel wall at SE. From there a densely overgrown stone-faced scarp (H 1m) extends eastwards along a natural break in slope for c. 40m until it abuts a N-S property boundary wall. Due to a forest plantation it was not possible to determine if the scarp extends further to the E. Remnants of an E-W wall can also be traced c. 20m downslope to S. A line of tall ferns, extending a short distance to SW from the cashel wall at W, may also indicate the remains of a wall. Immediately to W of the cashel is a large rectangular field which is indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Another forest drain lies immediately to N and trees have also been planted in the fosse. A mound barrow (SL031-018001-) lies immediately to N.

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture and forestry, on the S slopes of the Ox Mountains. A roughly circular area (24.5m N-S; 27m E-W) terraced into the hillslope at N and defined by a scarp NE-SW. The scarp is revetted NE-S by a drystone wall (H 1.8m) and in places by rock outcrop. Generally the interior slopes gently down to S and is c. 1m below external ground level along the N edge. Two flat areas have been created in the interior: one, a possible house (6m x 6m) (SL031-019002-) in the N half is defined by a scarp revetted with stones, the other, a possible hut site (2.7m x 5m) (SL031-019003-)is located immediately to S and is defined on the W side by a row of stones. Cultivation ridges cross the interior on a N-S axis. Rock outcrops were noted in the NW, NE and SE quadrants. Coniferous trees have been planted along the W perimeter. A N-S field boundary crosses the W half of the interior.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

There are no visible remains of the E half of the rath; farm buildings now occupy this area.

source_data.original_text:
On a platform of rocky pasture on a S-facing slope above the basin of the River Moy. The tomb is in a low mound of irregular outline (17m E-W; 8.5m N-S). A large rock at the E end of the mound seems to be an outcrop. An orthostat at the E end of the structure formed part of the S side of the entrance passage to the remains of a full court (L c. 6.5m) six stones of the N arm of which remain, one at the outer and five at the inner end. Two jambs mark the entrance to a chamber (L 3.8m; Wth 1.7m at its inner end) represented by three sidestones to the N and one to the S. There is a buttress-stone outside the inner of the three stones at the N and another outside the southern example. A pair of segmenting jambs at the inner end of the extant chamber shows that further gallery structure has been lost. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 59-60, no. 95)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough grazing, on a terrace on the lower S slopes of the Ox Mountains. All that survives of this castle are the sod-covered foundations (Wth c. 4m; H c. 1.75m) of an L-shaped structure (7.5m E-W; 14m N-S to W; 8.6m N-S to E) conjoined on its N side with three contiguous rectangular structures (c. 4.5m E-W; respectively 6.5m, 3.1m and 4.5m N-S). A short run of exterior wall-facing is exposed at the E end of the N side of the L-shaped structure, consisting of cut blocks of stone closely fitted together. Named 'Castle Carragh' on the 1838 OS 6-inch map this is the remains of an O'Hara castle (O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 14) which was already in ruins by 1636 (Wood-Martin 1882, 105, n. 1).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On rocky pasture at the edge of a plateau below the slopes of the Ox Mountains and commanding an extensive outlook to the S. A gallery (L 4.8m; Wth 1.6-2.6m) is preceded at the E by two stones representing the S arm of a court. There are three prostrate stones immediately N of the outer of the two courtstones. Just E of these there is a small limekiln (SL031-040001-) in a field fence that extends N-S about 5m in front of the gallery. Two jambs mark the entrance to the gallery and another pair divide it into two chambers. The gallery sides, each of five orthostats, and the backstone are in place. Just outside the N side of the gallery there is a large prostrate slab. There are slight traces of mound at the site most obviously to the N of the gallery. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 60, no. 96)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Not listed in either the SMR (1989) or RMP (1995). In upland rocky pasture, immediately SSW of a court tomb (SL031-040----) and built against the natural scarp that forms the S edge of the terrace on which the court tomb is sited. A small ruined and roofless circular, stone-built structure (int. diam. 1.5m) that is built into the natural slope. The interior is defined N-NW by a drystone wall (H 0.65m; T 0.9m) and NW-N, where recessed into the slope, by a stone-faced scarp (H 0.9m). A possible opening at E is obscured by rubble. This is probably post-1700 AD in date.

source_data.original_text:
In the NE quadrant of a circular enclosure (SL031-043001-). A roughly triangular burial ground (c. 22m N-S; c. 25m E-W) defined N-ENE by a low curving bank (Wth 1.5m; H 0.4m) which is also part of the enclosing element of the circular enclosure, defined on the straight W side mainly by the foundations of a drystone wall (Wth 1.1m) with an earthen bank (Wth 2.5m; H 0.5m) at the N end, and defined on the straight S side by a scarp (H 1.8m). The entrance (Wth c. 3m) is at NE. Along the N arc the burial ground is cut into the hillslope and overlooked by a scarp (H 0.8-1.2m). The interior slopes down to S. While the N half contains many uninscribed grave-markers, there are very few in the S half. According to local information, the graveyard was used as a burial ground for unbaptized children. Named 'Grave Yard' on the 1838 OS 6-inch map and indicated as a roughly triangular area (c. 40m NE-SW; c. 40m NW SE) abutting the now levelled field boundary along the SW side. Noted by Wood-Martin (1887-8, 275), as an unfenced burial ground 'wherein children and strangers are still buried' and 'until very lately even adults of the neighbourhood were laid in it'. There is a rath (SL031-044001-) c. 50m to NNE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the S-facing slope of a ridge in the foothills of the Ox Mountains. A raised circular area (41m N-S) defined by a curving hedgerow and road N-SE, by a scarp (H 1.2m) SE-NW and by a flat-topped earthen bank (Wth 2.5m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.4m) NW-N. source_data.original_text:
On top of a low narrow ridge of undulating elevated ground flanked by flat valleys of damp pasture and bog; just N of the centre of the older part of Kilvarnet graveyard (SL032-034002-) and within a possible ecclesiastical enclosure (SL032-034003-). The ruin of a rectangular church (int. 10.9m E-W; 5.95m N-S) built of uncoursed limestone in a lime mortar. Much of the N wall has fallen as has the top half of the E gable and the point of the W gable. It is entered through a very ruinous doorway, W of the centre, in the S wall. The interior is lit by two windows in the E gable, a central window high up on the W gable, and a window near the E end of the S wall. Only the lower portions of the E windows survive. These are identical embrasures, set side by side, each with a single light which has a right-angle rebate on its external edge. There is a similar rebate on the light in the W window (missing one of its jambstones) which has a pointed arch; the embrasure itself is covered by a rounded arch. There is a similar window embrasure in the S wall, which is missing the head and the E jamb of the light. Between the latter window and the SE corner is a recess (Wth 0.5m; H 0.85m) covered by a rounded arch which was probably a piscina though its basin is missing. On the line of the N wall is a pile of loose stones. The interior is covered by scrub overgrowth. Most of the E end is occupied by two 20th-century grave-plots, and there are two 19th-century headstones just W of the centre. This is the ruin of the medieval parish church of Kilvarnet which, according to Jordan (1996, 1) was founded by the O'Hara family of Annaghmore. It has been identified as the parish church recorded in the Papal taxation lists of 1302-06 where the Knights Templars are given as rectors (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 331).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on the summit of a knoll. A square platform (16.5m N-S; c. 16.5m E-W) with a smaller subrectangular enclosure or annexe (c.12.5m E-W; 10.3m N-S) appended to its E side. The square platform is defined on the S and W sides and at the NW corner by a scarp (H 1m) with a slight internal lip (H 0.1-0.2m). On the N side the enclosing element consists of a very degraded gapped sod-covered stony rise (Wth c. 1-1.2m; H 0.2m). On the E side the platform is poorly defined by a low irregular rise. Immediately outside the N bank the ground is uneven and disturbed in appearance with one shallow subrectangular depression (c. 4m E-W). Outside the scarp at S is a low terrace (Wth 3.4m; ext. H 0.2m). A shallow fosse exists at the base of the scarp on the W side. The interior is level and raised on the S and W sides to compensate for the hillslope. Shallow depressions were noted in the NW (diam. c. 2m) and SE (diam. c. 4m) quadrants of the interior. The junction between the annexe and the moated site is an area of disturbed and uneven ground. The interior of the annexe slopes down to E with the natural slope of ground and is enclosed on the N side by an earthen bank (Wth 1.8m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.6m) with a break (Wth 5m) at the W end. The N side of the annexe is in line with the N side of the main enclosure. The E side is defined by a scarp (H 0.6m). A large now overgrown quarry has cut into the S side of the annexe making it impossible to determine if the annexe once extended to the full width of the moated site.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

raw_items.raw_text: mid-15th-century Franciscan Third Order Regular foundation
The style of the church is consistent with a mid-15th-century date
the tower and transept are not later than the 16th century
An 18th-century burial vault of the O'Hara family

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, straddling a N-S rise; in the NW quadrant of a graveyard (SL032-047002-). A Franciscan foundation known locally as 'Court Abbey', the remains of which consist of a rectangular church with a central tower and a rectangular transept on its S side (see plan Harbison 2002, 97). Built of roughly coursed limestone in a lime mortar, except for the tower which is faced with limestone ashlar. The nave and chancel are of one phase but the tower and transept are later insertions. The interior of the church contains many 19th- and 20th-century burials. The chancel (surviving for c. 10m E-W; int. 6.5m N-S; ) is missing its E end; a slight break in slope, 12.3m from the tower, marks the line of the E wall; an illustration by Grose (1791, vol. 1, 52) shows the stump of it in this position. An 18th-century burial vault of the O'Hara family is set into the NW corner. The nave (int. 12m E-W; 6.5m N-S) walls stand to full height but are masked by ivy. In the centre of the W wall is a doorway, missing its surround. On its N side, on the internal wall-face, is a damaged stoup with a semicircular bowl. Near the W end of the S wall is another doorway. The rectangular tower (4.2m E-W; 6.5m N-S) occupies the full width of the church, between the nave and chancel. It rises from four rectangular piers, butted against the side-walls of the church. These form two identical bluntly pointed arched openings facing respectively into the nave and chancel; both arches have a moulded soffit rib. There is a doorway and window in the S wall of the church, between the piers. At approximately the level of the side-walls of the latter, the tower has a segmental wicker-centred vault (axis N-S) terminated at either end by a dressed limestone segmental arch. As the tower rises it narrows to approximately half the width of the church. On the W and E faces the flashing course for the apex of the church roof is evident. Below this on the W side is a doorway that must have accessed a wooden gallery overlooking the nave. In the same position on the E side is a small rectangular opening which probably gave access to an attic over the chancel. Above the roof level of the church, two string courses encircle the tower; the NE corner is missing above the level of the upper string course. At its uppermost level, on the W face, is a central window with a single ogee-headed light (much of the surround is missing). On the S face is a central window with a mullion and transom division and two ogee-headed lights with recessed spandrels and a hood-moulding. The battlements which once crowned the tower are missing but water-spouts draining the wall-walk are evident. An 18th-century plan (Harbison 2002, 97) shows a spiral stairs between the SE corner of the tower and the E wall of the transept but this is completely blocked up.
The transept (int. 10.9m N-S; 6.75m E-W) is built against the S wall of the church and a wide archway (Wth 3.95m) gives access to it from the nave. This arch is similar to those in the tower but rises from pillared imposts with plainly moulded capitals (the bases of the imposts are under ground level). The W wall of the transept is blank. In the centre of the S gable is a damaged ivy-clad window; the light is pointed and, judging by the stumps on the sill and jambs, had plain switchline tracery. The E wall has two similar side-altar recesses (Wth 3m). The recesses are square-set and then splayed inwards towards a central window light (most of both surrounds are missing); a tall rounded arch covers both embrasures. On the internal corner of both recesses, on the S side, are square recesses which are covered by quarter-domes. Each has a shallow basin with a drainage hole indicating that these are piscinae (Leask 1960, vol. 3, 181). Between the two side-altars recesses is a small rectangular mural chamber, the round-arched doorway of which is almost completely blocked by a late 18th-century headstone. Flanking this doorway are two flat projecting stones, at slightly different heights. Beneath the ivy cover on the areas of the W wall and the side-altars are faint traces of original paint on plaster rendering, which were noted by Grose (1797, vol. 1, 52). 
This was a mid-15th-century Franciscan Third Order Regular foundation, at which 'building had already begun in 1454' (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 270); unusually it was probably a joint community of both 'brothers and sisters' (Ó Clabaigh 2002, 93). A late 16th-century inquisition describes it as consisting of 'a thatched church, with cemetery, dormitory and two other thatched houses' (ibid.). The style of the church is consistent with a mid-15th-century date, whilst the tower and transept are not later than the 16th century. A field system (SL032-047004-) is evident to the E and S. The foundation at Kilcummin (SL031-006001-), c. 5km to the W, was described by Gwynn and Hadcock (1970, 271) as 'a small dependency' of Court Abbey. A rath (SL032-047003-) lies c. 20m to the ESE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

The oldest portion of the graveyard is rectangular (c. 50m E-W; c. 30m N-S) and contains the ruin of Court Abbey (SL032-047001-), in the NW corner. It was extended to the N and S in the 19th and 20th centuries and contains many headstones from these periods. The earliest headstone noted was dated 1789 and is located inside the abbey. An 18th-century burial vault of the O'Hara family is set into the NW corner of the chancel.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).
