source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a low N-S ridge bounded on the E and W sides by two streams. At least eleven small rectangular fields are evident to E and S of Abbey Court friary (SL032-047001-) and adjacent to a rath (SL032-047003-). The smallest field measures 12m x 21m while the largest measures 43m x 52m. The field boundaries consist of either low earthen banks (Wth 2-3m), sometimes with silted-up fosses, or scarps (H 0.1-0.4m). These fields may be the remains of gardens and paddocks associated with the abbey. There is a similar field system (SL032-188004-) associated with the ecclesiastical remains at Achonry (SL032-188001-), c. 3.5km to S.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the S-facing slope of a ridge. An oval area (41m N-S; 32.5m E-W) enclosed by an inner earthen bank, a dry flat-bottomed intervening fosse (Wth 6m) and an outer drystone wall. The inner bank (Wth 4.5m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 1.7m) is revetted in parts along the inner face with large boulders especially on its NE side. The grass-covered foundations of a drystone wall (Wth 2m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.2m) are evident around the edge of the fosse. There is an entrance (Wth 2m) at E through both banks, revetted on both sides by stones. The S portion of the interior is raised and the N portion is cut into the upslope to compensate for the hillslope. However, the interior retains a slope down to S. There is a souterrain (SL032-056002-) in the W half of the interior and a possible hut site (SL032-056003-) in the E half.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on top of a low rise. A roughly circular area (33m N-S; 30.5m E-W) enclosed by a flat-topped earthen inner bank (Wth 6m; int. H 0.6m; ext. H 3m), with a dry flat-bottomed intervening fosse (Wth 10.3m) and a flat-topped earthen outer bank (Wth 5.6m int. H 2.2m). There is a causewayed entrance at E, revetted by large stones on the N side where it cuts through the inner bank. The land to N and S of the rath has been quarried. A field boundary respects the rath to E and SE. There is a possible souterrain (SL032-064002-) in the W portion of the interior. According to O'Rorke (1878, 305), Mass was said 'on or near the rath of Fal-na-sugan' and 'a hedge-school' was taught on weekdays in the ditch of the rath. There are three other raths (SL032-037----; SL032-038----, SL032-039001-) in this townland and it is not known which was being referred to by O'Rorke.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a gentle SE-facing slope. A raised circular area (37m N-S) defined by an earthen bank with an external fosse. The bank (Wth 2.6m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 1m) is reduced on top to a low internal rim but has a pronounced external scarp. Occasional stones protrude randomly along the top of the bank. A section of the bank along the SW arc is higher and more substantial where it is incorporated into the line of a property fence. The shallow external fosse (Wth 3-3.5m) survives all round except to SW where it is truncated by a field boundary. A section of the fosse at N is infilled with fieldstones. There is a gap (Wth 1m) in the bank at NE with a corresponding causeway-like infilled section of the fosse (Wth 3-3.5m). The interior slopes very gently down to SE. In the centre there is a low sod-covered circular rise (diam. 7.9m NW-SE; 8.6m NE-SW; H 0.35-4m at NW; 0.6m at SE). The remains of NE-SW cultivation ridges cross the interior and are also evident on a NW-SE axis in the surrounding field to NE. There is a souterrain (SL032-073002-) in the NW quadrant.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on an E-facing slope. A raised rectangular area (15.8m NNE-SSW; 14m WNW-ESE) defined by a low scarp (H 0.4m at WNW; H 0.6m at ESE). The platform is built up on the ESE side to compensate for the natural slope but the interior retains a slight slope down to ESE. The scarp has an almost vertical external face with a hint of an internal lip in parts on the ESE and NNE sides. An infilled field drain (Wth 1m; D c. 0.2m), with the remains of a field boundary on its outer edge, is evident at the base of the scarp on the NNE side and extends to E and W. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as a small circular enclosure (diam. c. 15m).

In low-lying marshy ground, with a stream to N and E. There are a number of earthworks in close proximity consisting of a rectangular platform (10.7m NE-SW; 7m NW-SE; H 0.2m above ground level) enclosed by a fosse (Wth 2m; D 0.4m) and 8m to the E a rectangular depression (7.4m N-S; 6m E-W; D 1.5m) with a linear fosse extending N from it. source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified as 'Earthworks(s)' and 'Mill Race' respectively. In undulating pasture, on a gentle NE-facing slope near the SW bank of a stream. The foundations of a wedge-shaped structure (16m NE-SW; 10m SE-NW at NE end; 6m at SW end) are evident as low grass-covered earth and stone banks (Wth 1.8m; ext. H 1.1m; int. H 0.9m). A silted up millrace (Wth 1.8m; D 0.5m) can be traced for c. 300m to NW. The millrace runs around the SW end of the mill curving around a central low island (4m x 3m) at the S corner and then NE along the SE side of the mill. The tailrace runs NE for a short distance where it re-enters the small stream. Streamstown House (SL032-085----) is c. 100m to S. This is probably post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 14 December 2011

source_data.original_text:
In gently undulating pasture, on the S side of a stream. The remains of a rectangular house (ext: 13.29m NE-SW; 6.18m NW-SE) of which only the SW gable now stands above basement level. This shows the house had two storeys with an attic and a basement. It is of random rubble limestone construction (wall T 0.64m). The gable survives to full height, with very short returns (L c. 2m) of the NW and SE sidewalls. There is a wide internally projecting (Wth 4.9m) chimney stack rising the full height of the gable, narrowing above roof-level to a plain rectangular stack. At each floor level is a pair of brick-arched fireplaces. Also at each level is a window ope either side of the stack. The basement wall (ext: 13.29m NE-SW) on the SE side survives and has three blocked window opes. The foundations of the NW wall are evident. The interior is filled with mounds of grass-covered rubble and the NE end is quarried out. The walls of a three-storey lean-to structure stand immediately outside the SW gable. The fragmentary remains of farm buildings and the foundations of a circular structure (int. diam. 2m) lie immediately to the NE. A wide causeway bridge (Wth 6m), with a small stone arch, crosses the stream a short distance to the NE. There is also a narrow segmental-arched footbridge (Wth 0.85m) upstream to NW. According to local information, the house is known as 'Streamstown Castle'. It is shown as an inhabited house, named 'Streamstown Ho.' and surrounded by a small demesne, on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. The surviving remains are late-17th/early-18th century in appearance. A rath (SL032-086----) lies c. 90m to SSE and the site of a mill (SL032-084----) c. 100m to N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On an E-facing slope. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an embanked circular area (diam. c. 40m), covered with deciduous trees. The remains consist of a D-shaped raised area (dims. 25m E-W), with a straight E side (L 36m N-S), defined by a scarp (max. H 1.9m) all round with a dry external fosse (Wth 9m; max. The interior slopes gently down to E; a NE-SW field boundary crosses the N half of the interior. Outside and parallel to the scarp along the E arc is a disused stone wall that appears to be on the line of an avenue (indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map) to Streamstown House (SL032-085----) c. 90m to NNW.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a rise, with the ground falling steeply from the edge of the rath at NW to Loughanlea. A raised circular area (46m N-S) enclosed by a flat-topped inner earthen bank (Wth 8.3m; int. H 1.2m; ext. H 3.6m). A dry flat-bottomed intervening fosse (Wth 8.5m) is evident SSE-SE. A flat-topped outer earthen bank (Wth 3.6m; int. H 1.2m; ext. H 0.2m) is evident SSE-NE. The inner bank, which appears to contain numerous stones, is quarried into along the W arc. There is an entrance (Wth 1.8m) through the inner bank at SE which is partly revetted by stones. There is a souterrain (SL032-108002-) in the W portion of the interior and a hut site (SL032-108003-) in the NE quadrant. Between 30 and 60m away from the edge of the outer bank along the W, S and E arcs is a curving scarp (H 0.6-2m) on the lower slope of a rise. This scarp is cut by another rath (SL032-109----) c. 50m to SSE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On flat dry pasture, above bogland to S. A raised circular area (21m N-S) defined by an inner flat-topped earthen bank (Wth 2m; int. H 1m; ext. H 2.9m) SW-SSE and by a scarp (H 1.3m) elsewhere. An external flat-bottomed dry fosse (Wth 8.5m) is evident SSE-ENE. A low earthen bank (Wth 2m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 0.3m) follows the outer edge of the fosse SSW-NW. Large stones are incorporated into the inner earthen bank. The entrance (Wth c. 1.8m) is at E, revetted on its S side by large boulders. The interior slopes down to S. A NNW-SSE field boundary crosses the E half of the interior. The W two-thirds of the rath are under grass while the E third, to E of the field boundary, is overgrown with bushes and has coniferous trees planted along its edge. There is a souterrain (SL032-125002-) in the W half of the interior.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'House'. 
In a small field of undulating rough grazing. A raised rectangular stone-built structure (int. dims 3.2m N-S; 2.7m E-W) which is open at the E end. The walls (T 0.65m; max. H 0.85m) are of upright stone blocks bedded on their sides. Contiguous to, and to the W of this, is a second rectangular structure (int. dims. 3m E-W; 3.5m N-S), the walls of which are one slab thick (T 0.4m). The entrance (Wth 0.5m) is in the centre of the W wall. From the W end of this structure a pair of parallel walls, c. 3.2m apart and built of slabs laid lengthways, extend 10.3m to W, stopping short of a N-S field boundary. This house probably dates to the post AD 1700 period.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 11 January 2012

source_data.original_text:
Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'Mill'. On the SW bank of the Owenmore river, at the end of an old trackway flanked by a millrace. The mill is named 'Bleach Mill' on the 1838 edition of the OS 6-inch map. The remains of a rectangular structure (c. 26m NW-SE; c. 8m NE-SW) are built into a NE-facing slope. The SE wall stands to two storeys but elsewhere the walls are low. There are four stone arched window opes in the NE wall on the ground floor with remains of windows overhead. There is a central door ope in the SE wall. The remains of a two-storey projection is at the NW end of the NE wall. Two deep wheel-pit channels (long axis NE-SW), one with flowing water, cross the mill off centre to NW. A millrace (Wth 4m; D 1.35m) is taken from the river c. 350m to E. A bleach green named on the 1838 OS 6-inch map to S of the mill is now a pasture field. The remains of the 19th-century Thorn Hill Corn Mill are c. 200m to SE. The remains of a bridge over the Owenmore river survives between the two mills. The present bridge c. 400m to E, named Ballynacarrow Bridge, is a 19th-century five-arched bridge. This is probably post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 11 January 2012

source_data.original_text:
A road bridge (on a NW-SE axis; Wth 5.8m) over the Owenmore River and on the edge of the demesne of the late 17th-century Annaghmore house (SL026-049----). On the upstream side are seven low pointed segmental arches (span c. 2.5m) with shaped voussoirs. The downstream arches appear to be repaired in parts with concrete and underneath the arches have recently been heavily underpinned. Piers (Wth c. 2m) with pointed cutwaters on the upstream side form large V-shaped refuge niches in the parapet wall. There are low pointed concrete cutwaters on the downstream side. The bridge is medieval in appearance.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In the shallow waters of Lough Talt, c. 150m from the NW shoreline. Views are restricted due to the mountainous terrain. A circular high-cairn crannog (18.4m N-S;18.1m E-W; H 2.3m above the lake-bed). A central plateau (4m N-S; 5m E-W) consists of subangular stones (diam. 0.2-0.3m) and some flagstones that are loosely packed and rest on a firmer surface of shattered and fire-cracked stones. A pile of boulders (L 1.45m E-W; Wth 0.4m; H 0.65m) on the E half of the plateau may be the remains of a wall. The edge of the plateau drops down to a berm (Wth 2-4m) to N, E and S. The W edge of the plateau slopes less and connects to a jetty (5.7m N-S; 11m E-W; H 0.38m above the water) consisting of small stones (diam. 0.05-0.1m) topped with some boulders. On the N side of the jetty is a submerged flagstone path (4.9m NW-SE; 1.7m E-W). The edge of the crannog is distinct and consists of stones, which overspill for 1-2m into the water. It is moderately overgrown with briars and the plateau has a thin cover of soil and grass. Wood-Martin (1892, 274-5) mentioned a wooden beam, a bone arrowhead, fragments of polished and worked bone as well as teeth and bones of oxen, sheep and horses from this crannog. A possible crannog (SL030-003002-) is c. 1.2km to SSE in the S end of Lough Talt.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

The grass-covered raised centre has a thin soil cover with a scatter of flat stones (diam. 0.6-0.7m) on top of smaller subangular stones (diam. 0.2-0.3m) forming a firm surface. The edge of this raised area drops sharply down to the surrounding berm. The stony edge of the crannog slopes gradually into the water. The NW corner protrudes slightly and from it a submerged causeway leads out to the NW to another submerged platform which could not be inspected. A stony causeway (L 5m; Wth 0.4m) at S connects the crannog to the lakeshore. Another crannog (SL030-002----) is c. 1.2km to NNW in the N end of Lough Talt.

A rim (Wth 3m) of sod-covered collapsed stones lies immediately outside the cashel wall. The interior is level and largely covered with hawthorn bushes. source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on flat ground and on the E side of a road, named 'Stirabout Road' on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. Within the N half of Kilcummin graveyard (SL031-005002-) and also within a possible ecclesiastical enclosure (SL031-005003-). No trace is evident of the building indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as a rectangular structure (c. 20m E-W; c. 10m N-S) and named 'Abbey'. It was recorded in 1836 as 'an old abbey in ruins in Cill Cuimín' (OSL, 389). According to local information, 'considerable fragments' of the church remained up to the 1880s but these were all reused as grave-markers (SL031-005004-) (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 130-31). The base of a window and two jambstones are still evident in the graveyard (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). Part of the enclosing vallum may be extant (SL031-005003-). According to Gwynn and Hadcock (1970, 390), Kilcummin was founded 'perhaps by St. Caeman or by St. Coemgen'. The site of a friary (SL031-006001-) and a bullaun stone (SL031-006002-) are c. 60m and c. 130m to the NE respectively. An associated holy well, 'Tobar Cuimín' (SL031-005005-), remains unlocated.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
A trapezoidal area (37m E-W; 36.8m N-S at W end; c. 30m N-S at E end) enclosed by a stone wall. Access is through a gate in the W wall. The earliest inscribed headstone noted is dated 1777. The other inscribed examples date mainly to the first half of the 20th century. The majority of grave-markers are, however, uninscribed rectangular blocks which, according to O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 130-31), are reused fragments of the 'abbey' (SL031-005001-) which was in the N half of the interior. A scarp, possibly the remains of a monastic enclosure (SL031-005003-), occurs in the NW corner. An associated holy well (SL031-005005-), called 'Tober Cuimín', remains unlocated. There is a friary (SL031-006001-) c. 60m to the NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on the NE end of a low rise with boggy ground to E and NE. Indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as a roughly pear-shaped embanked area (diam. c. 25m). Only part of this rath is now evident, consisting of an arc (C 20.5m NW-SE) of scarp (H 1.8m) N-SE, topped in places by an earthen bank (Wth 2m; int. H 0.45m). A line of stones (Wth 1m; L 6m), possibly foundations of a drystone wall, extend in N-S direction from the scarp at N into the interior. Further stone foundations, possibly of a house, are in the N half of the interior. The slope immediately outside the scarp along the NE arc is poached by cattle. Eroded remains of a linear earthen bank (L 12.4m NW-SE; Wth 2m; ext. H 0.6m; int. H 1.1m) lie c. 40m WSW of the rath, with traces of inner facing consisting of up to five courses of drystone walling. A further short section of an earthen bank (L 1.5m NE-SW) was noted 5.5m SW of the former. A concrete cattle-shed has been built in the area between both these sections of bank. A hollow is indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map in this area.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

A further short section of an earthen bank (L 1.5m NE-SW) was noted 5.5m SW of the SE end of the main bank. This is possibly the remains of a house. A concrete cattle-shed has been built in the area between both sections of bank.

In pasture, on flat land c. 150m N of the River Moy. A slightly raised circular area (35m NW-SE) defined by a scarp (H 1m) NNW-SW and by a flat-topped earthen bank (Wth 4m; int. H 0.5m; ext. A boggy depression a short distance to SE is, according to local information, a silted-up well.

source_data.original_text:
A large oval enclosure (105m ENE-WSW; 97m NNW-SSE) (visible on an aerial photograph GSIAP, G 262-3) defined by a collapsed sod-covered stone wall (Wth 1.2-1.5m; max. H 0.6m) S-SW, by a low rise at WNW and N-NNE, and by a slight scarp NE-E. The enclosing element appears to be incorporated into the field boundary system NW-NNW. A linear NNW-SSE field boundary truncates it at W. A second field boundary (on a NNW-SSE axis) bisects the interior off-centre to SW. A possible church (SL032-141001-) and a possible graveyard (SL032-141002-) are situated in the interior off-centre to the E and a souterrain (SL032-141005-) occurs in the SW sector. Also in the interior, off-centre to the W, are the possible remains of a limekiln (SL032-141004-). A hut site (SL032-141006-) lies c. 50m to the SW. This enclosure is not indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
Listed in the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified 'Mound'. On a gentle S-facing slope, within a possible ecclesiastical enclosure (SL032-141003-) and c. 10m W of a possible graveyard (SL032-141002-). A small mound (7.5m N-S; 7.3m E-W; H 0.6m) of earth and stone which is square in plan with rounded corners. At roughly the centre of the top of the mound is a shallow depression (diam. 2.5m; D 0.3m) defined on its N and S sides by a slightly raised rim. Remnants of a field boundary extend to S from the NW corner. The function of this mound is not known but it may be the remains of a limekiln or a feature of relatively recent date. 


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

In the NW quadrant of a rath (SL032-163001-). According to local information, an opening to a drystone-built passage was blocked some time ago. The surface evidence for the souterrain now consists of a low sod-covered rise (Wth c. 2m) which extends from the bank of the rath at WNW for 10m south-eastwards into the interior. source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a gentle E-facing slope. The remains of a rectangular structure (int. c. 17m E-W; 5.5m N-S) are evident in places as a scarp and in other places by up to three courses of a mortared stone wall (Wth 1.3m; H 0.6-1m); the E end-wall does not survive. The orientation of the structure suggests the remains of a small church and it could be a chapel associated with the pilgrimage to Achonry (see O'Rorke 1878, 417). The main ecclesiastical remains at Achonry, which include the cathedral (SL032-188002-) and graveyard (SL032-188003-), lie c. 100m to the SW. O'Rorke (1878, 422) noted that 'some hundreds of paces to the north-east (of the graveyard) are the ruins and rubbish of a building, which the inhabitants of Achonry call The College'. He is probably referring to this structure.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
At the N end of Achonry graveyard (SL032-188003-) and immediately E of St Crumnathy's, an early 19th-century deconsecrated C of I cathedral. Part of the E gable (int. Wth 6.85m) and the N wall (surviving length 14.7m; H 1.2m) of the church survive in poor repair and heavily clad with ivy. In the centre of the E gable are the fragmentary remains of a window which had three sub-arches with switchline tracery above, cut in limestone, and is late 15th/early 16th century in form. The interior of the church is overshadowed by a sycamore tree, and partially covered by scrub undergrowth. A block of stone decorated with concentric circles, possibly a corbel, was recently found within it where it had been reused as a grave-marker (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). This is the site of a church founded by St Finnian in the 7th century though 'nothing further is known of the history of Achonry until the twelfth century' (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 60). Achonry was a separate diocese during part of the late medieval period (ibid.) and a cathedral is mentioned here in the 1680s (Ó Muraíle 2002, 240, n. 24), so this is probably the remains of this structure. It was inadvertently named 'R.C. Chapel' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map. A possible church (SL032-188001-) lies c. 100m to the NE and a holy well (SL032-188006-) is c. 100m to the SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

A subrectangular graveyard (c. 60m E-W; c. 30m N-S) with a 20th-century extension on its S side. At its N end is St Cromnathy's C of I cathedral immediately E of which is the ruin of a late medieval cathedral (SL032-188002-). The grave-markers appear to be mostly of 19th-century date and include two chest-tombs, one near the SE corner and another near the centre which stands on a rusticated plinth. Herity, Kelly and Mattenberger (1997, 118) recorded two cross-inscribed stones (SL032-188011-) and a carved stone (H c. 0.3m) (SL032-188009-) within the interior. The carved stone, with a human head in high relief at the centre of one face, was originally part of a larger piece. A possible church (SL032-188001-) lies c. 100m to NW and a holy well (SL032-188006-) is c. 100m to the SE. A field system (SL032-188004-) survives to the N and S of the graveyard.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a gentle NE-facing slope. The remains of relict field systems lie to the N and S of Achonry graveyard (SL032-188003-). The fields are mostly rectangular in shape, ranging in size from 12m x 15m to 83m x 30m, but some are D-shaped or irregular. The field boundaries are comprised of scarps, low earthen banks (Wth c. 3m), and parallel lines of limestone slabs with an earthen core. The best-preserved group of fields is that to the S of the graveyard. Crossing it is a disused road (Wth c. 6m) (SL032-188005-), cut into the slope on its SW side and bounded by a low earthen bank (Wth 3m; H c. 0.25m) on its NE side; it extends NE for c. 17m before turning SE where it can be traced for a further 90m. There is a similar field system (SL032-047004-) at Abbey Court friary, c. 3.5km to N. A second field system (SL038-016002-) lies c. 1km to SE in the same townland.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In wet pasture, in the S corner of a field and c. 100m SE of Achonry cathedral (SL032-188002-) and graveyard (SL032-188003-). The well consists of an oval pit (0.8m NW-SE; 1.3m NE-SW) enclosed by a partially collapsed moss and sod-covered stone wall (Wth 0.8m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 0.3m). Along the E-SW arc, where the well abuts the N side of a penitential cairn (SL032-188007-), the wall forms a stone facing (H 0.3m) against the base of the cairn. According to local information in 2002, the traditional 'pattern' day is still observed and is held on August 15th. O'Rorke (1878, 417) noted that 'patterns' were held on Saturday with as many as 'two or three hundred present on the Saturday that immediately preceded the 15th of August'. The well is named after St Finian of Clonard who with St Nathy is said to have founded a monastery here (ITA).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a NE-facing slope, in the S corner of a field, and on the S side of Toberfinane holy well (SL032-188006-). A field boundary curves NE-NW around the cairn. The cairn consists of a low circular almost entirely sod-covered mound of stones (4.5m N-S; 4.5m E-W; H 0.4m at S; 1.4m at N just above the well). On top of it is a small square flat-topped structure (1.2m NW-SE; 1.2m NE-SW; H 0.3m at SW; 0.75m at NE) of drystone construction. It is built up on the NE side to compensate for the sloping ground. Erected on top of the structure is a modern 'Celtic' cross, painted white, and in front of the cross, a horizontal slab which provides a flat table-like surface. The structure appears to serve as an altar (SL032-188010-). According to local information, the traditional pattern day, which is still observed, is held on the 15th of August. O'Rorke (1878, 417) stated that the 'great pile of stones' next to 'Tubber-Finneen' were 'deposited one after another by the crowds of devotees that used to frequent the place to invoke the intercession of that saint'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On level ground on N-facing slope of ridge. Three large boulders laid flat on the ground, two to the S and the other to the N, support a fourth which clearly has been deliberately placed on them. This raised boulder (3.55m x 2.55m; T 1.4m) is the largest of the four while the smallest of the others measures 2.25m x 1.6m x 0.9m T. There is a pad-stone (0.35m x 0.25m; T 0.2m) between the northern supporting boulder and the large raised boulder. The affinities of this curious structure may lie with boulder-burials. source_data.original_text:
On low-lying generally level pasture some 1.3km SW of Knocknashee Mountain. The tomb is represented by the remains of a SSE-facing gallery (L c. 8m). There is no evidence of a court but a transversely set jamb at the W would seem to have formed one side of the entrance. A large rectangular block of stone (2.1m x 1m x 0.7m) lying prostrate at the gallery entrance seems to be a displaced lintel. The W side of the gallery is represented by three orthostats and a fallen one. One orthostat adjoins the entrance jamb; next to this is a fallen one; the two other orthostats stand 1m apart at the inner end of the gallery. Two orthostats survive next to each other at the outer end of the E side of the gallery. An almost prostrate slab at the N end of the gallery seems to be the backstone.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, in gently undulating terrain on a natural elevation defined on the SE edge by a short length of exposed limestone rock face. Ground falls away to E−S, and more gently at SW. The steepest slope is at SE−S, dropping into a small valley of flat damp ground beyond which ground rises again. Knocknashee is clearly visible on the N skyline. Forestry plantations now cover much of the surrounding landscape. A possible enclosure (SL032-235002-) lies immediately to N. 
This cashel is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps; it is visible in aerial imagery. According to local information, it is traditionally known as ‘Cashleen’ and the field is known as the ‘Cashel field’.
The remains are ephemeral and difficult to trace at ground level. The cashel was originally roughly circular (28m N−S; 28-29m E−W) but the enclosing wall cannot now be traced on the W half, where it has been replaced by a N−S rubble field wall (Wth 1m; H 0.5-1m). On the E half, the outline of the original enclosing wall is defined at NE−SW by a moss-covered scarp from which occasional stones protrude; the scarp is most pronounced (H 2m, Wth slope 3m at SE; H 1.2m, Wth slope 2m at S) at SE−S where it merges with and is enhanced by the natural break of slope. At SE it incorporates the vertical bedrock face (H 1.2m L 2m). At NW-N the cashel appears to been truncated by possible enclosure (SL032-235002-).
The cashel interior slopes down slightly from N to S−SE. This drop in level is accentuated in the SE quadrant by a low mossy scarp which extends from the enclosing scarp at E in a shallow curve across the interior, terminating at its W end (roughly in the centre of the cashel) in a low heap (4m N−S; c. 2m E−W) of stones, obscured by sod, brambles and a hawthorn bush. Immediately to W of this, a subrectangular area (10m N−S; 7m E−W) is divided off in the SW quadrant by a barely discernible E−W linear rise on the N and E sides, by the cashel scarp at S and by the N−S field wall on the W side.
The cashel is grass-covered with a few hawthorn bushes on the scarp at S. An enclosure (SL032-187----) is located 340m to NNE and two ringbarrow (SL038-005----; SL038-006----) are 300m to SE.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a natural elevation in gently undulating terrain. Ground falls away to E and S and more gently at SW. Knocknashee is clearly visible on the N skyline. Forestry plantations now cover much of the surrounding landscape. There is a cashel (SL032-235001-) immediately to S. 
This possible enclosure is not shown on any edition of the OS 6-inch maps; it is visible in aerial imagery. The remains are scant and difficult to interpret. A roughly D-shaped area (18m E-W to wall at W; c. 22-24m N−S) is defined by a slight rise or scarp on the curving E side; the rise/scarp (Wth c. 2.5-3m, top Wth c. 1m), which is distinguished by shorter, yellower grass growth, barely rises above internal ground level and has a slumped external slope (ext. H 0.5-0.6m). There appears to be a break at E, possibly an entrance. The S arc is difficult to trace; it may overlie/truncate the N arc of a cashel (SL032-235001-) which lies immediately to S. A N−S field wall defines the straight W side; there is no trace of a continuation of the enclosure to W of this wall. 
On the N arc the enclosing scarp drops to an outer terrace (Wth 2-2.5m) defined on its outer edge by another low rise/scarp (ext. H 0.5m), which follows the natural contour, curving N−NE and then swinging to E for a few meters before petering out; it may be the remains of a later field boundary that skirted the elevated ground.
The interior is level with a possible hut site (SL032-235003-) in the N half, with a telegraph pole adjacent to it. An enclosure (SL032-187----) is located 340m to NNE and two ringbarrow (SL038-005----; SL038-006----) are 300m to SE.

It is visible in an aerial photograph (IASAP, 3034207-8) as a partially overgrown oval area with pits or hollows in the NE quadrant.

raw_items.raw_text: 1271 when it was 'broken down by Hugh O'Connor'

source_data.original_text:
In level pasture, on the N shore of Templehouse Lake. A rectangular (22m N-S; 12m E-W) two-storey structure (see plans in Lynn 1985-6, 106; Sweetman 1999, fig. 78), standing on the W side of a complex of ruined buildings (SL033-026002-, SL033-026003-; SL033-026004-), built of uncoursed limestone in a lime mortar, with a distinct base batter (H c. 2m). The partially ivy-clad walls stand to full height except the W wall which, apart from short returns at either end, does not survive. The structure was refurbished in the 15th/16th century and again in the 19th century. In the former case, vaulting was inserted over the ground floor and the floor levels changed slightly. In the latter case, parts of the interior were used for farm buildings and a bellcote was erected on top of the N wall; Lynn (1985-6, 108) suggests that the bellcote indicates a religious function for the building but bellcotes of this form are typical of 18th/19th-century demesne farmyards. 
The vaulting covered the entire ground floor and consisted of two segmental wicker-centred vaults springing from the E and W walls and an inserted medial wall which was arcaded. Only fragments of the vaulting and the medial wall now survive. There are four inserted 15th/16th-century embrasures at ground-floor level: one each in the N and E walls and two in the S wall. These were probably all windows; the best preserved is that in the N wall which has wicker-centred vaulting over the embrasure and a single light. Each one was adapted in the 19th century to take either a wooden door or window frame, fragments of which are still in situ. 
Slightly N of centre in the E wall, at 1st-floor level, is the original doorway; the inserted vaulting blocked the lower part of this doorway. The door-surround is composed of plain limestone blocks and has a bluntly pointed arch; the rear embrasure is square-set and has a tall pointed arch. South of the doorway is a very ruined embrasure and there are two further such embrasures in the S wall. There is a better preserved window embrasure in the N wall but this is now covered with ivy. From the E side of this window a narrow mural stairs rises to the NE corner where it is lit by two small slit windows. The stairs rises further through the E wall to wall-top level. The outside face of the E wall shows many repairs and alterations, including the plaster-scar of a building which stood against its S end.
The earliest reference to a castle here is dated 1271 when it was 'broken down by Hugh O'Connor' (Lynn 1985-6, 105). The identification of this structure as belonging to a Knights Templar foundation is extremely speculative (see SL033-026007-) though the base of an early medieval high cross (SL033-026005-) lies within the ruin. The original form of the building is much more typical of a 13th-century hall-house (Sweetman 1999, 100) than a religious foundation.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In level pasture, on the N shore of Templehouse Lake. A complex of ruined buildings (SL033-026001-; SL033-026003-; SL033-026004-) roughly arranged around a square area (L c. 40m). Judging by the appearance of the gate-tower (SL033-026003-) in the centre of the N side, the complex was turned into a tower house and bawn arrangement in the 15th/16th century with the 13th-century hall-house (SL033-026001-) converted into the main residential block. By the early 17th century a new residential block (SL033-026004-) was built in the SE corner of the bawn. In the 19th century when the nearby Templehouse country house was built (Bence-Jones 1988, 271) the complex was converted into a farmyard with servants' quarters. The only surviving section of the enclosing bawn wall (H c. 6m; T 1.65m) runs E (L c. 10m) from midway along the E wall of the gate-tower before turning at a right angle to the S (L c. 20m) where it eventually merges with the E wall of the 17th-century house. Midway along this latter section is a 19th-century archway; on the inside face of the keystone of this arch is a carved human head which is probably 15th/16th-century in date.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In level pasture, on the N shore of Templehouse Lake. The ivy-clad ruin of a square (5.95m E-W) two-storey gatehouse, stands on the N side of a complex of ruined buildings (SL033-026001-; SL033-026002-; SL033-026004-) and was probably the entrance into the bawn (see SL033-026002-). The tower stood to full height in the 19th century (see drawing O'Rorke 1878, 315) but now its S wall has entirely collapsed. The N wall still stands to near full height though its top is covered by ivy. Built of uncoursed limestone in a lime mortar, the walls have a distinct base-batter. There is a central ground-floor archway in the N wall (Wth 1.75m); the arch is pointed and the opening framed by dressed limestone blocks. The doorway is choked by fallen masonry and the area inside filled by rubble to 1st-floor level. This area was covered by a groin vault which has almost entirely fallen. Running E from the tower is a high wall set back 2.5m from its N face; the corresponding area on the W side is covered by rubble (see SL033-026002-). The 19th-century drawing (ibid.) shows a plain rectangular opening over the doorway but this area is now covered by ivy. This drawing also shows the remains of battlements on top of the tower. In general appearance the tower would appear to be 15th/16th-century in date and contemporary with the bawn wall (SL033-026002-).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In level pasture, on the N shore of Templehouse Lake. The fragmentary ruin of a two-storey gable-ended L-shaped house, standing at the SE corner of a complex of ruined buildings (SL033-026001-, SL033-026002- and SL033-026003-). The building is now reduced to rubble apart from its E wall (L 14m), a short return of the S wall (original L c. 12m), and a gable wall which formed the N gable of the eastern arm (L 8m); there is also a gable on the S half of the E wall. The house was extensively rebuilt in the 19th century as part of a farmyard complex but three original windows are evident on the E wall, one at ground-floor level and two above. These are very fragmentary apart from that on the S end at 1st-floor level which is now completely blocked up. The light is a rectangular frame divided by three mullions and a transom, and covered by a hood-moulding. This is typically of an early 17th-century date. Another original feature of the house are the contemporary red bricks which faced the inside wall. Also probably associated with the house is a stone-built chimney stack (H c. 6m) which stands close to the now missing SW corner of the house.
Lying on the ground nearby are fragments of a limestone door arch and an inscribed limestone mantelpiece (SL033-026006-), both of which probably come from the house. The mantelpiece (1.2m x 0.4m x 0.3m) has been damaged in places but its basic form is clear. On its front face are two side-by-side rectangular panels which bear a Latin inscription which O'Rorke (1878, 320) described as 'three pious proverbs'. Above the panels the face curves outwards, and above this is the flat top-surface of the mantel. O'Rorke (ibid.) also noted a stone 'over the hall-door' which bore the crest of the Croftons, their motto ('the generation of the righteous shall be blessed') and the year 1627; the Croftons had taken possession of Templehouse shortly before this date (O'Dowd 1991, 99). This feature is no longer visible. The complex featured in a siege in 1641 when it became a refuge for local protestant families (ibid., 118-22).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

raw_items.raw_text: possible Knights Templar foundation at Templehouse

source_data.original_text:
Lying on the ground on the line of the missing W wall of Templehouse hall-house (SL033-026001-) is a stone cross-base. This is a limestone block (H 0.4m; at base 0.7m x 0.55m) tapering gently to a rectangular top (0.6m x 0.45m). In the centre of the upper surface is a rectangular mortise-hole (0.3m x 0.22m; D 0.2m) which is surrounded by a plain rectangular rim (H 0.05m; Wth 0.08m), rounded in section. There appears to be no decoration on the stone though it is encrusted by lichen and moss. The form of the stone is characteristic of an early medieval high cross (Edwards 1990, 164-70). It has been suggested (Lynn 1985-6, 108) that the cross might be associated with a possible Knights Templar foundation at Templehouse of which there are no other obvious extant remains (see SL033-026007-). O'Rorke (1878, 320) noted a tradition where 'the country people' of the district called this stone a 'Holy Water Stone'. This stone is included by Harbison (1992b, vol. 1, 393) in a list of bases without crosses which are possibly 'earlier than 1200'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Lying on the ground within the Templehouse complex of ruined buildings (SL033-026002-) is a limestone mantelpiece (1.2m x 0.4m x 0.3m) which probably comes from the nearby ruined early 17th-century house (SL033-026004-). The stone has been damaged in places but its basic form is clear. On its front face are two side-by-side rectangular panels which bear a Latin inscription which O'Rorke (1878, 320) described as 'three pious proverbs'. Above the panels the face curves outwards, and above this is the flat top-surface of the mantel. The appearance of this stone is compatible with the date of the house, 1627.

Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC with revisions by Patrick F. O'Donovan and Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
According to Gwynn and Hadcock (1970, 330-31), there was a Knights Templers foundation at Templehouse. The evidence indicates that Temple House Castle (SL033-026001-)  and its lands formed a preceptory and manor belonging to the Knights Templar from some time before 1271 to the order’s suppression in 1312 (O’Conor and Nassens 2016, 127).There is a complex of ruinded monuments at this location (see SL033-026001-; SL033-026002-; SL033-026003-; SL033-026004-) including the base of an early medieval high cross (SL033-026005-) lying on the ground within the hall-house (SL033-026001-). (Ó Muraíle 2002, 240 n. 24; Egan et al. 2005, no. 2671)

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, immediately W of the Owenmore River and in an area known locally as Derreen. According to local information, a dry slightly domed subrectangular area (c. 15m E-W; c. 10m N-S), with rounded corners, defined on its S and W sides by drains and on its N side by a growth of irises, is known locally as a burial ground. Within this burial ground are 100-120 grass-covered hummocks (L 0.5m; Wth 0.3m; H 0.2m), aligned E-W, arranged in six rows. The date of this burial ground is not known but it is believed locally to have been used for famine victims. (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In a small sub-circular sinkhole (E-W 26m; N-S 23m; D 2.5m along N; which presumably formed after the monument was constructed) in an area of numerous sinkholes on the bog-grown S-facing slope of the Ox Mountains (Slieve Gamph). This is a grass-grown circular cairn (diam. 11.5m to 12.5m; H c. 2m) at the top of which the upper part of the N side of a well-built drystone wall is exposed. A C-shaped arc of walling (SL036-001002-) survives and outlines a space measuring 1.7m E-W and 1m N-S. Up to four courses of walling (H 0.8m) are exposed. The wall is built of small stones laid in corbel fashion so that it inclines inwardly as it rises. The wall is part of a burial chamber the design and nature of which is uncertain. The elevated location of the site and the presence of a circular cairn suggest it might belong in the passage tomb tradition. (Aldridge 1960-1, 89-90)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On the bog-covered plateau below the higher slopes of the Ox Mountains and commanding an extensive view S and E across the basin of the River Moy. The tomb, in an oval bog-grown cairn (20.5m E-W; max. 13m N-S; H 1.5m), consists of a gallery (L 6m; Wth 1.5-3.3m) preceded at the E by the N side of a court. Two of the courtstones adjoin the gallery entrance and four others are 1.5m to the E. The outer two of these four may represent the side of an entrance passage leading to the court which may have been quite small. The well-preserved gallery narrows to both front and rear and its sides are doubled in places. Two jambs set at an angle to each other form the entrance to the gallery and another pair, the northern of the two split into three pieces, divide it into two chambers. The site is littered with displaced stones, some of them quite large. There is a low wall around the tomb probably built with stones taken from the cairn. Another court tomb (SL036-003----) c. 300m to S and a possible megalithic tomb (SL036-002001-) c. 30m to SW. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 70-1, no. 112)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

On a bog-grown plateau below the higher slopes of the Ox Mountains and 30m SW of a court tomb (SL036-002----). Some eight stones remain of what may be a ruined gallery aligned NE-SW, possibly c. 8m long. It is exposed in a grassy hollow (c. 8m x 7m) surrounded by bog. The stones are of generally slight proportions. At the NE there is a set stone (0.4m x 0.4m; H 0.2m). Some 0.8m to the SW there is a possible sidestone (L 1m; H 0.3m) leaning against which there is another stone, possibly a displaced corbel. Immediately SW of these there is a jamb-like stone (0.55m x 0.55m; H 0.5m). Some 0.6m further to the SW a partly buried stone, possibly a split boulder (1.4m x 0.35m; H 1m), may not be in situ. Just SW of the last a thin firmly set stone (0.8m x 0.15m; H 0.6m) stands at right angles to the alignment of the structure. It could be a jamb. A set stone (0.8m x 0.1m; H 0.7m) lies 0.4m to the SW and 0.8m beyond this there is another (0.7m x 0.2m; H 0.2m).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

A National Monument (No. 479) in state guardianship. On a bog-grown plateau below the higher slopes of the Ox Mountains and c. 300m S of another court tomb (SL036-002----) and on the same bog-covered plateau. The rear chamber (L 3.3m; max. Wth 2.2m) of a NE-facing court tomb is exposed at about mid-length in a bog-grown mound (L 34.5m; Wth 12m NE end, 7m SW end; H 3m). At the front of the chamber there are two jambs either side of a sill-stone. The sides, each of three orthostats, and backstone of the chamber support well-preserved corbelling which seems to extend beyond the jambs and sill into the concealed front part of the gallery. A largely concealed roofstone covers the back of the chamber. The peat cover above this is 0.6m thick. A slight depression in the mound, c. 5m from its NE end, may indicate the presence of a buried court. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 71-2, no. 113)

source_data.original_text:
In a marshy hollow, on the lower NE-facing slope of the Ox Mountains and just above Lough Talt River. This well is evident as a natural spring which forms a stream. There is no evidence of recent veneration here. In 1942-4 it was recorded that people prayed at the well 'asking St. Barbara to intercede for them in obtaining their request on visiting St. Attracta's well' after which they bless themselves with water from the well (ITA). Wood-Martin (1892, 358) noted that the 'stations' here were generally performed about the same date as those at St Attracta's well (SL036-009---) while O'Rorke ([1889], vol. 2, 152) states that it is supposed to have got its name from some companion of St Attracta. St. Attracta's well (SL036-009----) lies c. 190m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On a NE-facing slope of the Ox Mountains, above the Lough Talt River. The spring well, which is dedicated to St Attracta, is c. 1.5m below ground level with stone steps leading down to it, revetted and surrounded by a large D-shaped cairn of stones. There is a cross, depicted in white marble, above the well. Rosary beads adorn surrounding bushes and trees and Mass is celebrated here on 15th August each year. According to local tradition, a monster living in the glen was killed by St Athy or Araght, who came form the North of Ireland with a blessed staff given to her by St Patrick (Wood-Martin 1892, 357; O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 152). In 1942-4 it was recorded that close to the well is a place called 'Lug na paiste or Hollow of the Beast' (ITA). It was also recorded that the pilgrimage to the well commences on the last Sunday in July and continues until the end of August, with 'the annual pilgrimage day being the Sunday within the octave of the feast of St Attracta' (ITA). St Barbara's well (SL036-008----) lies c. 190m to NW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In the Ox Mountains, SW of Lough Talt, adjoining the Sligo-Mayo border. A linear earthwork, named the 'Black Ditch' extends, in a SE direction, from the Sligo-Mayo border for a distance of 3km. It forms the townland boundary between Kilmacteige to the N and Letterbrone to the S. Two small lakes, Lough Nablaneybaun and Lough Hure, interrupt the earthwork at 1.45km and 2km, respectively, from the Mayo border. Condit and Gibbons (1991, 10) described the earthwork as a trackway with a raised bank on one side and suggest that it may have been an ancient droveway or a property division or frontier boundary. Although not indicated on the OS 6-inch map as continuing into Mayo, the earthwork 'is said locally to go towards Ballina [county Mayo]' (ibid.).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In a hollow covered with overgrowth, beside a stream. This is a spring well, with the surrounding ground poached by cattle. There is no evidence of recent veneration here. According to Wood-Martin (1892, 357), a small ash tree beside 'Tubber-Keeran, or St. Keeran's-well', is covered in rags and frequented by country people for many reasons but mainly by 'farmers wives and daughters whose cows are sick or not producing as much butter as they expected'. Pilgrimage to the well was on the last Sunday in July with a procession from Kilmacteige church (SL036-021001-), c. 200m to S, to the well where three circles of the Rosary were said (ITA). The origin of the name Keerann may come from the Irish for mountain ash 'Caerthain, pronounced caraun' or from a corruption of Tubber Ciaran, well of Ciaran (O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 152). According to Wood-Martin (1892, 357, n. 1), there were possible bullaun stones (see SL036-021006-) close to the well.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on an E-facing slope. There is no evident trace in Kilmacteige graveyard (SL036-021003-) of the medieval parish church (SL036-021002-) which had disappeared by 1836 (OSL, 389). In the NW quadrant is the roofless ruin of the 18th/19th-century C of I parish church. This is a small gable-ended rectangular structure (ext. 14.7m E-W; 7.02m N-S) whose walls (T 0.60m) are built of rendered random-rubble limestone, with ashlar (limestone) details. There is a square-headed doorway in the W gable, two round-headed windows in the S wall, and a single large round-headed window in the E gable. According to Mason (1816, vol. 2, 358), it was damaged in the rebellion of 1798, 'but has since been put into decent repair' though it contained only 'four pews'; it was again in a state of disrepair by the 1830s (Bowen 1970, 211). Pilgrimages from this church to 'Tober Keerann' holy well (SL036-020----) were held on the last Sunday in July (ITA). Wood-Martin (1892, 357, n. 1) recorded a number of possible bullaun stones (SL036-021006-) in the immediate vicinity of the church.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Mason (1816, vol. 2, 358) referred to the 'ruins of ancient building which is said to have been a college, or place of education for young men intended for the priesthood' in the graveyard. According to O'Rorke (1890, vol. 2, 141), this building was a church which 'stood on the site of the present Protestant church [SL036-021001-], where some ruins may still be seen'. There are no remains of this church now visible.

A roughly rectangular area (max. dims. 60m WNW-ESE; 36m SSW-NNE) enclosed by a stone wall and accessed through a gate and stile in the W wall. The E half of the S wall curves outwards in an arc, possibly following the line of an earlier enclosure (SL036-021005-). There are grave-markers and headstones throughout which are 18th-, 19th- and 20th-century in date. In the NW quadrant is the ruin of the 18th-century C of I parish church of Kilmacteige, on the site of a medieval parish church (SL036-021001-). A cross-slab (SL036-021004-) is located in the SE quadrant and Wood-Martin (1892, 357, n. 1) recorded a number of possible bullaun stones (SL036-021006-) in the immediate vicinity of the church.

source_data.original_text:
In a broad valley among foothills at the SW end of the Ox Mountains. It lies to the E of a field fence on land reclaimed from the bog. A well-preserved SW-facing gallery (L 8.7m) opens onto a flat facade which links it to flanking lines of outer-walling. A curved line (L c. 8m) of seven orthostats between 2m and 4m beyond the more northerly side of the outer-walling seems to represent a kerb. The whole stands in a low mound (16.5m N-S; 12m E-W; max. H 0.75m). A high septal-stone divides the gallery into a portico (L 2m; Wth 2.1m at front, 1.8m at the septal-stone) and main chamber (L 6.2m; Wth 1.6m at front, narrowing to c. 0.8m at rear). Single stones form the portico sides. The septal-stone, now split from base to top towards its N end, is inset in the gallery walls and rises 0.2m above the portico sides. Two broken and partly concealed roofstones lie to the E of the septal-stone and there are other smaller displaced stones beyond these. The N side of the main chamber is formed by eight orthostats some of which partly overlap each other. Only three stones, alongside to the W, remain of the opposite side. Ten outer-wall stones are in position to both N and S and the eastern two examples at both sides turn inwards towards the backstone of the gallery. A single façade-stone joins the front of the gallery to the outer wall at each side. Adjoining the inner end of each facade-stone is an orthostat. These two stones stand at either side of the portico entrance (Wth 0.8m). Another wedge tomb (SL036-036----) lies c. 1km to NE in the same valley. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 72-3, no. 114)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On a little knoll in the same valley as another wedge-tomb (SL036-035----) c. 1km to SW. A WNW-facing gallery (L at least 7m; Wth 1.85m at front, narrows sharply to rear), flanked at the S by the slight remains of an outer wall, stands on a D-shaped platform (H 0.5m to 1m) which appears to be artificial. There are vague traces of mound at the back and along the N side of the gallery. A number of displaced and largely concealed roofstones cover the E end of the structure. Three orthostats are in position at the front of the more northerly side of the gallery, the first set outside the line of the other two. Beyond these, two largely concealed slabs, apparently sidestones, have collapsed inwards. About 1m beyond these another inward-leaning stone, now split, also appears to be a sidestone. Four orthostats are in position at the outer end of the more southerly side of the gallery, the second set outside the line of the others. About 1.5m beyond these an outwards-leaning stone may also be a sidestone. There are three buttress-stones outside the N side of the gallery, one at right angles to the inner end of the first orthostat and there are two just beyond the collapsed easternmost sidestone. There is another buttress-stone outside the more westerly end of the second sidestone at the S. Outside and parallel to the opposite end of the same orthostat there is a low stone perhaps like the buttress-stone intended to support the gallery side. There are two outer-wall stones alongside some 1.5m beyond the end of the S side of the gallery. A large stone in front of the tomb is displaced. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 73-4, 116, no. 116)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on the southern slopes of the Ox Mountains and c. 90m to S of stream. A roughly circular area (30.5m N-S; 32.5m E-W) enclosed by a partially collapsed drystone wall (Wth 3.1m; int. H 1.75m; ext. H 2.2m) along the E, S and W arcs. A stone field boundary has been built on top of the foundations of a drystone wall along the N arc. The inner and outer faces of the wall are constructed of large rectangular blocks of stone, and the core is filled with smaller stones. A large amount of collapsed stone from the wall now lies in the interior. The entrance (Wth 1.2m) is at SSE, roofed by large lintels. The interior is bisected by a field boundary on a N-S axis. There is a steep natural slope down to S in the N third of the interior. The remainder of the interior is level as it has been raised to compensate for the hillslope. There is a possible souterrain (SL036-037002-) in the interior.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture on the slopes of the Ox Mountains and commanding an extensive outlook to the S and SW. An orthostat to the W and two alongside 2.5m to the E represent the S side (L 7m) of a WSW-facing gallery. A displaced stone lies against each of the latter two orthostats. Two orthostats of the N side of the gallery are in place, one opposite the gap in the southern side and the second 0.7m to the E. There is a displaced stone alongside the western of these two orthostats. It is clear that the gallery both narrowed and decreased in height from W to E. There are slight traces of a mound at the W end of the structure. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 73, no. 115)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In level upland pasture, adjacent to a cashel (SL036-040001-), on the southern slopes of the Ox Mountains. The adjoining fields to SW and SE of the cashel are under coniferous forest. The cashel is within a large rectangular field which overlaps or supersedes the remains of the walls shown radiating to W, NE and E from the perimeter of the cashel on the 1914 OS 6-inch map. These walls remain as moss-covered jumbles of stone (Wth c. 1.5m; H 0.3-0.5m) two of which, 15m apart, subdivide the NE end of the rectangular field. There are remains of similar walls nearby.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On a terrace, on the southern slopes of the Ox Mountains. An oval area (35.5m N-S; 38m E-W) enclosed by a partially collapsed drystone wall (Wth 1.9m; ext. H 1.9m). Internally the wall survives to a height of 0.4-1m and there is a large amount of collapsed material from the wall around the edge of the interior. An intervening fosse (Wth 8m) and an outer earthen bank (int. H 1.2m; ext. H 1.75m) are evident NNE-SW. The bank is revetted internally and externally in parts by a drystone wall. A linear N-S field boundary lies immediately outside the stone wall to W. The outer bank is indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as continuing around to W outside the linear field boundary. This is now part of the lawn adjoining a bungalow. The interior is overgrown with bushes and briars and there is a souterrain (SL036-041002-) in the W half. A drainage channel lies to the N of the cashel.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a terrace overlooking the Bellanamean River. Only the ivy-clad N corner now stands of a rectangular structure (int. c. 7m NW-SE; c. 5m NE-SW) otherwise reduced to sod-covered foundations. The corner stands to approximately third-floor level and incorporates the remains of a spiral stone stairs (diam. c. 0.9m). Two windows lighting the stairs survive, each with a flat rear arch and a broken light. In the 1940s the tower was described as 'square in shape ... and approximately 30 feet [9.14m] high ... with no architectural features' (ITA). There are no visible remains of the 'court yard, enclosed by a very thick strong wall' mentioned by Mason (1816, vol. 2, 358-9). A castle of the O'Hara's (Mason 1816, vol. 2, 358-9; O'Rorke [1889], vol. 2, 149).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture on a natural rise with a fall of ground to the stream at SE. This possible rath is indicated as an embanked circular area (diam. c. 40m) on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. The rath is levelled but visible as a roughly circular area (c. 27m N-S; 26m E-W) defined W-NW by gentle undulation, NNW-NNE by the slope of a natural rise and NE-ESE by the remnants of a scarp (H 0.6m) cut into the natural slope. A band of brambles appears to mark the S limits and may be related to a linear cropmark (Wth c. 2m) of long grass, rushes and gorse which extends W from the SW edge of the possible rath. This cropmark is probably a levelled field fence that skirted the possible rath. The interior is fairly level but it has an uneven surface, broken by shallow hollows and low hummocks.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On the bog-grown southern slopes of the Ox Mountains. A heather-grown, bog-covered cairn of trapezoidal outline (L 37m E-W; Wth 14.7m E end, 9m W end; H 2m). The stones of the cairn are exposed in two holes in the bog cover. One is some 5m from the W end of the cairn and the other is about 12m further to the E. A large displaced stone exposed in the more easterly opening is jammed in an upright position among cairn stones. A shallow U-shaped inturn in the broader end of the mound may indicate the presence of a buried court.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

A circular area (diam. 25m) terraced into the hillside, with the N half up to 1.2m below and the S half up to 0.6m above the external ground level. In the W half of the interior of a rath (SL037-002001-). Two parallel rectangular stone-built corbelled chambers are linked by creepway with a possible third chamber to E. Chamber 1 (L 5.5m E-W; Wth 2.2m; H c. 2m) has a collapsed entrance at W and a creepway (Wth 0.6m; L 1.2m) at the E end of the N wall which leads to chamber 2 (L 5.5m E-W; Wth 2.5m; H c. 2m). A stone step along the E wall gives access to a collapsed creepway (Wth c. 0.6m; L 1.6m) which leads to a possible third chamber, now inaccessible, and only visible as a surface depression.

In pasture, on the N-facing slope of a rise. Remains of a roughly circular area (27.1m N-S; 31m E-W) defined by a scarp (H 1m) along the N arc and rising ground (H 0.9m) along the S arc. The N portion of the interior is raised and the S portion is cut into the upslope to compensate for the hillslope. Nevertheless the interior still slopes gently from SW to NE, is concave in profile, possibly due to the remains of levelled earthen banks. The rath was levelled in 1985 and a low rise with faint traces of an earthen bank E-W and a scarp W-E were noted during a subsequent inspection in 1985 (SMR (1989) file) as well as a souterrain (SL037-003002-) on the N edge.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, on top of the NE-facing slope of a low rise. An oval area (27.3m N-S; 23.5m E-W) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 8m; int. H 1m; ext. H 1.75m) SE-NE; the bank is levelled NE-SE. The remains of a second annexe (30m E-W; 10m N-S) to the N are defined by low, slightly curving relict earthen field boundaries at E and W, by the N bank of the rath to S and by a linear modern field boundary to N. Two other raths (SL037-015---- and SL037-016----) are c. 100m to NW and c. 100m to SW, respectively.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a N-facing slope overlooking a stream c. 70m to the N; on the W side of a graveyard (SL037-037002-). Fragmentary remains of a rectangular church (int. c. 18m E-W; 7m N-S). Only the W gable with short returns of the N and S walls (H c. 2m), and a short section of the E end of the S wall (H c. 1.2m), stand. Otherwise the lines of the N and S walls are defined by a scarped edge, and three large 19th-century grave-plots occupy the line of the E wall. The surviving walls (T 1.2m; max. H 2.5m) are built of coursed limestone blocks. The church is indicated as an L-shaped structure (20m E-W) on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. The remains of a castle (SL037-039----) lie c. 200m to ENE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

A rectangular graveyard (55m E-W; 35m N-S) enclosed by a drystone wall. Access is via a stile in the E wall and there is a flat stone on top of the wall immediately to the N of the stile on which coffins were placed while the mourners entered the graveyard (pers. comm. M. A. Timoney). Headstones date to the 19th century and there is a 19th-century baptismal font in the SE corner. The remains of a church (SL037-037001-) are in the W side of the interior. A castle (SL037-039----) lies c. 200m to the ENE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rough pasture, on a gentle SW-facing slope with a stream c. 100m to SW. It was listed in 1633-6 as 'a good Castle . . . and a lowe Irish mill' (Wood-Martin 1889, 158): the exact location of the mill (SL037-111----) is unknown. The area of the castle has been surface quarried and is now covered by quarry scars and spoil heaps. Four pieces of fallen masonry lie on the S side of a slight rise. Immediately NE of these is a linear depression (L 25m; Wth 5m; D 0.3m), wet in places, which may be the remains of a fosse. The castle was indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as a roughly rectangular structure (35m NE-SW; 30m NW-SE), with a small rectangular enclosure (c. 15m NE-SW; c. 20m NW-SE) and three small structures adjacent to SE. A late 18th-century drawing shows a complex of ruined buildings here, part of which appears to stand to 1st-floor level (Grose 1791, vol. 2, facing p. 47). In 1836 it was recorded as an O'Hara castle in ruins (OSL, 388-9). A church and graveyard (SL037-037001-; SL037-037002-) lie c. 200m to WSW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Revised by: Paul Walsh

Date of upload: 31 July 2012

source_data.original_text:
In pasture. A natural hill (diam. c. 200m) defined at its base NNW-SE by a curving scarp with a broad fosse and traces of an external bank and elsewhere to S and W by linear field boundaries, that at S being an earthen stone-faced townland boundary (Wth 2m; H 1.4m). The scarp (H 1.7-2m) which marks an abrupt break of slope at the base of the hill and may be partly natural, peters out at each of its termini. Generally the slope of the scarp is broad but it is almost vertical at SE. Traces of a field boundary (Wth 1.2m) are evident on top of the scarp at SE and a low rise (Wth c. 2m) is evident at ENE. The fosse is broad and shallow (Wth c. 5m at top and 3m at base). Remnants of an outer bank (Wth c. 1.8-2m) are evident SE-SSE and at NE where it takes the form of a very low rise (Wth c. 2.5m). The interior slopes gently down towards the perimeter. There is a rath (SL037-046001-) in the interior off-centre to W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008
