On the W bank of the River Moy; at the E end of Banada graveyard (SL037-068005-), directly on top of a steep slope rising from the bank of the river. Only the E end of the church of this Augustinian foundation stands though a much-greater part of the complex stood until 1897 (Harbison 2002, 92-5). The surviving structure consists of the E end of the N (int. L 7.1m) and S walls (int. L 10.15m) of the chancel and the base of the E end-wall (int. L 6.55m) (see plan Lynn 1985-6, 96). These are built of uncoursed limestone in a lime mortar; the surviving walls are heavily enveloped by ivy. 
The N wall is featureless save for a broken window ope. A 15th-century 'relief carving of human head with elaborate head dress' (SL037-068006-) (ibid., 98), formerly lying in the N half of the graveyard, has been built into its internal wall-face. Externally along the base of the wall is the battered face of 'coarser, random rubble masonry' which Lynn (ibid.) interpreted as the remains of a 13th-century castle (SL037-06804-). 
Near the E end of the S wall is a two-seater sedilia. The front elevation (see sketch in Lynn 1985-6, 96) consists of two round arches rising from a central twisted column and a pilaster at either end (pilaster to E is missing). These have plain octagonal bases and capitals. Over each is an ogee hood rising to a moulded finial, and there are stylised floral mouldings set on the shoulders of the hood. A short distance W of the sedilia is a doorway facing into the church; the ground level here is halfway up its jambs. The doorway has a two-centred pointed arch. It leads to a short mural passage which is very ruined but has an opening on its W side leading to the base of a spiral stairs. The stairs, which rises clockwise, is lit by a small slit window looking into the choir. The S wall runs a short distance further W before breaking off. 
Lying within the graveyard are many carved limestone blocks derived from the friary. These include the central piece of a cusped ogee-headed window light, the side of a cusped round-arched window-head, and a number of chamfered blocks which were probably window-light jambs. Also in the graveyard are two gutter-stones from the wall-walk of the church, which were reused as grave-markers. There are some further chamfered blocks (SL037-067----) in a garden 350m to the SW. A drawing of the ruin in 1779 (Harbison 2002, figs. 71 and 72) shows the that the building had a tower of 15th-century form, slim in profile and built of coursed ashlar. 
This Augustinian foundation was established in 1423 by Donnchadh O'Hara (Gwynn and Hadcock 1970, 296; Ó Muraíle 2002, 240, n. 27); the surviving architectural features confirm the 15th-century date. A bridge (SL037-068007-) over the river Moy is indicated on the Down Survey (1655-6) map of County Sligo in the vicinity of this friary.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

This is listed as a 'tomb' in the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995). The source of this reference is F. Grose, Antiquities of Ireland (1797, 57) where he notes that 'There are two handsome antient tombs in the church.' It is possible that Grose mistakenly misinterpreted the sedilia at the E end of the S wall of the chancel for one of these tombs. Alternatively, there may have been two tombs visible there when he recorded the friary as there was much more in existence when he drew his sketches.

Compiled by: Paul Walsh

source_data.original_text:
Lynn (1985-6, 95-8) suggested than the battered plinth (H 1.5m) of coursed limestone under the N chancel wall of Banada Abbey (SL037-068001-) is the remains of a mid-13th-century castle erected by Maurice Fitzgerald. Apart from being slightly battered, the plinth shows no other 'castle' features. Lynn's suggestion that it is unusual to find the E end of such a church built on steeply sloping ground can be countered by sites such as Buttevant (Power et al. 2000, Inv. no. 14871) and Timoleague (Power et al. 1992, Inv. no. 3065) in county Cork.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
A roughly rectangular graveyard (c. 80m ESE-WNW; c. 55m SSW-NNE) enclosed on the S, W and N sides by a stone wall and defined on the E side by a steep slope down to the river. The ruins of an Augustinian friary (SL037-068001-) are at the E side. There are many 18th- and 19th-century headstones and crosses, the earliest noted was dated 1775. Amongst the grave-markers are numerous architectural pieces derived from the friary, and the area immediately around the ruin is strewn with rubble, broken headstones and tomb surrounds. The graveyard has recently been partially cleared of overgrowth. The enclosed burial ground for the nearby convent of the Sisters of Charity of Banada Abbey, who are associated with Banada since the 1860s (McDonnell-Garvey 1999/2000, 9-11), is at the S side of the graveyard.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In rough pasture, on a gentle NW-facing slope overlooking the River Moy to NW. An oval area (32.6m NE-SW; 20.4m NW-SE) is defined by a low bank (Wth 2m; int. H 0.25m; ext. H 0.55m) with an external fosse (Wth 1.7m; D 0.4m) NE-SE and elsewhere by a scarp (H 0.9m) with a low internal rim and a shallow external depression (D 0.2m). The W portion of the interior is raised to compensate for the hillslope. The level interior is bisected NE of centre by a low sod-covered bank (Wth 1.2m; H 0.3m) on a NW-SE axis; on the NE side of this bank are traces of cultivation ridges. Five mature beech trees are close to or on the enclosing bank and a few hawthorn bushes and brambles are scattered around the perimeter.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a broad level hilltop with commanding views of the surrounding countryside. Indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map by an arc of hachures W-NNE. The present remains consist of a semicircular area (33m NE-SW) defined by a scarp (H 1.1m) SSW-NE with a flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 5.5m) and a gapped external bank (Wth 4.5m; int. H 1.2m; ext. H 0.8m) WSW-NE. No trace of the enclosing elements are visible NE-SSW where the interior merges with the surrounding field. The interior is generally level though there is a slight slope to SSW in the S half. The rath is densely overgrown with hawthorn bushes. A NW-SE field boundary may incorporate a short section of the external bank at SW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a low hill. The rath is covered in a dense thicket of blackthorn, hazel and brambles. A raised roughly circular area (diam. c. 25m N-S; 29m E-W) defined by a scarp (H c. 0.3m) and enclosed by a flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 5.7m) with an external flat-topped earthen bank (Wth 5.5m; int. H 1.7m; ext. H 0.9m) SE-N. A field boundary has replaced the external bank N-SE. An external fosse (Wth 6.5m) is evident W-NW. Some stones protrude from the inner face of the external bank. There is a possible entrance at NE where the scarp is reduced to very shallow ramp-like slope. There is a corresponding gap (Wth c. 12m) in the outer bank which has been infilled by an earth and stone field boundary. The interior is level and clear of overgrowth and, like the bank, is poached by cattle in places. A small quarry-hole abuts the outer bank at W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In a rath (SL037-074001-), now entered through a small opening on the inside of the bank of the rath at NW. A rectangular stone-built chamber (7m NE-SW; 2m NW-SE; H 1.7m) with corbelled walls and a lintelled roof. At the SE end it turns at right angles towards NE, leading to possible second chamber or entrance.

There is a souterrain (SL037-078002-) in the NW quadrant adjacent to the scarp. The interior is poached by cattle and is densely covered with overgrowth as well as damaged by badger setts. There is a small quarry to NE and a field boundary clips the fosse at W and S.

Not listed in either the SMR (1989) or RMP (1995). A small, approximately rectangular building is marked at this location on the 1838 edition of the OS 6-inch map. On a small level terrace, on the SW bank of a stream, on a S-facing slope of the Ox mountains. A circular earthen structure (int. diam. 2.5m E-W; 2.3m N-S) with vertical sides which are topped by an irregular rim of earth and stone (Wth 3m; ext. H 0.65m). The interior, which is sunken to a depth of 0.6m below the external ground level, is flat and damp. The opening (Wth 0.5m) is at ENE and is approached by a passage (L 1m) which narrows (Wth 0.35m) at its outer edge where it is flanked by two large partially embedded boulders. The structure is engulfed with ferns and moss and there are rushes growing in the interior. Another limekiln (SL031-065001-) is c. 100m to NW. This is probably post-1700 AD in date.


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

source_data.original_text:
Located in rough upland pasture, in the S-facing foothills of the Ox Mountains, adjacent to a small cluster of ruined 18th/19th-century cottages.
This cross-inscribed stone is broken; it now consists of a roughly T-shaped sandstone boulder (L 0.39m) with a cross and two symbols inscribed on one face. The stone appears to have been chosen for its unusual natural form; the edges are smooth and rounded, and there is no evidence of sculpting to create the T-shape. The narrow part of the stone or stem of the ‘T’ (L c. 0.22m; Wth 0.21m; T 0.11m) is bulbous at its terminal, from where it narrows slightly before expanding in a gently sweeping curve into the ‘bar’ (Wth 0.39m) of the T. The stone is broken at this broad end, presenting a straight, sheared-off surface. 
The incised cross (H 0.08m; Wth at arms 0.09m) is located at the neck of the stone, and is outlined by narrow, shallow incised grooves. The upright element of the cross has long bar terminals, with each bar having a slight expansion at its terminals. The horizontal element (arms) of the cross extends the full width of the stone, and has a slight expansion at each terminal. The cross as a whole is crude and asymmetrical in execution.
Two widely spaced, incised symbols are evident at the broad end of the stone, both are truncated by the broken edge. One symbol is triangular (H 0.06m; Wth 0.07m) with very slightly bowed sides, the other is roughly D-shaped (H 0.03-0.04m; Wth 0.075m) with a short linear extension or ‘tail’ at one side. It is not now possible to determine their significance. They may be an attempt to outline a more elaborate cross-like carving on the broader part of the stone, or they may represent letters. The D-shaped symbol, for instance, resembles the top of a D in typical early medieval half-uncial script, although this resemblance may be entirely fortuitous.
As the stone is incomplete, and its provenance unknown, it is difficult to date with certainty. The crude execution of the incised symbols and the choice of a stone of unusual natural shape might suggests a relatively late date, perhaps Penal Era/17th- or 18th-century. However, an early medieval date is not impossible: this style of incised cross occurs on early medieval slabs.
There is no known burial ground or ecclesiastical site in the immediate vicinity of the find spot. A cashel (SL031-003-----), reused as a burial ground (SL031-003002-), is located 1km to SE, and Kilcummin graveyard (SL036-006002-), site of a church (SL031-006001-), is 1.5km to S.  

Attached images:

SL031-067---_01.JPG Cross-inscribed stone
SL031-067---_02.JPG Close-up of the incised symbols
SL031-067---_03.JPG Set upright, in profile

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 5 July 2019

source_data.original_text:
In rolling pasture within 100m of the River Moy. Three orthostats stand on an oval stony mound (11.7m E-W; 7.7m N-S; H 0.6m). Two of the orthostats, both low stones, are opposite each other close to the middle of the mound and seem to represent a gallery aligned approximately E-W. Immediately E of these the tops of some small stones are exposed at the surface but their status is unclear. Some 2.5m to the W of the opposed orthostats there is a tall example set transversely to the line of the presumed gallery, possibly a backstone. There are a number of displaced stones on the mound. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 61, no. 98)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On level pasture S of the Ox Mountains. The monument is very ruined and difficult to interpret. A fence extends along its N side. A chamber (L 2.7m) opening to the NW seems to be the rear of a gallery. Two jambs and an intervening sillstone mark the front of the chamber. One stone is in place on its more southerly side and a prostrate stone at the opposite side may be a fallen orthostat. A large inward-leaning stone forms the back of the chamber. A considerable number of stones extend for some 8m forward of the chamber. Most of these do not appear to be in situ but two of them, both tall stones now leaning, and c. 2m apart, stand more or less opposite each other about 4m from the front of the chamber. There are some traces of mound at this end of the structure. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 61, no. 97)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On the lowermost north-western slopes of Knocknashee Mountain. A spring well revetted by a drystone wall and roofed by lintels. There is no evidence of recent veneration at this well. It may be the well which Wood-Martin (1892, 355-6, n. 1) mentioned in Cashel North which had been 'formerly held in estimation as "holy"'.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

On the table-top plateau of Knocknashee hill, commanding extensive views in all directions to the Ox Mountains and South Sligo. The generally level plateau is comprised of a series of natural terraces of limestone bedrock declining gradually from the centre of the plateau outwards to the abrupt break of slope that marks the outer edge. Described by Condit, Gibbons and Timoney (1991, 59-62) as a roughly oval-shaped area (c. 700m NNE-SSW; c. 350m E-W), comprising c. 21.5 hectares and enclosed by two earth-and-stone banks. The inner bank (Wth 3.8m; max. H 1.5m) is constructed from a series of quarry hollows contiguous to the inner bank face and forming an inner fosse in parts and is topped by a later field boundary wall along the E side (ibid.). A second rampart was described along the E and S arcs, parallel to the inner bank and utilising a natural terrace and turning sharply downhill at NE (ibid.). Along the sheltered E half of the interior are about 30 hut sites, possibly a Neolithic settlement (SL032-013004-). Two possible passage tombs (SL032-013002-; SL032-013003-) c. 120m apart are located at the N end of the plateau. A D-shaped enclosure (SL032-013005-) abuts the inner bank at E. Further evidence of settlement might be provided by the presence of 'scoops and hollows situated at the south and south-west in the hillfort' (ibid., 61).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Close to the N end of flat-topped Knocknashee Mountain, commanding an extensive outlook and within a hillfort (SL032-013001-). This possible passage tomb lies at the N limit of the possible Neolithic settlement (SL032-013004-). Another possible passage tomb (SL032-013003-) lies c. 120m to NE.

source_data.original_text:
On the plateau-like top of Knocknashee Hill and widely distributed over the grass and heather-covered terraces in the E half of a hillfort (SL032-013001-). A complex of c. 30 huts in clusters of two, three and occasionally more, separated by distances of 2-15m; one instance of two conjoined huts was noted. The huts are often in N-S rows following the contours of the natural terracing. Although the degree of preservation of the huts varies, they are remarkably uniform in size and form. A typical hut consists of a flat circular area (diam. 8-11m) defined by a stony wall (Wth 1.6m; H 0.3-0.5m). Most are entirely sod-covered but where the enclosing wall is exposed it appears to be composed of a jumble of angular limestone rubble. A number of the huts are surrounded by a fosse (Wth 1.5-2m; D 0.3-0.5m) immediately outside the enclosing wall. However, in most cases, instead of a continuous fosse there are two or three discrete depressions outside the wall. A clearly defined entrance gap is not always evident but where entrances were identified they usually occurred in the SE quadrant. Condit, Gibbons and Timoney (1991, 61) noted that further evidence for individual settlement sites might be provided by the presence of scoops and hollows situated at the S and SW within the hillfort. The complex is clearly visible in aerial photographs taken in 1968 (CUCAP, AVJ 1, 4, 5; CUCAP, AVI 95-6). Two possible passage tombs (SL032-013002-; SL032-013003-), c. 120m apart, lie at the N limit of the huts and within the hillfort. A similar complex of huts (SL040-108----) at Mullaghfarna, c. 22km to the SE, has been tentatively dated to the Neolithic period. (Norman and St Joseph 1969, 24-5)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

On the plateau-like top of Knocknashee hill, at a break of slope on the E side and abutting the inner defences of the hillfort (SL032-013001-) at E. A D-shaped area (dims. 29m E-W) defined by a ruinous stone wall that survives as a sod-covered stony rise (Wth 2m). A roughly constructed field boundary wall (Wth 0.6m) borders the straight side (L 64.5m N-S) at E. A jumble of stones barely protruding from the base of the field boundary wall is the remains of the hillfort wall. The interior slopes down gently to E and encompasses an area of uneven stony ground. Just inside the enclosing wall at WNW is a low circular sod-covered platform (10.4m N-S; 9m E-W; H 0.3m) with stones protruding randomly from the sod around the perimeter. Adjacent at N is a sod-covered stony area, possibly an expanse of limestone bedrock. A ruined sod-covered wall (Wth 1-1.2m; H 0.3m) partitions off the S third of the interior. Within this area abutting the enclosure wall at SW is a roughly circular stony rise (c. 6m NW-SE; 5m NE-SW; H 0.3m).

source_data.original_text:
Located in the S half of a rath (MA032-016001-).
Indicated as 'Cave' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map, this drystone-built souterrain consists of a N−S passage, which connects at its S end via a short creep to a subrectangular chamber. The walls are constructed of roughly coursed limestone rubble, consisting of irregular-shaped medium and large stones and boulders, with smaller stones filling the interstices. The passage and chamber are each roofed by a row of contiguous large limestone slabs. The roof lintels and the stones in the upper courses of the walls are covered in a thick white coating of calcium carbonate .
A surface opening (H c. 0.55m; Wth c. 1m) leads into the passage (L c. 3.6m N−S; Wth 1m E−W), which slopes downwards to S. Displaced earth, incorporating a large boulder, partly blocks the access hole. The walls of the passage are composed of between four to six courses and incline inwards gently towards the top to support four large lintel slabs, laid transversely. The sloping floor gives the passage a height of 1.12m close to the entrance at N and of 1.5m at the lower S end. The floor is covered by loose stone rubble. In the S wall of the passage there is short creep (H 0.69m; Wth 0.68m at base, 0.6m at top; L 0.75m). The opening to the creep spans almost the full width of the S wall of the passage, with its W side wall being almost flush with the W wall of the passage, and its E wall separated from the E wall of the passage by a short offset/corner. The creep is roofed by a single lintel, which does not extend the full N−S length of the creep; the S end of the creep is roofed by two roughly-set boulders.
The creep opens into the N end of a subrectangular chamber (L 2.55m N−S; Wth 1.98m E−W; H 2.1m) with gently rounded corners. The walls of the chamber rise in six to eight rough courses, with the upper courses slightly corbelled to support three massive roof lintels, set transversely. A fourth smaller subsidiary lintel fills a gap at the SE end of the roof. In the centre of the E wall, at a height of 0.3m (one course) above current floor level, there is a rectangular recess or wall cupboard (H 0.64m; Wth 0.46m N−S), which extends to a depth of 1.07m (E−W). The sides of the recess are of 2-3 courses of large stones; it is roofed by a single large lintel slab (L 1.2m N−S; Wth 0.7m E−W) which does not span the full depth of the recess. A large boulder forms the floor, but this is largely concealed by displaced earth spilling from the back wall of the recess, which is cut into natural subsoil and is not faced with stone. The chamber floor is overspread with a layer of loose limestone rubble, with accumulations of gravelly soil beneath the wall recess and in the SW corner of the chamber.
A quernstone fragment (SL032-016003-) was found close to the souterrain (NMI).

Compiled by: Jane O’Shaughnessy

Date of revised upload: 22 March 2020

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on top of a knoll on the summit of a rise. A roughly circular area (22.5m N-S; 25.5m E-W) raised a max. of 3.5m above the surrounding ground level. The edge of the interior is defined by the remains of grass-covered foundations of a drystone wall (Wth 1m; int. H 0.3m). A dry flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 2.5m) surrounds the raised interior, 2.7m below the top of the bank, and in turn is defined by a counterscarp bank (Wth 4m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 1.4m). There is a ramped entrance at SW. The interior slopes gently down to S. The rath is partially overgrown with hawthorn and the remainder is heavily poached by cattle. Field boundaries respect the rath to W, N and E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In the NW quadrant of a rath (SL038-035003-). A lintelled opening at the SSW end of a depression (c. 2.5m NNE-SSW; D 1m) leads to two lintelled stone-lined passages linked by a creepway. Passage 1 (4.1m NE-SW; 1.3m NW-SE; H 1.5m) is entered through a modern opening at the NE end. Two niches in the NW wall and one in SE wall were noted. A creepway (Wth 0.8m; H 1m) at the SW end gives access to a second passage at right angles to passage 1. Passage 2 (3.3m E-W; 1.4m N-S; H 1.7m) ends with a blocked creepway (Wth 0.9m; H 0.9m; L 3m) at the E end. The area around the entrance is overgrown with bushes. The site of another souterrain (SL038-035002-) is in the SW quadrant of the rath.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In rocky pasture, on the E outskirts of Tobercurry town and in the NW corner of a field bordered to the N by a road and to the W by a disused lane. A dense thicket of blackthorn bushes and brambles now covers the rath which appears to survive as a roughly circular area (diam. c. 25m) defined by remnants of a stony scarp (H c. 7m) visible along the E arc and truncated by field boundary along its W arc. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an embanked circular area (diam. c. 30m) truncated at W by a field boundary and at N by a road. The 1838 map also shows two souterrains (SL038-035001-; SL038-035002-) named 'Caves', one on the NW edge and the other within the SW quadrant of the rath.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On gently rolling pasture. A SW-facing gallery (L 7m; max. Wth 2m) stands in a diamond-shaped mound (11.5m NE-SW; 9m NW-SE; max. H 1m). The more northerly side of the gallery is intact and formed of seven orthostats. Adjoining the western of these seven stones is a facade-stone. Eight stones are in position on the opposite side of the gallery, three to the W of a gap and five to the E. A stone divides the gallery entrance into two parts. There are two partly buried slabs and a displaced stone in the rear half of the gallery. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 74, no. 117)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
The monument, destroyed sometime between 1914 and 1942, stood on rolling pasture about 1km SW of Tobercurry town. A sketch of the tomb by Wakeman (1878-82, drawing book 1, folio 109) and a plan by Wood-Martin (1886-7, 276; 1888, 214) show a dual court tomb, aligned more or less E-W, consisting of two two-chambered galleries set back to back and 3.8m apart. The western chamber was c. 5.5m long and the eastern c. 7.5m long. Two jambs stood at the entrance to both galleries and a single courtstone adjoined the southern of the two at the eastern gallery. Two sidestones on each side, the southern segmenting jamb and the backstone of the western gallery were then in place as were four sidestones to the S, one to the N, the northern segmenting jamb and the backstone of the eastern gallery. An OS 1:2500 field trace (1914) depicts two galleries aligned NE-SW within a roughly rectangular enclosure which seems to represent a mound (L 25m; Wth 15m). (Ó Nualláin 1989, 74-5, no. 118)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a SE-facing slope. A raised circular area (38.5m N-S; 39.5m E-W) defined by a scarp (H 1.25m). Remains of a stone wall (Wth 1.2m; int. H 0.2m) are evident on top of the edge of the scarp WSW-NW. An external dry flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 5.5m; D 0.7m) is evident SW-NW and at SE. Short stretches of an outer earthen bank (Wth 3.5m; ext. H 0.7m) are evident at SW and NW, revetted in places by upright stones. The interior is also encircled by a stone wall (Wth 1m; H 1.8m) c. 2m inside and concentric with the line of the inner enclosing wall of the cashel and possibly built reusing stones from the latter. A small rectangular stone-built structure (5m x 2.5m) is built as a lean-to on the inner face of this wall at SW. There are rock outcrops in the N half of the interior.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on a gentle SW-facing slope overlooking a bog. A roughly oval area (40m NE-SW; 33.5m NW-SE) enclosed by two earthen banks with an intervening fosse (Wth 5m). The interior is enclosed by a curving bank (Wth 3.5m; int. H 0.65m; ext. H 0.9m) NNE-S, by a scarp (H 0.9m) S-SW, by a curving bank SW-W and elsewhere by a linear bank which forms a right angled corner at NW. The outer bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.55m; ext. H 0.4m) is evident all round, topped by a field boundary NW-NNE. There is a stone-revetted entrance (Wth 2m) at ESE through the inner and outer banks, with a causeway across the fosse. The S and SW portions of the interior are raised c. 0.7m above the external ground level and the N and NE portions are cut into the hillslope to compensate for slope, though the interior still retains a gentle slope down to SW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

A scarp (H 0.5m) curving W-NE just S of centre marks a change in ground level and to S of this the interior is slightly lower with a soft and damp surface. The rath is densely overgrown with blackthorn and hawthorn bushes and brambles.

In marshy ground, on a gentle NE-facing slope. A D-shaped area (dims. 30.5m NE-SW; 19m NW-SE), with a straight SE side, is enclosed by two banks and an intervening fosse. The inner bank of earth and stone (Wth 2.7m; int. H 0.65m) is evident all round except for a short section at NE where the interior is defined by a scarp. The fosse (Wth 5m; D 0.7m) is evident all around. An outer earthen bank (Wth 2m; ext. H 0.3m) is evident NW-NNW and at SE. The interior is used for rough grazing. A small wedge-shaped annexe (L 10m N-S; Wth at N end 11m; Wth at S end 7m), raised 0.7m above the ground, lies immediately outside the fosse at N.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on gentle S and SW-facing slopes amid rock outcrops; there are several large natural hollows in the area. A field system covering an area c. 600m NW-SE x c. 350m NE-SW is overlain by a modern rectilinear grid of fields on a NE-SW axis. The older field system is comprised of rectangular, D-shaped or irregular fields enclosed by stone walls or stone-faced scarps. The walls are constructed of a rubble core faced with contiguous stones but most survive as low sod-covered rises or as irregular gapped lines of stones. The fields in general respect or utilise the natural contours and terraces in the area. Linear seams and scarps of limestone, many on a NW-SE axis, are incorporated into the field boundaries. A cashel (SL038-110001-) and two hut sites (SL038-110002-; SL038-110007-) lie within the SE part of the field system. Roughly in the centre of the system is a complex of monuments including a souterrain (SL038-110004-), a possible souterrain (SL038-110003-), a cashel (SL038-110010-), two enclosures (SL038-110012-; SL038-110017-), a rectangular enclosure (SL038-110014-), a circular enclosure (SL038-110009-) and four hut sites (SL038-110006-; SL038-110008-; SL038-110011-; SL038-110013-). Also within the field system are the remains of several rectangular houses of unknown date, one (15m NW-SE; 3m NE-SW) of which is divided into three compartments with the largest compartment (7m NW-SE) in the centre (SL038-110006-).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In flat reclaimed pasture, c. 1.5km E of Moylough. A dense concentration of moss-covered stones, varying greatly in size from medium-sized rounded stones to large boulders and irregular slabs, is spread over a roughly oval area (c. 28m NW-SE; 25m NE-SW) and engulfed in a thicket of hawthorn bushes. The largest stones occur on the outer limit of the spread and while the general impression is of a dense and chaotic spread there are some possible N-S rows of upright stones. At NE and E there is a very slight rise around the perimeter, possibly the remains of the earthen bank which, according to local information, once enclosed the burial ground. According to local information, unbaptised babies were buried here until c. 1960. It is named 'Burial Ground' on the 1838 OS 6-inch map.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In an undulating meadow. According to local information, a rectangular area (37m E-W; c. 50m N-S) defined by a natural limestone scarp (H 1-1.5m) on its W, N and E sides, is regarded by local tradition as the site of a castle. This could be either of the 'two old castles' referred to in this townland in 1836 (OSNB vol. 1, 33). 
Topping the scarp on the W and N sides are gapped sod-covered wall footings (Wth 0.7m; H 0.3m) of large contiguous stones (L 0.5-1m). On the W side, at one point, two courses of the footing are evident. The N half of the interior is level but there is a slope down from the centre to the S where it merges into the surrounding field. At the base of the scarp, outside the N half of the E side, is a subrectangular area of disturbed ground (c. 17m N-S; c. 5m E-W) marked by low sod-covered mounds and heaps of angular stones. This may be the remains of the foundations of the rectangular structure (20m NW-SE; 4.5m SW-NE), divided internally into four separate rooms by cross-walls and known locally as 'the stables', that was noted here in 1991 (SMR (1989) file). A length of mortared wall (6m N-S; T 0.65m; H 2m) stands just outside the SE corner of the rectangular area. Traces of rendering are evident on its E face and there is a roughly circular break (0.7m N-S; H 0.8m) in its centre. Immediately to E is a roughly rectangular area of disturbed ground containing limestone rubble suggesting that it may have been the W wall of a collapsed rectangular structure. Further to S is another rectangular area (c. 10m N-S; c. 5m E-W), recessed into the slope, which may be the trace of a similar structure. A rath (SL038-047----) lies c. 50m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a slight rise. Discovered in 1928 during sand quarrying and described by Morris (1929, 113-5) as a cist (L 29in [0.73m]; Wth 16in [0.4m]; D 12in [0.3m]) formed of four thin slabs with a stone floor and a covering slab. It contained cremated human bone and a corroded and shrivelled bronze halberd. The underside of the covering slab was decorated with a faint wavy band of pitting (L 3ft [0.9m]; Wth 1in [0.025m]). This short cist has not been precisely located and it is possible that it is in that part of Moylough townland which is on OS 6-inch map 43. (Waddell 1990, 133)

In pasture, on a gentle SW-facing slope; in the narrow N end of a field. A circular area (int. diam. c. 29m N-S) defined by a scarp (H 0.6m) E-NNE with an external dry flat-bottomed fosse (Wth 0.6m; D 0.1m) evident SE-WSW and NNW-N. The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In wet pasture, bordering a broad expanse of flat bogland that stretches to S and SE. A kidney-shaped mound (15m ENE-WSW; 8.7m NNW-SSE; H 0.95m) of heat-shattered stones and dark soil. There is a shallow oval depression (3m NE-SW; 2m NW-SE) in the W half. The NW end is adjacent to a low flat-topped rise bounded by bedrock. A possible fulacht fia (SL038-139002-) lies 8m to SSW and a small stone-lined well, associated with a nearby ruined 19th-century cottage, c. 8m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In a sand quarry, adjacent to a farmyard. According to local information, a grave-like feature (max. dims. c. 0.75m) made of stone slabs and containing some bones was revealed during sand extraction c. 1983. It was found c. 1.2m below the top of a sandy hillock. The feature was subsequently destroyed when that part of the hillock in which it was contained was quarried away and a barn partially built over it.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on top of a low rise, with bog to N and S. A slightly raised area (c. 20m N-S; c. 23m E-W) surrounded by a wide fosse (Wth 3.4m) and a broad external earthen bank (Wth 7.3m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.65m). The fosse appears in parts to be higher than the surrounding ground level. From N-NNE the earthen bank is evident only as a barely perceptible rise. The bank is narrower and higher for short sections along the E and W arcs. This may be due to disturbance by a lane and farmyard buildings abutting the bank to E and W respectively as shown on the 1838 OS 6-inch map. A depression remains where the farm building once stood. Numerous gaps were noted in the bank. The interior is level and raised at max. 0.45m above the base of the fosse. The barrow is grass-covered and heavily poached by cattle. According to local information, it was used as a children's burial ground (SL042-001001-).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
On top of a low E-W ridge. A trapezoidal area (41.5m E-W; 47m N-S at W end; 39m N-S at E end) enclosed by a stone wall. The entrance is at the W end of the N wall, with a stile at the opposite corner. The S two thirds of the graveyard are raised (max. H 2.6m) above the external ground level, with the mortared stonework of a limekiln (SL042-004006-) (indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map) acting as a revetment. At the N edge of the raised area, an arc (C 19m) formed by a scarp N-E may be the remains of an early ecclesiastical enclosure (SL042-004005-). The headstones date to the 19th and 20th centuries and there are also many uninscribed grave-markers. There is a bullaun stone (SL042-004003-) in the E half of the interior. This may also be the site of a nunnery (SL042-004002-). The NW portion of the townland, in which this graveyard is located, is named 'Killeen' on the 1910-11 OS 6-inch map.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Listed in both the SMR (1989) and RMP (1995) and classified 'Grave-slab'. In the E half of Montiagh graveyard (SL042-004001-). A rougly shaped slab (H 0.55m; Wth 0.5m; T 0.06m) with a simple Latin cross incised on one face. Thinly incised lines represent the shaft (H 0.2m) and the arms (Wth 0.14m) of the cross, with a slight expansion or indentation marking the terminals. The base of the shaft is flanked by the letters 'P' and 'B', incised similarly to the cross. The distance between the letters and the cross is unequal, the 'P' being furthest away. This is probably a grave-marker, perhaps 19th or even 20th century in date (pers. comm. M. B. Timoney). (Herity, Kelly and Mattenberger 1997, 121).


Compiled by: Archaeological Survey Unit, UCC

Date of upload: 10 January 2012

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

The rath is heavily overgrown with blackthorn bushes.

source_data.original_text:
In flat dry land, on the E side of Bellahy village and c. 200m N of the Sligo-Mayo border at Charlestown. The fortification is depicted on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as a square enclosure (c. 40m N-S; c. 40m E-W) with an angled bastion at each corner, all enclosed by an external fosse (see plan in Kerrigan 1995, fig. 51). The NE bastion survives as a D-shaped mound (straight side 19m NNE-SSW, projecting 11m to ESE; H 1.55m) with a flat rectangular top (12m NNE-SSW; 5m ESE-WNW) and an external fosse (Wth 9.4m; max. D 0.6m). A field boundary respects the mound on the N and W sides and extends SSW apparently on the line of the E rampart. The faint outline of the outer edge of the fosse extends SSW for c. 35m, on the E side of the field boundary and beyond. During a previous inspection in 1994 (SMR (1989) file) it was recorded that the northern part of the fort was fairly intact with the NW and NE angled bastions clearly visible and standing 1.5-2m above the ground; this area has since been levelled by intensive horticultural activity and roadworks. This fort was under construction in 1655-6, under the supervision of the engineer William Webb, and was known as 'Fort Cromwell' (O'Dowd 1991, 131). It was built to house a garrison of 100 men (Kerrigan 1995, 102). It was constructed 'of earthworks faced with masonry walls' inside which were 'timber-framed houses' (Kerrigan 1980, 147; Kerrigan 1995, 97-8). On the E side of the area formerly the interior of the fort are the grass-covered foundations of a rectangular stone-built structure (14m NNE-SSW; 7m WNW-ESE; wall T c. 0.4-1m) (SL042-029001-), which according to local information is the remains of a church and is likely to date from the 18th century.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, c. 200m E of Ballylaur. A flat-topped roughly rectangular grass-covered mound (15m N-S; 8m E-W; H 0.75m) with broadly sloping sides known locally as a 'killeen'. According to local information, it was used as a children's burial ground with the last interments taking place in the early 20th century. Also according to local information, the mound was partially levelled in the 1980s and prior to that several stone grave-markers had been visible. During road building in the 1940s, a hole was dug to extract gravel immediately to S of the mound and several adult human bones were exposed which were later reburied; a grass-covered depression is now visible in this area.

H 1.4m). The inner fosse (Wth 4.8m; D 0.7m from interior) is boggy. The outer fosse (Wth 6m; D 0.4m) is evident N-SE and a wide band of rushes may indicate its continuation S-SW. source_data.original_text:
In rough, rush-grown damp pasture, in generally lowlying, poorly drained terrain. Slightly raised, oval area (30m N−S; 22m E−W) defined by remnants of a bank (Wth c. 2m), largely reduced to a scarp (ext. H 0.5-0.6m), and enclosed by a fosse which is evident as a shallow depression (Wth c. 2m; ext. D 0.3m). The bank retains a slight internal rise or lip in parts at S and at W−N. There are several eroded sections or gaps: at W (Wth 2m), at NNE (Wth c. 3m), at E (Wth c. 4m), at SE (c. 1.5m). The fosse is very shallow/poorly defined in parts at E and S but no clearly defined causeway is evident. The interior is level. In the NE quadrant, a low, upright stone (L 1.1m NW−SE; max. T 0.25m; H 0.45m) protrudes from the ground. It leans sharply to SW. Immediately adjacent on its W side, another stone (L 1.35m NW−SE; Wth 0.6m) lies concealed beneath the grass. The field is planted with forestry but an exclusion zone protects the enclosure.

Compiled by: Jane O'Shaughnessy

Date of upload: 9 December 2016

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a SE-facing slope with a steep natural drop to W and SW. A circular area (diam. c. 32m) enclosed by the remains of a stone wall (int. H c. 1m; T 2.2-6m) of large limestone stones and boulders with a rubble and earth core. The internal face of the wall is topped by a recent field boundary. A low earthen bank (Wth 2-3m; H c. 0.2m) curves across the S half of the interior. There is a possible souterrain (SL038-002002-) in the NW quadrant. The interior is cut into the hillslope with the S half raised c. 1m to compensate for the slope. Recorded in 1836 as 'Caiseal Loga, i.e. Lughaidh's stone fort' (OSNB vol. 1, 17).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In undulating pasture. The remains of a field system, underlying the present field system, are visible in an aerial photograph (IASAP, 3033062-3) as linear and curvilinear field boundaries. No complete field can be identified in the aerial photograph or on the ground but traces of low earthen banks (Wth 4m; H 0.4-0.6m) are visible at ground level. These consist of an arc of earthen bank (C c. 30m) on the S side of a modern E-W field boundary from which a similar but straight earthen bank extends in a SE direction for c. 100m. A branch of this extending to SW, visible in the aerial photograph, is not visible at ground level nor is a continuation of the arc in a northerly direction. This field system is possibly associated with a circular enclosure (SL038-016003-) c. 40m to W. A second field system (SL032-188004-) lies c. 1km to NW in the same townland.

In level pasture, with good views of the surrounding countryside. Indicated as a circular hillock (diam. c. 40m) on the 1838 OS 6-inch map with the accompanying name 'Carn'. The hillock is named 'Sheeaun' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map and the cairn as 'Carn (site of)'. A slightly raised circular area (diam. 25m) enclosed by three low earthen banks and intervening fosses. The inner bank (Wth c. 4m; ext. H 1.15m) is the widest though its internal edge is evident only as a slight lip or differential vegetation pattern. H 0.7m) is evident SE-N, possibly incorporated into a field boundary NE-ENE and levelled ENE-SE. The inner fosse (Wth 2.7m) and middle fosse (Wth 2m) are evident all round. In undulating pasture, on the E-facing slope of a ridge. A slightly raised circular area (28m WNW-ESE) enclosed by an earthen bank, apart from a section (L 16m) NW-N where the bank has been levelled. The bank (Wth 3.7m; int. H 0.9m; ext. H 0.85m) has traces of possible internal and external stone facing. A slight external depression (Wth 3m), evident SSW-WSW, may be remains of a fosse. There is a possible entrance (Wth 1.2m) at S and a further two gaps in the bank at SSE and ESE. The interior is grass-covered. The E portion of the interior is raised to compensate for the hillslope though there is still a gradual slope down towards E. There is a small field clearance cairn in the centre. There is a field boundary to W, immediately outside the bank. A complete bank is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map, but by the 1914 OS 6-inch map the section at NW had been levelled.

In pasture, on a low rise. A slightly raised oval area (49.7m NNW-SSE; 70.4m ENE-WSW) enclosed by an earthen bank and an external fosse. The bank (Wth 3.7m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 2m) has an almost vertical external face and is incorporated into a field boundary WSW-WNW. There is a possible entrance (Wth 2m) at NE with a low causeway across the fosse. Gaps occur in the bank at SE, S and SW, ranging in width from 1-2m. A quarry pit (12m N-S; 10m E-W; D 1.2m) abuts the external face of the bank at ENE. The fosse (Wth 3m; D 1m) is evident N-NE; elsewhere the line of the fosse is marked by a slight depression and a dense growth of irises. A slight rise (Wth c. 2.4m) on the external side of the fosse at NE may be remains of an outer bank though there is no further evidence of such. The interior is grass-covered and slopes gently down to S and SE. There is a souterrain (SL025-055002-) in the SW quadrant and a rectangular enclosure, with a slightly sunken interior, in the E half. The latter consists of a rectangular area (18.3m WNW-ESE; 24.5m NNE-SSW) enclosed by an earthen bank (Wth 2.2m; int. H 0.9m; ext. H 0.4m) which is best evident on the N and W sides, low and eroded on the E and S sides with boulders lining the internal face on the N side.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
On a flat tract of ground in rolling pasture. Two groups of orthostats stand 3.6m apart, four to the SW and three to the NE. Each group seems to represent a chamber. The four to the SW include two opposed orthostats (H 0.8m), 1.75m apart, standing at either side of a stone set transversely between them. This seems to be a sillstone (H 0.5m). Some 1.5m W of the more southerly of the two opposed stones there is another orthostat, apparently a sidestone. The chamber represented by the second group of orthostats seems to have been of polygonal outline. It measures 2.3m N-S and is represented by three orthostats, one at N, E and S. There are some prostrate and partly concealed stones at the site. Faint traces of mound adjoin the southern side of each chamber. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 57, no. 90)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

In pasture, on the summit of a ridge with excellent views of the surrounding countryside, the Ox Mountains to NE and Knocknashee Hill to SW. Indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as a small circular mound. It is now evident as a roughly D-shaped mound (diam. c. 9m) of uneven height with a straight E side (H 1.4m). In pasture, on a gentle NE-facing slope with excellent views of the surrounding countryside. A raised circular area (24m NW-SE) defined by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse. In the W half, against the internal face of the bank, is a low terrace (c. 5m E-W; c. 10m N-S; H 0.35m) with a stone kerb along its outer edge. The N end of this terrace is more well defined than the rest. A field boundary has been built against the external edge of the inner bank, on the line of the fosse N-NE. A mound barrow (SL025-061----) lies c. 80m to SW.

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, prominently sited on top of a NNW-SSE ridge, with extensive views in all directions. A roughly square earthen platform (c. 20m N-S; c. 18-19m E-W; H 2m at W; 1.4m at E) with rounded corners except at SW where the platform is truncated by a quarry pit (c.10m across). The high scarp on the W side utilises the natural fall of ground and drops to a narrow terrace (Wth c.4m) from which the ground falls away again for c. 1.5-2m. The terrace is truncated at N and S. The linear scarps defining the N and S sides of the rath appear to be the result of quarrying. The scarp on the E side also appears to have been modified. The top of the platform is generally level but with several shallow surface depressions; there is a low rise in the SE corner. A field boundary skirts the rath N-SE. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an embanked circular area (diam. c. 30m) and on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as a roughly circular raised area (diam. c. 15m).

In pasture, on a low rise. A raised oval area (27.5m NW-SE; 30.9m NE-SW) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 3.1m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1m) apart for a short section at N which is defined by a scarp. There is a sod-covered field clearance cairn (diam. 2m; H 0.3m) in the interior close to the gap. There is a limekiln (SL025-065001-) c. 40m to NE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

Not listed in either the SMR (1989) or RMP (1995). Depicted as a small subrectangular structure on the 1838 edition of the OS 6-inch map. In pasture, on a gentle NE-facing slope, c. 40m NE of rath (SL025-065----). A small oval stone-lined pit (c. 2m x 4m; D 0.7m) defined on its outer edge E-N by a low irregular sod-covered stony rim (Wth 1-1.5m). Outside of the rim E-NW is a shallow hollow or quarried area (Wth 1.5m; D 0.4m). This limekiln probably dates to the post-1700 AD period.

In undulating pasture, straddling the top of a narrow ridge. The south-westernmost of two conjoined raths (see SL025-068----). In undulating pasture, on the E side of a low rise. A slightly raised circular area (diam. 29.5m) enclosed by an inner bank, an intervening fosse and a counterscarp bank. The inner bank (Wth 4.4m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 1.5m) is low internally all round and is levelled for a short section to W. Traces of internal stone revetment were noted. The fosse and counterscarp bank (Wth 2.4m; int. H 0.75m; ext. H 0.2m) are evident SSW-N. An E-W field boundary at S obscures the line of the fosse. There is a narrow gap (Wth 1.4m) in the bank at SSE, partially lined with stones. The interior slopes down to E. There is a thick band of nettles inside the bank in the W half of the interior. There is a heap of stones (3m E-W; 1.5m N-S; H 0.4m) roughly in the centre of the N half of the interior and another similar heap (diam. 2m; H 0.2m) in the S half, to E of which is rough arc of stones (C 4m). The bank is ringed with hawthorn bushes.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In undulating pasture, on a natural rise and densely covered with undergrowth and trees. The natural rise is utilised to form a high flat-topped circular platform (24.6m NW-SE) defined on top by an earthen bank (Wth 3m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 4.8m) S-N and by a scarp N-S. A tumble of loose stones was noted on the external slope of the bank. The base of the platform is enclosed all round by a fosse (Wth 3m) with an external bank (Wth 5m; int. H 1.5m; ext. H c. 3.6m). A tumble of loose stones is evident on the internal and external slopes of this bank, most noticeably at NW. The interior is mostly level with a slight slope down to SE. A shallow depression (Wth 1.4m; D 0.15m) skirts the bank internally S-N. At NNE a sunken pathway (Wth 1.6m) through the outer bank leads to a series of steps, bordered on the W side by remnants of a low stone wall, which have been cut into the external slope of the platform. Another pathway approaches the barrow from the road to the E and curves up the slope of the hill to an eroded section of the outer bank at SE where a causeway (Wth 1.8m) crosses the fosse. A field boundary abuts the outer bank at WNW and another crosses the fosse at SSE. A large boulder (1.3m x 1.4m; H 0.75m) in the fosse at NNE is known locally as a mass-rock (SL025-071003-). A cist (SL025-071002-) containing an urn is said to have been found on the summit (Wood-Martin 1887-8, 270-72).

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
Wood-Martin (1887-8, 270-72) described an urn, then in the museum of the Royal Irish Academy, which was found on the summit of an ancient rath (presumably SL025-071001-) in Rathbarran townland. The urn was discovered within a 'square coffer of flagstones placed on edge' and measured '43/4 inches [0.12m] high, 6 inches [0.15m] broad and 53/4 [0.14m] wide in the mouth' (ibid., 271-2). It was decorated all over, except for the base, with incised lines and 'enriched about the middle with five raised bands, more or less ornamented with chevrons, and wavy oblique lines' (ibid., 271). It contained cremated bones and a stone disc and a polished stone axehead was found with it. There are no visible remains of this cist. It is one of three cists known from Rathbarran townland (see SL025-051002- and SL025-151----). (Waddell 1990, 133; Ó Ríordáin and Waddell 1993, 131)

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

Not included in the SMR (1989) but listed in the RMP (1995) and classified 'Mass Rock'. In the fosse at the NNE of Rathbarran barrow (SL025-071001-) is a large boulder (1.3m x 1.4m; H 0.75m). It is known by the people in the locality as a mass-rock. The classification mass-rock is likely to be post-1700 AD in date.

In undulating pasture, close to the break of slope on the NW side of a ridge. A raised circular area (26m NW-SE) enclosed by two earthen banks and an intervening fosse (Wth 4m). The inner bank (Wth 10.8m; int. H 1.35m; ext. H 4.7m) has an entrance (Wth 3.5m) at S with a causeway across the fosse and there is a corresponding entrance in the outer bank. The outer bank (Wth 5.7m; int. H 1.55m; ext. H 1.4m) has much tumbled stone on its internal face along the W arc. The W portion of the interior is raised to compensate for the hillslope and is covered with nettles. The remainder of the interior is covered with thistles. Both banks are ringed with hawthorn bushes. Immediately to W of rath is a natural terrace (c. 20m E-W; 40m N-S).

source_data.original_text:
In level pasture. A slightly raised circular area (22.4m N-S; 20.7m E-W) defined SE-NE by the remains of an earth and stone bank and truncated NE-SE by a linear field boundary, probably incorporating the bank. The bank (Wth 2.5m; int. H 0.4m; ext. H 0.8m) is evident as a low sod-covered rise with protruding stones. Traces of possible stone revetment are evident on the external face of the bank at S and several low eroded areas were noted at NE, NW and SE. According to local information, the bank was partially levelled to allow access to the interior. The interior is level with a possible field clearance cairn (diam. 2.5m; H 0.3m) situated off centre to W. Immediately to the W of the cairn are two rectangular closely set stones (N stone: H 0.5m; Wth 0.35m; T 0.2m, S stone: H 0.5m; Wth 0.35m; T 0.17m) leaning at an oblique angle. Narrow vertical grooves, noted on the E- and S-facing sides of the N stone and on the S-facing side of the S stone, are probably natural. There is a local tradition that these stones are grave-markers. E-W cultivation ridges were noted in the surrounding field.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

In pasture, on a gentle SE-facing slope. A slightly raised circular area (26.8m NNE-SSW) defined by the remains of an earthen bank (Wth 4.2m; int. H 0.7m; ext. H 1.2m) N-NNE and by a scarp (H 1m) elsewhere. The scarp is covered in places with sod-covered stoned possibly upcast from adjacent quarrying. There is a gap (Wth 6m) at NW. A possible external fosse (Wth 4m; D 0.7m) is evident SSW-W. A band of quarrying (Wth 8-12m) is immediately outside the perimeter NW-SE. A low arc of bank (Wth 2.5m; int. H 0.5m; ext. H 0.7m) built against the slope of the scarp at SE is probably of recent origin. The interior slopes down to SE and is covered with irises. The perimeter is ringed with hawthorn bushes. A spring, indicated on the 1914 OS 6-inch map c. 20m to E, and a field boundary abutting the SW edge of the rath are no longer evident.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

This monument stood in rolling pasture dominated by the Ox Mountain range to the N. In 1951 a gallery opening onto a flat facade at the SW and surrounded by an outer wall could be distinguished in heavy growth. Examination of the monument during the course of its destruction in 1959 indicated the presence of a portico. A quantity of unburnt bone recovered at this time was deposited in the National Museum. (Ó Nualláin 1989, 57-8, no. 91)

In pasture, on a gentle SSE-facing slope and c. 40m W of a cashel (SL025-083----). A slightly raised circular area (8.2m E-W; 8.8m N-S) defined by a sod-covered bank of earth and stone. The bank (Wth 2.6m; int. H 0.45m; ext. H 0.5m) bulges outwards at NW. There is a gap (Wth 2m) in the bank at S. The interior slopes gently down to S. A field-clearance cairn abuts the internal face of the bank at NW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a level area on a gentle S-facing slope. A slightly raised circular area (diam. c. 31m) enclosed by a collapsed sod-covered stone wall (Wth 3m; int. H 0.25m; ext. H 0.75m), topped by a modern drystone wall NW-SE. Immediately to the S is a field boundary on an E-W axis and immediately to W is a disused field boundary on a N-S axis. Three hollows (max. dims. 5m x 3m; D 0.7m) were noted in the wall at SW, probably the result of stones being robbed. The interior is strewn with sod-covered stones; the remains of a hut site (SL025-083001-) are visible in the NW quadrant. There is a hut site (SL025-082----) c. 40m to W of cashel and a small coniferous plantation immediately to E.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a gentle SE-facing slope. A slightly raised circular area (diam. c. 20m) enclosed by an earth and stone bank with an external fosse. The bank (Wth 4.2m; int. H 0.8m; ext. H 1.2m), best evident W-ESE, is possibly incorporated into a field fence at SE and difficult to trace due to disturbance and overgrowth elsewhere. A field boundary respects the line of the bank NW-NE and probably marks the outer edge of a silted-up fosse at this point. The fosse is evident as a shallow depression (Wth 3m) WSW-WNW. The interior is densely overgrown with trees and bushes and has been extensively disturbed by quarrying. Apart from a narrow band inside the bank W-E, the surface of the interior has been quarried away to a depth of 1.3m. Beneath the overgrowth, large boulders and heaps of stones were noted. There is a field boundary immediately E of the rath.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In gently undulating pasture. A linear sod-covered mound (7.5m NW-SE; 3.5m NE-SW; H 0.55m) incorporating some irregularly shaped stones. Though named 'Giants Grave' on the 1914 OS 6-inch map there is insufficient evidence to classify it as a megalithic structure (Ó Nualláin 1989, 98, no. 20). There is an enclosure (SL025-086----) c. 80m to SE.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a low rise. Indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as a circular enclosure (diam. c. 15m) and on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as a raised rectangular area bounded on the NW and NE sides by field boundaries. Now evident as a roughly square platform (c. 20m NW-SE; c. 19m NE-SW; H 1m) bounded on the NW and NE sides by field boundaries and densely overgrown with bushes. Traces of a drystone revetment are evident on the SW side. A large portion (Wth c. 10m) of the interior on the SW side has been quarried away to a depth of c. 1m and a small section of the platform has been levelled on the SE side close to the E corner. A miscellaneous mound (SL025-085----) lies c. 80m to NW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, at the gently sloping SW end of a ridge. This rath is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an embanked oval area (35m NW-SE; 20m NE-SW) straddling a NW-SE field boundary. The rath is now mostly levelled and is evident as slightly raised roughly circular area (37.5m NW-SE; 33.7m NE-SW) defined by an earthen bank (Wth 3.2m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 1.1m) S-WNW and by a slight scarp elsewhere. A NW-SE field boundary crosses the W half of the interior. An opening to a possible souterrain (SL025-087001-) is in the outer face of the bank at W.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005).

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a low rise c. 40m W of a disused railway line. The rath is indicated on the 1838 OS 6-inch map as an embanked oval area and on the 1914 OS 6-inch map as an arc of hachures SE-NE indicating a raised area. The rath is now evident as a circular platform (33.4m NW-SE) with the remnants of an earthen bank (Wth 5.5m; int. H 0.2m; ext. H 0.7m) NW-N. The S edge is incorporated into a now disused field boundary. The E arc is mostly levelled and the perimeter is only barely discernible. The interior slopes gently down to E. A stone slab (c. 5m x 2m) rests against the external slope at S. A small quarry pit lies immediately to NW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008

source_data.original_text:
In pasture, on a gentle W-facing slope. A slightly raised circular area (30.5m N-S; 28m E-W) enclosed by two banks and an intervening fosse (Wth 2.6m). The inner bank is broad, low and stony (Wth 7.8m; int. H 0.3m; ext. H 1.3m) and within it is a slightly higher rim (Wth 3.8m) outside of which c. 4m of the stony spread slopes gradually down to the fosse. The outer earthen bank (Wth 2.7m; int. H 0.95m; ext. H 0.5m) has a rounded profile with stones protruding from the sod on both the internal and external faces and is evident all round apart from a levelled section (L 15m) at N. The interior is level; over half of it is occupied by an internal enclosure (SL025-089003-). There is a souterrain (SL025-089002-) in the NW quadrant. A disused railway line lies c. 70m to E. A rath (SL025-090001-) lies c. 150m to SSW.

The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Sligo' compiled by Ursula Egan, Elizabeth Byrne, Mary Sleeman with Sheila Ronan and Connie Murphy (Dublin Stationery Office, 2005). 

Date of upload: 18 January 2008
